docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
The augmented form of the course's initial LP models replaces each \(\le\) functional constraint by an equality with a nonnegative slack variable. For \(Ax\le b\), \(x\ge0\), this gives

\[ Ax+s=b,\qquad x\ge0,\quad s\ge0, \]

with the same objective in the original variables.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: Adding slacks changes the algebraic representation, not the allowed original decisions. Each original feasible vector determines exactly one vector of slack values.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Count auxiliary variables when determining the dimension of the equality system used for a basis.
  • For \(m\) independent equalities in \(n\) augmented variables, a basis contains \(m\) variables.
  • Artificial variables used for other constraint types require a feasibility phase; they cannot simply remain free in the final model.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• Two original variables and two slack variables give four augmented variables.
  • The constraints \(2x_1+x_2+s_1=10\) and \(x_1+3x_2+s_2=15\) have initial solution \((0,0,10,15)\).

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: The augmenting path algorithm starts with a feasible flow, initially zero in the course examples. Find a source-to-sink augmenting path, augment by its bottleneck \(\delta\), decrease each traversed residual capacity by \(\delta\), increase the opposite residual capacity by \(\delta\), and repeat. If no augmenting path remains, the current flow is maximum.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: The residual network allows both new routing and correction of earlier routing. The stopping condition certifies that no further flow increase is possible.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Maintain flow conservation after every augmentation.
  • The integer capacities in the exercises allow integer augmentations and finite termination.
  • Recover original flows from the final residual values, taking edge directions into account.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• The main example augments by \(5,2,1,4,1,2\), totalling 15.
  • The last residual network cannot reach T from S through positive residual directions.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
An augmenting path is a source-to-sink path in the residual network with strictly positive residual capacity in every traversed direction. Its residual capacity, or bottleneck, is

\[ \delta=\min\{r_e:e\text{ is traversed along the path}\}. \]

An additional \(\delta\) units of net source-to-sink flow can be assigned along it.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: The smallest remaining capacity limits the whole path. A backward residual segment reduces an original flow while still increasing the total source-to-sink value.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• All residual directions on the path must be feasible.
  • Augmenting by the bottleneck saturates at least one residual direction.
  • A path may use both forward and reverse directions relative to original edges.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• The first S-A-D-T augmentation in the video has bottleneck 5.
  • A later S-B-E-D-A-C-T path cancels part of the earlier A-D flow and adds two units overall.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: A basic feasible solution is a basic solution of an equality-form LP with all its variables nonnegative. A basic solution with a negative variable is a basic infeasible solution.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: Simplex maintains this combination of algebraic structure and feasibility. It can then improve the objective without leaving the allowed region.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Nonbasic variables are set to zero; feasibility is checked through the resulting basic values.
  • A basic variable may be zero in a degenerate solution.
  • For the course LPs with a finite optimum, an optimal basic feasible solution exists.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• \((x_1,x_2,s_1,s_2)=(0,0,10,15)\) is basic feasible in the main simplex example.
  • \((0,10,0,-15)\) is basic but infeasible.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: For \(m\) independent linear equality constraints in \(n\) variables, a basic solution is obtained by choosing \(n-m\) variables to be nonbasic and setting them to zero, then uniquely solving for the other \(m\) variables. The chosen basic columns must be linearly independent.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: Choosing a basis selects an algebraic candidate for a corner. Some choices fail to give a unique solution and some give negative values, so not every choice is a feasible candidate.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• There are at most \(\binom{n}{m}\) basis choices.
  • A basic solution may be feasible or infeasible.
  • Different bases can represent the same degenerate solution.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• The four-variable example has at most \(\binom42=6\) bases.
  • Week 2 practice 4 has five variables and two equalities, but only eight basic solutions from ten candidate choices.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: A basic variable belongs to the selected basis of an equality-form LP. Its value is obtained from the constraint equations after the nonbasic variables have been set to zero. With \(m\) independent equalities, the basis contains \(m\) variables.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: The bin packing problem assigns every item to a container, subject to a common capacity per container, and minimizes the number of containers used. If item \(i\) has weight \(w_i\) and a container has capacity \(C\), the weights assigned to each container must sum to at most \(C\).

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: Combining items efficiently can reduce the number of containers. A simple packing rule is easy to apply, but need not find the best combination.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Each item must be packed exactly once without splitting it.
  • Any feasible packing provides an upper bound on the minimum number of containers.
  • The total-weight bound is \(\lceil\sum_i w_i/C\rceil\); it need not be attainable. This follows by aggregating the capacity requirements.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• The exercise has 15 items and container capacity 50.
  • First-fit uses five containers, while the solution sheet states that four suffice.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: A binary integer program (BIP) is a linear optimization model in which all decision variables are binary. For variables \(y_1,\ldots,y_n\), the domain is \(y\in\{0,1\}^n\) before imposing the remaining constraints.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: BIPs describe combinations of yes-or-no choices. Even a moderate number of choices creates many candidate combinations, motivating methods such as branch-and-bound.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• There are \(2^n\) binary assignments before functional constraints eliminate infeasible combinations.
  • Its LP relaxation replaces each binary restriction by \(0\le y_j\le1\).
  • The objective can count selected alternatives or weight them by costs or returns.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• Project selection maximizes the return from projects under yearly budgets.
  • Ambulance location minimizes the number of selected station sites.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
A binary variable is a decision variable restricted to \(\{0,1\}\). For a yes-or-no choice \(j\), the course convention is

\[ y_j=\begin{cases}1,&\text{if decision }j\text{ is yes},\\0,&\text{if decision }j\text{ is no}.\end{cases} \]

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: Binary variables convert discrete choices into quantities that linear expressions can combine. Their practical meaning must be stated explicitly.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• The continuous bounds \(0\le y_j\le1\) alone do not enforce binarity.
  • Summing binary variables counts the selected decisions.
  • Auxiliary binary variables can activate or relax constraints.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• A station-location variable is 1 exactly when an ambulance station is built in that town.
  • \(y_1+y_2\le1\) prohibits selecting both alternatives.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: A bipartite matching pairs entities from two distinct groups, with each selected pair containing one member of each group and no entity used in more than one pair. A complete one-to-one assignment between equally sized groups is a perfect bipartite matching.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: The separation into two groups distinguishes assignment from pairing odd-degree vertices in the Chinese postman problem. This special structure supports the Hungarian algorithm.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Agents and tasks form the two groups in an assignment problem.
  • A matching need not use every entity unless completeness is required.
  • Maximum zero-cost matching can be represented as a unit-capacity flow problem.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• A machine-job pair connects the machine group to the job group.
  • The CPP odd-vertex pairing is nonbipartite because all paired vertices belong to one common set.

docs.title: Proposition
docs.text: For a maximization integer program with incumbent value \(L\), a branch-and-bound node can be pruned if its LP relaxation is infeasible, its relaxed optimizer satisfies all integer restrictions, or its relaxed upper bound \(U\) satisfies \(U\le L\). In the integral case, update the incumbent if appropriate. For minimization, reverse the bound comparison.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: Each condition proves that further subdivision of that node cannot improve the best known value. This is what makes the method more efficient than full enumeration.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• For maximization, a valid global upper bound is the maximum of the incumbent value and the LP bounds of active unresolved nodes.
  • At completion the incumbent proves the optimal value.
  • Pruning equality with the incumbent is sufficient to find the optimum value, but can discard other equally optimal solutions.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• A node with upper bound 3.3 can be discarded once the incumbent is 3.4.
  • In week 3 practice 9, the branch \(x_3\ge7\) is infeasible because \(x_2+3x_3\le20\) and \(x_2\ge0\).

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
Branch-and-bound solves an integer program by solving LP relaxations of subproblems, splitting subproblems when restricted variables are fractional, and discarding subproblems whose bounds cannot improve the best feasible integer solution. If \(x_j=v\) is fractional, branch into

\[ x_j\le\lfloor v\rfloor\qquad\text{and}\qquad x_j\ge\lceil v\rceil. \]

For a binary variable these branches fix it to 0 and 1.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: The branches retain every possible integer solution while excluding the current fractional value. Bounds prevent unnecessary exploration of parts of the search tree.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Carry all ancestor branching constraints into each child.
  • Prune for infeasibility, an integral relaxed optimum, or an uncompetitive bound.
  • Continue until every remaining possibility is resolved or bounded by the incumbent.
  • Branching choices affect the work required but not the correctly proven optimum.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• A fractional value \(x_1=3.3\) yields branches \(x_1\le3\) and \(x_1\ge4\).
  • The development-project model has optimum 3.4; the supplied tree has incorrect intermediate LP values, documented in coverage.md.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
The bus scheduling model chooses nonnegative integer counts \(x_i\) of buses starting in each of six consecutive four-hour intervals. Each bus operates for two intervals. With requirements \(d=(4,8,10,7,12,4)\), the cyclic model is

\[ \min\sum_{i=1}^6x_i,\qquad x_{i-1}+x_i\ge d_i\ (i=1,\ldots,6),\qquad x_i\in\mathbb Z_{\ge0}, \]

where \(x_0=x_6\).

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: The variables count shift starts, while each coverage constraint counts all buses operating in an interval. The wrap-around term links the last daily shift to the first interval.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Eight-hour operation covers exactly two consecutive four-hour intervals.
  • Coverage may exceed the minimum demand.
  • The repeating daily interpretation is the assumption used to formulate the midnight boundary.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• The midnight-to-4 AM constraint is \(x_6+x_1\ge4\).
  • The 4 PM-to-8 PM requirement gives \(x_4+x_5\ge12\).

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: The Chinese postman problem (CPP) finds a minimum-length closed route traversing every edge at least once in a connected undirected network with nonnegative edge lengths. To solve the course version, find a minimum-cost pairing of the odd-degree vertices using shortest-path distances, duplicate the corresponding paths, and construct an Euler tour in the resulting network.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: Every street must be covered. Repeated edges are necessary only to make a closed covering route possible, and the matching step chooses a minimum total extra length.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• If every vertex already has even degree, any Euler tour is optimal.
  • The optimal cost is the sum of original edge lengths plus the minimum pairing cost.
  • The shortest path between paired vertices can contain intermediate vertices.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• The five-vertex example has total edge length 25 and minimum pairing cost 7, giving CPP value 32.
  • Pairing A with D duplicates A-C-D, while pairing B with E duplicates B-E.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
The classical EOQ model assumes deterministic constant demand rate \(D>0\), instantaneous batch replenishment, no shortages, fixed setup cost \(K>0\) per order, and holding cost \(h>0\) per unit per unit time. A constant unit purchasing price can be excluded when optimizing. For batch size \(y>0\), relevant cost per unit time is

\[ TCU(y)=\frac{KD}{y}+\frac{hy}{2}. \]

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: Inventory repeatedly drops linearly from the batch size to zero. Large batches reduce setup frequency but increase average stock.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Average stock is \(y/2\) and cycle length is \(y/D\).
  • The cost is strictly convex for positive \(y\).
  • The model optimizes a continuous order quantity; discrete purchasing units require checking feasible nearby quantities.
  • Using a mean demand to approximate stochastic demand does not incorporate its variability.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• The phone data \(D=2\), \(K=605\), \(h=5\) give an optimal batch of 22.
  • The exercise uses average weekly demand 100 while explicitly omitting its standard deviation 10 from the EOQ calculation.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: An undirected network is connected if every pair of vertices can be joined by a path. It is unconnected if at least one pair cannot be joined.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: Connectedness establishes that all parts of the network can be reached from one another. The spanning-tree and undirected routing problems in the course assume it.

• A disconnected network has no spanning tree covering all its vertices.
  • A tree is connected as well as cycle-free.
  • For a directed flow network, available directed routes must still be checked; undirected connectedness alone does not imply flow to the sink.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• A chain of roads linking A to B and B to C connects all three towns.
  • Two groups of towns with no road between the groups are unconnected.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
A constraint is a requirement that an allowed decision must satisfy. A linear functional constraint has the form

\[ a_{i1}x_1+\cdots+a_{in}x_n\le b_i, \]

or the corresponding equality or \(\ge\) inequality. The \(a_{ij}\) are constraint coefficients and \(b_i\) is the right-hand side.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: Constraints translate capacity limits, demand requirements, and other restrictions into mathematics. Feasibility requires all constraints to hold together.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• A capacity limit commonly gives a \(\le\) constraint; a minimum requirement commonly gives a \(\ge\) constraint.
  • An equality represents an exact requirement or balance.
  • Multiplication by a negative number reverses an inequality.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• \(x_s+x_t\le80\) limits carpentry use.
  • \(800x_A+1000x_B\ge8000\) requires enough calories.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
Contingent decisions are binary choices whose admissibility depends on other choices. If decision 2 is allowed only when decision 1 is yes, the implication is represented by

\[ y_2\le y_1,\qquad y_1,y_2\in\{0,1\}. \]

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: The inequality prohibits precisely the combination “decision 2 yes, decision 1 no.” It does not force decision 2 to be selected when decision 1 is selected.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• If decision 2 must be yes when decision 1 is no, use \(y_1+y_2\ge1\).
  • If decision 3 is allowed only when both decisions 1 and 2 are yes, use \(y_3\le y_1\) and \(y_3\le y_2\).
  • If \(y_1=1\) and \(y_2=0\) must imply \(y_3=0\), use \(y_1-y_2+y_3\le1\).

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• \(W_{LA}\le F_{LA}\) requires a local factory before a warehouse can be built.
  • \(y_1+y_2+y_3\le2\) rules out all three yes decisions together.

docs.title: Proposition
docs.text:
For continuous demand with finite mean and CDF \(F\), the newsvendor expected cost satisfies

\[ G'(y)=(b+h)F(y)-b. \]

If \(F\) is continuous and strictly increasing through \(\beta=b/(b+h)\) and that quantile lies in the allowed quantity domain, the unique optimum is

\[ y^*=F^{-1}(\beta). \]

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: The optimal stock is a quantile of demand, determined by the cost balance. Continuity alone does not guarantee uniqueness if the CDF has a flat segment at the critical probability.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• For uniform demand on \([a,u]\), the optimum is \(a+(u-a)\beta\).
  • For the course normal approximation, it is \(\mu+\sigma\Phi^{-1}(\beta)\).
  • A continuous demand approximation may give a noninteger answer even when actual items are indivisible.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• Meal demand uniform on \([80,120]\) with \(\beta=0.6\) gives 104 meals.
  • Normal meal demand with mean 100 and standard deviation 20 gives about 105.07.

docs.title: Proposition
docs.text:
If \(x^{(1)},\ldots,x^{(k)}\) are optimal solutions of the same LP and \(\alpha_j\ge0\) with \(\sum_{j=1}^k\alpha_j=1\), then

\[ x=\sum_{j=1}^k\alpha_jx^{(j)} \]

is also optimal. Such a weighted average is a convex combination.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: Linear constraints are preserved by these weighted averages, and the linear objective remains equal to the common optimum. Two optimal corners therefore generate an entire optimal segment.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Weights must be nonnegative and sum to one.
  • For two points use \(\alpha\) and \(1-\alpha\), with \(0\le\alpha\le1\).
  • The property concerns continuous LP feasibility; averaging integer solutions need not preserve integrality.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• Combining \((5,0)\) and \((3,4)\) gives \((3+2\alpha,4-4\alpha)\), all with value 20.
  • Combining \((2,3)\) and \((0,6)\) gives \((2\alpha,6-3\alpha)\); \(\alpha=1/2\) gives \((1,9/2)\).

docs.title: Proposition
docs.text: For the LPs in the course with a nonempty feasible region in nonnegative variables, if a finite optimum exists, at least one feasible corner point attains it. Consequently, a unique optimal solution must be a feasible corner point. If a bounded feasible region has multiple optimal solutions, at least two of its corner points are optimal.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: This result allows an LP to be solved without testing every point in its feasible region. Simplex uses the algebraic counterparts of these corners.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• The existence of a finite optimum is essential.
  • The bounded-region qualification in the multiple-corner statement matters when the feasible region has rays.
  • Every convex combination of optimal corners is optimal.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• The manufacturing optimum \((2,5)\) is a feasible corner.
  • For the course LP with objective \(4x_1+2x_2\) and boundary \(2x_1+x_2\le11\), an entire feasible boundary segment attains 22.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: In an LP with \(n\) decision variables, a corner point is a point determined by the intersection of constraint boundaries with \(n\) independent boundary equations. At least \(n\) constraints are therefore active there, counting nonnegativity boundaries. A corner point is feasible only if it satisfies all constraints.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: Corner points are the finite candidates exploited by the graphical and simplex methods in the course. Merely counting repeated or dependent constraints does not determine a corner.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• In two dimensions, two nonparallel active boundaries determine a corner.
  • Extra active constraints can occur at a degenerate corner.
  • Not every intersection of boundaries is feasible.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• The lines \(x_2=5\) and \(2x_1+x_2=9\) intersect at \((2,5)\).
  • The nonnegativity boundaries meet at the origin \((0,0)\).

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
For newsvendor overage cost \(h>0\) and underage cost \(b>0\), the critical ratio is

\[ \beta=\frac{b}{b+h}=\frac{p-c}{p-s},\qquad 0<\beta<1. \]

It is the cumulative-demand probability used to select the optimal stock quantile.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: A large underage cost justifies a higher demand quantile; a large overage cost justifies a lower one. The ratio balances the two marginal risks.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• For integer demand, increasing from \(y\) to \(y+1\) helps while \(F(y)<\beta\).
  • For the continuous strictly increasing CDFs used in the examples, the optimum solves \(F(y^*)=\beta\).
  • The ratio is not the expected fraction of demand served.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• Newspapers with \(b=1.5\) and \(h=2\) have \(\beta=3/7\).
  • Meals with \(b=3.3\) and \(h=2.2\) have \(\beta=0.6\).

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: In the course's network terminology, a cycle or tour is a path that starts and ends at the same vertex. Because its path convention requires distinct edges, no edge is repeated within such a cycle.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: Cycles return to their starting point. They are useful for routes that must return home and are excluded when constructing a tree.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• An Euler tour is a closed traversal using every edge exactly once.
  • A tree contains no cycles.
  • In the Chinese postman problem, “tour” is also used for a closed route that may repeat original edges; repeated copies are distinct in the augmented network.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• Three edges \(A-B\), \(B-C\), and \(C-A\) form a cycle.
  • Adding an edge between two already connected vertices of a tree creates a cycle.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: A degenerate basic feasible solution has at least one basic variable equal to zero. A degenerate pivot has a zero step length and can change the basis without changing the solution vector or objective value.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: At a degenerate point, several constraints become active together. More than one basis may describe the same point, so a simplex iteration need not correspond to visible movement.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• A tie for the minimum ratio can produce a degenerate basic feasible solution.
  • Zero ratios must be considered when the pivot-column coefficient is positive.
  • The basic/nonbasic distinction is determined by the basis, not by whether a value is zero.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• With \(x_1-x_2\le1\) and \(2x_1+x_2\le2\), increasing \(x_1\) gives tied ratios of 1.
  • At \((x_1,x_2,s_1,s_2)=(1,0,0,0)\), exchanging \(s_2\) for \(x_2\) leaves the point and \(z=3\) unchanged.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
The course's diet problem chooses pounds \(x_A,x_B\) of two feeds to minimize daily feed cost while satisfying calorie, vitamin, and composition requirements:

\[ \begin{aligned} \min\quad &0.4x_A+0.8x_B\\ \text{subject to}\quad &800x_A+1000x_B\ge8000,\\ &140x_A+70x_B\ge700,\\ &2x_A-x_B\le0,\\ &x_A,x_B\ge0. \end{aligned} \]

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: This is a minimum-cost mixture model. The composition restriction prevents cheap feed A from exceeding one-third of total feed weight.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• The share constraint follows from \(x_A\le(x_A+x_B)/3\).
  • Nutrient requirements are lower bounds, so their inequalities point toward greater nutrient intake.
  • The optimal solution is \(x_A=20/7\), \(x_B=40/7\), with cost \(40/7\).

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• The optimal mixture contains exactly one-third feed A.
  • At the optimum the calorie requirement is tight, while vitamin intake is \(800\ge700\).

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: The Dijkstra-Prim method constructs a minimum spanning tree in a connected undirected network with nonnegative edge lengths. Start with an arbitrary vertex in \(U\) and no selected edges. Repeatedly select a shortest edge joining a vertex in \(U\) to a vertex outside \(U\), add that edge, and add the outside endpoint to \(U\). Stop when every vertex belongs to \(U\).

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: The method grows one connected tree. Each new edge connects one previously unreached vertex at the smallest available joining cost.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Compare edges crossing from the whole set \(U\), not only from the last added vertex.
  • Ties can be broken arbitrarily.
  • The starting vertex can change the construction order without changing the minimum total value.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• In the Euclidean example, starting with \(U=\{1\}\) selects edge \(1-7\) of length \(\sqrt{13}\).
  • The next edge is \(1-4\), of length 5.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: A directed network is a network whose edges have specified orientations. An edge \(i\to j\) allows traversal or flow from \(i\) to \(j\); reverse traversal is not implied by its existence.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: Direction represents asymmetric connections such as one-way movement or the order in which activities must occur.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Incoming and outgoing edges have different roles at a vertex.
  • Maximum-flow constraints respect the original edge directions.
  • A backward residual edge cancels assigned flow; it is not necessarily an original directed edge.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• The maximum-flow network has outgoing edges at the source and incoming edges at the sink.
  • An activity edge \(i\to j\) points from its preceding event to its following event.

docs.title: Proposition
docs.text:
Let demand be a nonnegative integer-valued random variable with CDF \(F\), finite mean, and newsvendor costs \(b,h>0\). Over nonnegative integer order quantities, a smallest optimal quantity is

\[ y^*=\min\{y\in\mathbb Z_{\ge0}:F(y)\ge\beta\},\qquad\beta=\frac{b}{b+h}. \]

The marginal expected-cost difference is

\[ G(y+1)-G(y)=(b+h)F(y)-b. \]

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: Add another item while its expected lost-margin saving exceeds its expected leftover loss. Stop at the first CDF value reaching the critical ratio.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• If \(F(y)=\beta\), quantities \(y\) and \(y+1\) have equal expected cost.
  • All integer optimal quantities satisfy \(F(y-1)\le\beta\le F(y)\), taking \(F(-1)=0\).
  • Compute the expected cost with the actual discrete probabilities, not only the critical ratio.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• For the newspaper distribution, \(F(16)=0.25<3/7\le F(17)=0.50\), so the smallest optimum is 17; expected cost is 1.975.
  • The dress example has \(\beta=0.75\), optimal quantity 10, and expected cost 138.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: A dummy assignment makes a rectangular assignment matrix square by adding fictitious agents or tasks with zero assignment costs. Add dummy agents when there are fewer agents than tasks; add dummy tasks when there are fewer tasks than agents.

  • A real agent assigned to a dummy task remains unused.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
The dynamic lot-size model chooses order quantities over \(n\) discrete periods with known varying demands, no shortages, and no lead time. In the detailed course notation, \(y_i\) is the period-\(i\) order, \(D_i\) demand, \(x_i\) starting stock, \(K_i\) setup cost, and \(h_i\) holding cost per unit carried to the next period. Then

\[ x_{i+1}=x_i+y_i-D_i\ge0,\qquad C_i(y_i)=\begin{cases}0,&y_i=0,\\K_i+c_i(y_i),&y_i>0.\end{cases} \]

Minimize \(\sum_{i=1}^n[C_i(y_i)+h_ix_{i+1}]\), with given \(x_1\) and terminal stock \(x_{n+1}=0\) in the course examples.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: The model balances setup costs against carrying inventory into later periods. Unlike EOQ, demand and costs can change over the finite planning horizon.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• The course tables enumerate nonnegative integer order and stock quantities.
  • Variable ordering cost \(c_i(y_i)\) may depend nonlinearly on the batch size.
  • The model is introduced in the week 5 overview and developed in week 6.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• For demands \((2,1,3)\), the worked optimum orders \((2,2,2)\) at total cost 79.
  • Week 6 practice 2 has two optimal policies, \((4,0,4,0)\) and \((6,0,0,2)\), both costing 31.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: Dynamic programming (DP) decomposes an optimization problem into related subproblems and computes their optimal values recursively. A state records the information needed to connect stages, and the optimum for a smaller subproblem becomes an input to the next calculation.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: Rather than enumerate every complete policy separately, the method reuses solutions to subproblems with the same state. In this course, periods are stages and inventory levels are states.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Specify the state, decision, transition, cost, boundary conditions, and recursion.
  • Store minimizing decisions as well as costs to reconstruct an optimal policy.
  • Keep every minimizing decision if all optimal policies are required.

docs.text:
• \(f_i(x_{i+1})\) records the least cost through period \(i\) for a specified ending inventory.

docs.title: Proposition
docs.text:
Under the classical EOQ assumptions with \(D,K,h>0\), the unique order quantity minimizing \(TCU(y)=KD/y+hy/2\) over \(y>0\) is

\[ y^*=\sqrt{\frac{2KD}{h}},\qquad t_0^*=\frac{y^*}{D}=\sqrt{\frac{2K}{Dh}}. \]

The optimal policy orders \(y^*\) units when stock reaches zero.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: The formula balances the two policy-dependent cost components. Demand and setup cost favour larger batches; expensive holding favours smaller ones.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• At the optimum, \(KD/y^*=hy^*/2\).
  • The minimum relevant cost rate is \(\sqrt{2KDh}\).
  • Increasing demand raises the batch size but shortens the cycle.
  • The formula follows from \(-KD/y^2+h/2=0\) and strict convexity.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• The phone shop orders 22 units every 11 days and incurs relevant daily cost 110.
  • The snack bar obtains \(y^*=\sqrt{2(50)(10)/(3/7)}\approx48.30\) kilograms.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
For a repeating EOQ cycle of length \(t_0^*>0\) and fixed lead time \(L\ge0\), the effective lead time is

\[ L_e=L-nt_0^*,\qquad n=\left\lfloor\frac{L}{t_0^*}\right\rfloor. \]

Thus \(0\le L_e<t_0^*\). The course's on-hand reorder level is \(DL_e\).

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: The formula removes complete ordering cycles from the delay. It locates the ordering moment within a repeating stock cycle when orders from earlier cycles can still be in transit.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• For a lead time shorter than a cycle, \(L_e=L\).
  • The quantity \(L_e\) is a cycle remainder, not a shorter physical delivery delay.
  • If the delay is an exact multiple of the cycle, the remainder is zero; ordering and receipt events must be interpreted at that common cycle boundary.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• \(L=20\) weeks and \(t_0^*=7\) weeks give \(L_e=6\) weeks.
  • The snack bar has \(L=12\) days and \(t_0^*\approx4.83\), giving \(L_e\approx2.34\) days.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
To require at least one of \(a^Tx\le b\) and \(d^Tx\le e\), introduce \(y\in\{0,1\}\) and write

\[ a^Tx\le b+My,\qquad d^Tx\le e+M(1-y). \]

The finite constant \(M\) must be large enough that the relaxed inequality imposes no unintended restriction over the relevant variable domain.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: One inequality is enforced while the other is allowed to relax. Both original inequalities may still hold, so this formulation expresses inclusive “or.”

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• For \(y=0\), the first inequality is enforced; for \(y=1\), the second is enforced.
  • A valid value of \(M\) requires information about bounds on the expressions being relaxed.
  • This is a modelling device; it does not mean multiplying two decision variables.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• \(3x_1+2x_2\le18+My\) and \(x_1+4x_2\le16+M(1-y)\) implement the video example.
  • The week 3 exercise applies the same switch to two inequalities involving four variables.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: The EOQ model with lead times retains constant known demand, no shortages, and the classical setup and holding costs, but an order arrives after a fixed delay \(L\ge0\). The optimal quantity remains \(y^*=\sqrt{2KD/h}\). In the course's repeating on-hand-stock convention, order when stock falls to \(DL_e\), where \(L_e\) is the effective lead time.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: Lead time changes when an order must be placed so that replenishment arrives at the required moment. It does not change the EOQ under these deterministic assumptions.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• If \(L<t_0^*\), the reorder stock level is \(DL\).
  • If lead time exceeds a cycle, several orders can be outstanding; use the course effective-lead-time construction.
  • The on-hand trigger describes steady-state cycles, not the initial setup of an empty supply pipeline.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
The EOQ model with planned shortages allows all unmet demand to be backordered until instantaneous replenishment. With constant \(D>0\), setup \(K>0\), holding rate \(h>0\), and backlog penalty \(p>0\), choose batch size \(y>0\) and stock just after replenishment \(0\le s\le y\). Maximum backlog is \(y-s\), and

\[ TCU(y,s)=\frac{KD}{y}+\frac{hs^2}{2y}+\frac{p(y-s)^2}{2y}. \]

The optimum is

\[ y^*=\sqrt{\frac{2KD}{h}}\sqrt{\frac{p+h}{p}},\qquad s^*=\sqrt{\frac{2KD}{h}}\sqrt{\frac{p}{p+h}}. \]

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: The policy deliberately balances periods with positive stock and periods with waiting customers. Replenishment first clears the backlog, leaving \(s\) units on hand.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Order \(y^*\) when backlog reaches \(y^*-s^*\).
  • Cycle length is \(y^*/D\); the fraction of time without shortage is \(p/(p+h)\).
  • The stock-phase mean \(s/2\) is not the whole-cycle average; the latter is \(s^2/(2y)\).
  • For finite positive \(p\), the optimal batch is larger than the classical EOQ.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• With the phone data and \(p=6\), \(y^*=22\sqrt{11/6}\approx29.79\) and \(s^*=22\sqrt{6/11}\approx16.25\).
  • With \(p=h\), the model is out of stock for half the cycle.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
The course's EOQ model with price breaks gives an all-unit discount: every ordered unit has price \(c_2<c_1\) when the batch meets a threshold \(q\). Following the “at least” convention of the worked examples,

\[ c(y)=\begin{cases}c_1,&0<y<q,\\c_2,&y\ge q,\end{cases}\qquad TCU(y)=Dc(y)+\frac{KD}{y}+\frac{hy}{2}. \]

Holding rate \(h\) is fixed across price levels; demand is constant, replenishment instantaneous, and shortages prohibited.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: A larger batch may be worth buying to reduce the price of every unit. Purchasing cost must therefore be included in the comparison.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Let \(y_m=\sqrt{2KD/h}\). If \(y_m\ge q\), order \(y_m\) at the discount price.
  • If \(y_m<q\), compare the full costs at \(y_m\) and \(q\) and choose the cheaper; both are optimal at equality.
  • The introductory PDF uses \(y>q\), inconsistent with its later recommendation \(y=q\). This page explicitly follows the worked-example convention.
  • The discount is all-unit, not a discount only on units above the threshold.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• For phones, \(y_m=22\): cost at 22 is 450 per day, while cost at the qualifying 35 is about 442.07; order 35.
  • For the snack bar, the 100-kilogram threshold is not worthwhile; the optimal quantity remains about 48.30.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
In the course's Euclidean network, cities have plane coordinates \((x_i,y_i)\), an edge may join every pair of cities, and its length is

\[ d_{ij}=\sqrt{(x_i-x_j)^2+(y_i-y_j)^2}. \]

The resulting distances provide the weights for the minimum spanning tree problem.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: Coordinates turn a location problem into a complete weighted network. Distances are straight-line lengths rather than road travel times.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Distances are symmetric: \(d_{ij}=d_{ji}\).
  • Use sufficient precision when comparing close distances.
  • The usual spanning-tree algorithms apply once the distance matrix is computed.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• Between \((13,6)\) and \((15,9)\) the distance is \(\sqrt{13}\approx3.61\).
  • The seven-city example has tree length about 27.29 using the displayed rounded distances.

docs.title: Proposition
docs.text: A finite connected undirected network has an Euler tour if and only if every vertex has even degree. Such a network is called an Euler network.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: Even degree is necessary because each arrival along an edge must be paired with a departure. The cycle-splicing construction establishes sufficiency.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• One odd-degree vertex is enough to rule out an Euler tour.
  • Connectedness is required to traverse all edges in one tour.
  • Parallel copies introduced by the Chinese postman construction are counted as separate edges.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• The seven-bridge network violates the even-degree condition.
  • Duplicating suitable paths between odd-degree vertices makes their endpoint degrees even.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: For a connected undirected Euler network, the course's Euler tour algorithm starts at a vertex \(s\), follows unused edges until returning to \(s\), and calls the resulting cycle \(\Omega\). If unused edges remain, choose a vertex \(v\) on \(\Omega\) incident to an unused edge, build another closed unused-edge traversal \(\Omega_1\) from \(v\), and splice \(\Omega_1\) into \(\Omega\) at \(v\). Repeat until every edge is used.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: The method builds a complete tour from smaller cycles. Even degree ensures that an unused-edge excursion can close at its starting vertex.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Keep track of used edge identities, especially with parallel copies.
  • The splice inserts one closed excursion into another without losing any previously used edge.
  • Arbitrary eligible choices can give different valid Euler tours.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• The worked example begins its first cycle at A.
  • It later adds a cycle through B and then one through D to include all 12 edges.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: An Euler tour is a closed traversal of a network that uses every edge exactly once. Vertices may be revisited. A network possessing an Euler tour is called an Euler network.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: The requirement concerns visiting edges, not visiting each vertex once. It models a route that covers every street without retracing an edge.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• At each vertex, arrivals and departures balance.
  • For connected undirected networks, an Euler tour exists exactly when every vertex has even degree.
  • In a weighted Euler network, every Euler tour has length equal to the sum of all edge lengths.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• The Königsberg bridge network has no Euler tour because its vertices have odd degree.
  • The course weighted Euler example has total edge length 24, so its Euler tours have length 24.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
The feasible region is the set of all feasible solutions of a model:

\[ F=\{x:x\text{ satisfies every model constraint}\}. \]

For a two-variable LP it is obtained by intersecting the allowed half-planes and equality lines, including variable-domain restrictions.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: The feasible region shows the choices available before the objective is considered. Each extra constraint can retain or reduce this set.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Removing a constraint cannot shrink the feasible region.
  • An empty feasible region means the model is infeasible.
  • An unbounded feasible region does not by itself imply an unbounded objective value.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• \(x_1,x_2\ge0\) restrict the region to the first quadrant.
  • The diet requirements define the intersection of calorie, vitamin, and feed-share half-planes.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: A feasible solution assigns values to all decision variables and satisfies every constraint, including their domain restrictions. A solution violating at least one constraint is infeasible.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: Feasibility asks whether a decision is allowed. It must be checked before the decision's objective value can be used as a practical candidate.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• An attractive objective value does not compensate for a violated constraint.
  • An LP-feasible fractional solution may be infeasible after integer restrictions are imposed.
  • Every optimal solution is feasible.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• For \(x_1\le4\), \(x_2\le5\), \(2x_1+x_2\le9\), \(x_1,x_2\ge0\), \((2,5)\) is feasible.
  • In the same model, \((4,5)\) is infeasible because \(2(4)+5=13>9\).

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
A linear expression can be restricted to one of the listed values \(d_1,\ldots,d_N\) by introducing binary variables \(y_i\) and writing

\[ a_1x_1+\cdots+a_nx_n=\sum_{i=1}^Nd_iy_i,\qquad \sum_{i=1}^Ny_i=1,\qquad y_i\in\{0,1\}. \]

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: Exactly one indicator selects the allowed value of the expression. This avoids writing a separate alternative constraint for every possible value.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• The sum-to-one equality ensures that a value is actually selected.
  • The \(d_i\) are fixed data, so \(d_iy_i\) is linear.
  • Relaxing the indicators to continuous fractions would generally allow values between the listed values.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• For allowed totals 3, 5, or 8, write \(x_1+x_2=3y_1+5y_2+8y_3\).
  • An even number of three yes decisions can take only the values 0 and 2.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: The first-fit heuristic processes packing items in their given order. Place the current item into the first previously opened container with enough unused capacity. If no such container exists, open a new container and place the item there. Assume every item individually fits in a container.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: The rule makes each placement using the current packing, without searching all arrangements. Both item order and container order affect its decisions.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Every produced packing respects capacity.
  • Its container count is an upper bound, not a proof of optimality.
  • The exercise gives this procedure without a name; first-fit is its conventional search name.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• In the course exercise, items 1, 2, 3, and 9 fill container 1 to weight 49.
  • Items 6, 7, and 8 fill another container to weight 49; the full heuristic packing uses five containers.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: A forbidden assignment is an agent-task pair that is not allowed. In the course's Hungarian cost matrix, represent this pair by \(\infty\) and leave that entry infinite during all transformations.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: The infinite cost acts as a prohibition rather than an expensive ordinary choice. A finite feasible complete assignment must avoid every prohibited pair.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Do not apply finite row or column adjustments as if they made an infinite entry available.
  • If no complete assignment avoiding forbidden pairs exists, the intended assignment problem is infeasible.
  • In a binary formulation, the equivalent restriction is \(x_{ij}=0\).

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• A machine unable to process job 3 receives an infinite entry in that job's column.
  • A feasible assignment must choose another machine for that job.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: Graphical integer programming solves a two-variable integer model by plotting its continuous constraints and considering only the lattice points satisfying all restrictions. Evaluate the objective at feasible integer points to identify the best value.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: The continuous feasible region helps locate the permitted integer points. Unlike an LP, the best integer point need not be a corner of that continuous region.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Both coordinates must satisfy the stated integrality restrictions.
  • An LP-optimal fractional corner is not an integer-feasible decision.
  • For a small bounded example, explicit comparison of feasible lattice points proves optimality.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• The integer work-order model uses \(3.2T+2.4S\le16\) and \(2T+3S\le15\).
  • Its best integer decision is \((T,S)=(0,5)\), with profit 750.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: The graphical method solves a two-variable LP by drawing each constraint boundary, identifying the common feasible region, drawing a constant-objective line, and moving that line in the direction of improvement until the best feasible contact is reached. Intersecting the relevant boundary equations gives exact coordinates.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: The method makes feasibility and optimality visible. It also reveals whether the best value is attained at one point or along a segment.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Determine the allowed side of each boundary from the inequality; do not assume it is always below the line.
  • Check the direction of improvement from the objective, especially with negative coefficients.
  • Also allow for an empty feasible region or an objective that can improve without bound.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• Maximizing \(x_1+2x_2\) with \(x_1\le4\), \(x_2\le5\), \(2x_1+x_2\le9\) gives \((2,5)\).
  • For \(z=2x_1-3x_2\), increasing \(z\) moves its objective line downward.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: A heuristic is a solution method designed to obtain a good feasible solution without a general guarantee that it is optimal. In this course, a heuristic solution is required to satisfy the original problem's constraints.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: Heuristics are useful when finding an exact optimum is too difficult or time-consuming. A good feasible decision can be valuable even before its distance from optimality is known.

  • For maximization, a feasible heuristic value is a lower bound.
  • A relaxation can supply an opposing bound that measures solution quality.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: The Hungarian algorithm solves the square minimum-cost assignment problem. Subtract each row minimum, then each column minimum. Cover all zeros of the resulting matrix with a minimum number of rows and columns. If \(n\) lines are needed, select \(n\) independent zeros, one per row and column. Otherwise let \(k\) be the smallest uncovered entry, subtract \(k\) from uncovered entries, add \(k\) to doubly covered entries, leave singly covered entries unchanged, and repeat the covering step.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: The transformations preserve the optimal assignment while creating enough zero entries for a complete assignment. The final cost must be evaluated in the original matrix.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• The zero cover must use the minimum number of lines.
  • A set of independent zeros has no two in the same row or column.
  • The minimum line-cover size equals the maximum number of independent zero assignments in this construction.
  • Do not add together transformed zero costs to report the original objective value.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• The worked four-machine matrix initially needs three covering lines; an adjustment with k=2 enables a complete assignment.
  • The final original cost is \(2+5+6+7=20\).

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: The incumbent solution in branch-and-bound is the best feasible solution of the original integer problem found so far. Its objective value supplies a lower bound for maximization and an upper bound for minimization.

docs.title: Interpretation

  • A fractional relaxed optimizer cannot become the incumbent.
  • Without a known feasible solution there is no incumbent value, although an obvious feasible point may already be available.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: An infeasible linear program has no decision vector satisfying all its constraints. Equivalently, its feasible region is empty. In the two-phase method, a negative optimal value of \(r=-\sum_iR_i\) proves infeasibility.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: Conflicting requirements can make a model impossible even when each requirement is individually sensible. The objective cannot resolve this conflict.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• An infeasible model has no optimal feasible solution.
  • A positive remaining artificial variable at the phase-I optimum indicates an unsatisfied original requirement.
  • Infeasibility differs from an unbounded objective, which requires feasible points.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• \(2x_1+x_2\le2\), \(3x_1+4x_2\ge12\), \(x_1,x_2\ge0\) is infeasible: the first constraint implies \(3x_1+4x_2\le8\).
  • A negative phase-I optimum, such as \(r^*=-4\), cannot be repaired by beginning Phase II.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: An integer linear program (ILP) is a linear optimization model in which some or all decision variables must take integer values. The linear objective and functional constraints are retained, with restrictions such as \(x_j\in\mathbb Z\) added to the specified variables.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: Integrality represents indivisible decisions and also supports modelling of logical conditions. It changes the feasible set and can make the problem substantially harder to solve.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Pure integer programs require all decision variables to be integer.
  • Mixed integer programs include both integer and continuous variables.
  • Binary integer programs restrict every decision variable to 0 or 1.
  • Rounding an LP solution need not preserve feasibility or optimality.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: An inventory policy specifies when to replenish stock and how much to order. Inventory theory constructs and analyses models to choose these decisions while accounting for demand and relevant costs.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: Ordering frequently reduces stock held but increases the number of setups. Larger, less frequent orders reverse that trade-off. The appropriate model depends on the demand setting.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• The EOQ models use a constant deterministic demand rate.
  • Dynamic lot sizing uses known demand varying by discrete period.
  • The newsvendor model uses stochastic demand for one selling period.
  • A complete policy states both the quantity and the ordering trigger or period.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• A classical EOQ policy orders a fixed quantity whenever inventory reaches zero.
  • A newsvendor policy chooses one stock quantity before seasonal demand is observed.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
The job sequencing model orders nonpreemptive jobs on one machine to minimize total lateness penalties. Let \(s_i\ge0\) be job \(i\)'s start, \(p_i\) its duration, \(d_i\) its due date, \(T_i\ge0\) its tardiness, and \(w_i\) its penalty rate. Minimize \(\sum_iw_iT_i\) subject to \(T_i\ge s_i+p_i-d_i\). For each pair \(i<j\), impose

\[ s_i+p_i\le s_j+M(1-y_{ij}),\qquad s_j+p_j\le s_i+My_{ij},\qquad y_{ij}\in\{0,1\}. \]

Here \(y_{ij}=1\) means \(i\) precedes \(j\), and \(M\) must be valid for the scheduling horizon.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: Pairwise alternatives prevent overlapping processing. Tardiness variables charge for finishing after the due date while imposing no penalty for early completion.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• For the supplied three jobs, total processing time is 40; a no-idle schedule starts at zero and lies within that horizon.
  • Nonnegative penalty rates make unnecessary idle time avoidable.
  • This formulation is derived from the exercise and the preceding either-or technique; the video PDF contains the problem statement only.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• The course has processing times \((5,20,15)\) and due dates \((24,22,35)\).
  • Sequence \(2,1,3\) completes at 20, 25, 40 and incurs \(12(0)+19(1)+34(5)=189\).

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
To require at least \(K\) of \(N\) inequalities \(a_i^Tx\le d_i\), introduce binary relaxation indicators \(y_i\) and impose

\[ a_i^Tx\le d_i+My_i\quad(i=1,\ldots,N),\qquad \sum_{i=1}^Ny_i\le N-K. \]

Here \(0\le K\le N\) and \(M\) must validly relax each marked inequality. The video's equality \(\sum_i y_i=N-K\) gives the same allowed \(x\) values when such relaxation is valid.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: At most \(N-K\) inequalities may be released, so at least \(K\) remain enforced. A released inequality is allowed to hold as well.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• The formulation does not require exactly \(K\) original inequalities to be true.
  • The practice solution uses the inequality version; the video uses equality.
  • For \(K=N\), no constraint may be relaxed.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• At least two of four constraints can be enforced using \(y_1+y_2+y_3+y_4\le2\).
  • At least two of three constraints leave at most one relaxation indicator equal to 1.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: The Königsberg bridge problem asks whether a closed walk can cross each of the city's seven bridges exactly once. Represent each land region by a vertex and each bridge by an edge. The resulting four-vertex network asks whether an Euler tour exists.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: The geographical details are reduced to a connection problem. The impossibility follows from vertex degrees rather than from testing every possible walk.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Parallel bridges are separate edges between the same vertices.
  • The illustrated degrees are 5, 3, 3, and 3, so the even-degree condition fails.
  • The requested return to the starting point is part of the problem.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• The central land region has five incident bridge edges.
  • At an odd-degree region, a closed traversal cannot pair all arrivals and departures.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: The Kruskal method constructs a minimum spanning tree by starting with no selected edges and repeatedly choosing a shortest unselected edge that does not create a cycle with the already selected edges. Stop once the selected edges connect all vertices.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: The selected edges may initially form several separate pieces. The method joins those pieces while avoiding unnecessary loops.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Equivalently, inspect edges in nondecreasing order and reject any that create a cycle.
  • For \(n\) vertices, a completed tree has \(n-1\) selected edges.
  • Equal-length eligible edges may be chosen in any order.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• If A-B and B-C are already selected, adding A-C would create a cycle and must be rejected.
  • Week 4 practice 3 has three independent binary tie choices, giving \(2^3=8\) minimum trees.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: Linear program formulation converts a practical description into an LP by organizing the data, stating the objective in words, defining decision variables, writing the objective function, and writing all constraints including variable restrictions.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: The formulation should be understandable without guessing what its symbols mean. The main task is to translate the problem's choices and requirements accurately.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• State variable meanings before using them in formulas.
  • Use consistent measurement units in each constraint.
  • A percentage requirement can often be rearranged into a linear inequality.
  • Do not add integrality to a requested LP unless the intended model requires an integer program.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• A maximum one-third share of feed A becomes \(x_A\le(x_A+x_B)/3\).
  • Tow-bar production uses \(3.5x_t+2.5x_s\le18\) for machine 1.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
A linear program (LP) maximizes or minimizes a linear objective function subject to linear equality and/or inequality constraints. Its decision variables are continuous unless additional integer restrictions are imposed. For example,

\[ \max z=\sum_{j=1}^n c_jx_j,\qquad \sum_{j=1}^n a_{ij}x_j\le b_i\ (i=1,\ldots,m),\qquad x_j\ge0. \]

Other inequality directions and equalities are also allowed in an LP.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: Linearity makes large planning models tractable by methods such as simplex. A model with indivisible decisions needs explicit integer restrictions to rule out fractional choices.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Products of decision variables and powers such as \(x_j^2\) are not linear.
  • Negative coefficients are allowed.
  • The graphical method is useful for two variables; simplex handles larger models.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• Giapetto maximizes \(3x_s+2x_t\) under linear labour and demand limits.
  • The feeding-pigs model minimizes cost under nutrient and composition requirements.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
Let \(f_i(x_{i+1})\) be the minimum cost through period \(i\), including its ending-stock holding cost, conditional on stock \(x_{i+1}\). For given initial stock \(x_1\), the course's forward lot-size recursion is

\[ f_1(x_2)=C_1(D_1+x_2-x_1)+h_1x_2 \]

when the required order is nonnegative, and \(+\infty\) otherwise. For \(i\ge2\),

\[ f_i(x_{i+1})=\min_{0\le y_i\le D_i+x_{i+1}} \left\{C_i(y_i)+h_ix_{i+1}+f_{i-1}(x_{i+1}+D_i-y_i)\right\}. \]

Use integer states and decisions in the course tables; unreachable predecessor states have value \(+\infty\). The required final value is \(f_n(0)\).

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: The previous stock level is inferred from the ending stock and current order. The recursion compares all feasible ways to reach the same ending state.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• The bound on \(y_i\) ensures nonnegative predecessor inventory.
  • Reconstruct from \(x_{n+1}=0\) using stored minimizers and \(x_i=x_{i+1}+D_i-y_i\).
  • In the course examples, states need not exceed the remaining future demand.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• The three-period example gives \(f_2(1)=53\) and \(f_3(0)=26+53=79\).
  • Backward reconstruction gives \(y_3=2\), \(x_3=1\), \(y_2=2\), \(x_2=0\), \(y_1=2\).

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: The LP relaxation of an integer linear program removes its integrality requirements and keeps the objective and all other restrictions. In particular, a binary variable becomes a continuous variable satisfying \(0\le x_j\le1\).

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: The relaxation is easier to solve and includes every integer-feasible decision. Its optimum bounds the original integer optimum.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Its value is an upper bound for maximization and a lower bound for minimization.
  • If a relaxed optimizer satisfies every original integrality restriction, it is also integer-optimal.
  • Do not drop binary upper bounds when dropping binarity.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• The project-selection relaxation allows \(x_3=0.2\) and obtains 3.52 at the root.
  • An integral relaxed solution such as \((1,0,1,1,0)\) is a feasible candidate for the original project model.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
For the course network with only outgoing source edges and only incoming sink edges, the maximum flow LP uses continuous variables \(x_{ij}\) and solves

\[ \begin{aligned} \max\quad &\sum_jx_{sj}\\ \text{subject to}\quad &\sum_jx_{ji}=\sum_jx_{ij}\quad(i\ne s,t),\\ &0\le x_{ij}\le c_{ij}\quad\text{for every directed edge }(i,j). \end{aligned} \]

Here \(c_{ij}\) is the edge capacity and sums run over existing edges.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: The formulation separates the objective at the source from conservation at intermediate vertices. Capacities constrain individual directed flows.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Source outflow equals sink inflow by summing conservation equations.
  • No binary selection variable is needed: an edge may carry any feasible flow amount.
  • The formulation is derived from the video prompt and the previously taught flow conditions.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• The example objective is \(x_{SA}+x_{SB}\).
  • At A, conservation is \(x_{SA}=x_{AB}+x_{AC}+x_{AD}\).

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: The maximum flow problem assigns nonnegative flow \(x_{ij}\) to the edges of a directed network, subject to capacities \(x_{ij}\le c_{ij}\) and flow conservation at every transshipment vertex. The course assumes the source has only outgoing edges and the sink only incoming edges. The objective is to maximize total source outflow, equivalently total sink inflow.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: Intermediate vertices pass flow through the network rather than create or consume it. Capacities limit how much can travel on each directed connection.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Flow into each intermediate vertex equals flow out.
  • The same maximum value can have several feasible edge-flow assignments.
  • Residual reverse capacity permits earlier routing choices to be revised.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• The main example sends maximum flow 15 from S to T.
  • Week 4 practice 7 reaches 16, with 9 entering T from D and 7 from E.

docs.title: Proposition
docs.text: Over the same feasible set, minimizing \(f(x)\) is equivalent to maximizing \(-f(x)\). The two problems have the same optimal solution vectors, and their optimal objective values have opposite signs.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: The course presents simplex for maximization. Negating a minimization objective allows that procedure to be used while leaving the constraints unchanged.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Negate every objective coefficient.
  • Recover the original optimal value by changing the sign back.
  • Only the objective changes; the allowed decisions remain the same.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• Minimizing \(3x_1-5x_2\) becomes maximizing \(-3x_1+5x_2\).
  • In week 2 practice 8, transformed value 10 corresponds to original minimum \(-10\).

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
For a feasible canonical tableau and an entering variable with constraint-column coefficients \(a_{ik}\) and right-hand sides \(b_i\ge0\), the minimum-ratio test selects

\[ \theta=\min_{i:a_{ik}>0}\frac{b_i}{a_{ik}}. \]

A row attaining the minimum supplies the leaving basic variable. Zero ratios are eligible; only the denominator must be strictly positive.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: The test finds the first basic variable that reaches zero as the entering variable increases. A larger step would violate nonnegativity.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Rows with zero or negative pivot-column coefficients do not restrict the increase.
  • A tie may be broken arbitrarily in the course procedure and can lead to degeneracy.
  • If there is no positive coefficient and the objective improves along this column, the objective is unbounded.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• The initial ratios \(10/2=5\) and \(15/1=15\) make \(s_1\) leave.
  • The next ratios are \(5/(1/2)=10\) and \(10/(5/2)=4\), so \(s_2\) leaves.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: Given a connected undirected network with nonnegative edge lengths, a minimum spanning tree is a spanning tree whose total selected edge length is smallest among all spanning trees of that network.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: The objective is to connect every location at minimum total construction length. It does not minimize travel distance from one selected origin.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Both Dijkstra-Prim and Kruskal methods produce a minimum spanning tree.
  • There may be several minimum trees with the same total length.
  • Tie choices may be explored to identify alternative minimum trees.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• Roads can be selected to connect all cities while minimizing total road length.
  • Week 4 practice 1 has two minimum spanning trees, differing by the choice B-F or F-G.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
In the CPP construction, a minimum-weight perfect matching pairs the odd-degree vertices so that each belongs to exactly one pair and the sum of pair costs is minimized. The cost \(d_{ij}\) of a pair is its shortest-path distance. With a binary variable for each unordered pair,

\[ \min\sum_{i<j}d_{ij}x_{ij},\qquad \sum_{j<i}x_{ji}+\sum_{j>i}x_{ij}=1\quad\text{for each odd vertex }i. \]

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: This selects which odd vertices should be linked by duplicated paths. Pairing must be optimized jointly, since a locally cheap pair may leave expensive remaining pairs.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Each pair variable is binary.
  • For four odd vertices there are three complete pairings to compare.
  • This is a nonbipartite matching problem because the vertices are not separated into two assignment groups.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• The pairings AB/DE, AD/BE, and AE/BD cost 8, 7, and 8.
  • The optimum selects \(x_{AD}=x_{BE}=1\).

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: A minimum zero cover is a smallest set of matrix rows and columns covering all zero entries. Starting from a maximum independent zero assignment, mark all unassigned rows; repeatedly mark columns containing zeros in marked rows and rows assigned to marked columns. When marking stops, cover all marked columns and all unmarked rows.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: This procedure supplies the minimum line cover required by the Hungarian algorithm. A merely maximal partial assignment is insufficient; use a maximum one.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• For an \(n\times n\) matrix, \(n\) required covering lines indicate that a complete zero-cost assignment exists.
  • The cover size equals the size of the maximum independent zero assignment.
  • Rows and columns marked during the search are not the same as the final lines: the final rows are the unmarked ones.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• Week 5 practice 5(b) covers columns 1 and 2 and rows 2 and 3.
  • The ten-job example covers columns 1, 3, 4, 5, 8, 9 and rows 2, 10: eight lines.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: A mixed integer program (MIP) is an integer linear program containing both integer-restricted decision variables and continuous decision variables. Binary variables may be used for the discrete decisions.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: A single model can select a discrete action and determine continuous quantities conditional on it. The domain of each variable must therefore be stated individually.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• An LP relaxation removes integrality only from the restricted variables.
  • Continuous variables should not accidentally be forced to integer values.
  • Logical modelling often introduces auxiliary binary variables alongside quantities.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• \(x_1+x_2\le100+50y\) combines continuous production with a binary machine-purchase decision.
  • Continuous job start times can be combined with binary variables specifying which job comes first.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: A model parameter is a given numerical input to the optimization model. In the course's LP notation, parameters include objective coefficients \(c_j\), constraint coefficients \(a_{ij}\), and right-hand sides \(b_i\).

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: Parameters describe the circumstances under which decisions are made. A parameter may be an estimate even though the optimization treats its supplied value as fixed.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Changing parameters can change both the optimal decision and the optimal value.
  • Units must agree within an equation or inequality.
  • Sensitivity analysis investigates the effect of parameter changes.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• The coefficient \(3\) in \(3x_s+2x_t\) is profit per soldier.
  • The right-hand side \(100\) in \(2x_s+x_t\le100\) is available painting time.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: An optimization problem has multiple optimal solutions if distinct feasible decision vectors attain the same optimal objective value. In an LP, every convex combination of two optimal solutions is also optimal.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: Different decisions can be equally good under the stated objective. In a two-variable LP, this often appears as an objective line coinciding with a feasible boundary segment.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• A zero objective-row coefficient for a nonbasic variable in an optimal simplex tableau suggests an alternative optimum.
  • A positive feasible movement in that direction produces a distinct optimum; a zero-length degenerate pivot alone does not establish a different decision vector.
  • Additional requirements can select one point from an optimal segment.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• In the week 3 example, \((5,0)\) and \((3,4)\) both give \(4x_1+2x_2=20\).
  • In practice exercise 3 of week 3, imposing \(x_1=1\) selects \((1,9/2)\) from the optimal segment.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
For binary variables \(y_1,\ldots,y_k\), mutually exclusive decisions allow at most one variable to equal 1:

\[ \sum_{j=1}^ky_j\le1. \]

If one alternative must be chosen, use \(\sum_{j=1}^ky_j=1\) instead.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: The inequality permits choosing none, while the equality requires one choice. This distinction matters when translating phrases such as “at most one” and “exactly one.”

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Binarity is essential to interpret the sum as the number of yes decisions.
  • Exactly one implies at most one, but the reverse is false.
  • This restriction concerns decisions, not an either-or condition on continuous inequalities.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• \(W_{LA}+W_{SF}\le1\) permits at most one warehouse.
  • \(y_1+y_2+y_3=1\) selects exactly one allowed quantity value.

docs.text: The negative right-hand-side transformation multiplies an entire constraint by \(-1\) when its right-hand side is negative. An inequality reverses direction; an equality remains an equality.

  • A \(\le\) constraint can become a \(\ge\) constraint and consequently require a surplus and an artificial variable.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: A network consists of a set of vertices and edges connecting specified pairs of vertices. Vertices represent entities or locations; edges represent connections. Depending on the problem, edges may have directions and numerical values such as distances, costs, or capacities.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: A network separates the connection structure of a problem from its physical setting. The same mathematical representation can describe roads, communication links, or project activities.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Vertices are also commonly called nodes.
  • An edge may be used only in its specified direction in a directed network.
  • The meaning of an edge value depends on the problem: distance and capacity are different quantities.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• A road network connects cities by roads.
  • A project network represents activities and their precedence relations.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text: • No additional prerequisites.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
The newsvendor model chooses a single order quantity \(y\ge0\) before observing random demand \(D\). With unit purchase cost \(c\), selling price \(p>c\), and salvage value \(s<c\), define overage cost \(h=c-s\) and underage cost \(b=p-c\). Minimize

\[ G(y)=h\,\mathbb E[(y-D)^+]+b\,\mathbb E[(D-y)^+], \]

where \(u^+=\max\{u,0\}\) and the expectations are finite. Sales equal \(\min\{y,D\}\).

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: Too much stock leaves costly leftovers; too little misses profitable demand. The optimal quantity balances those risks through the demand distribution.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Salvage value can be zero or negative.
  • \(G(y)\) is convex; an optimum occurs where increasing stock stops reducing expected cost.
  • \(G(y)\) measures overage and underage loss, not gross purchasing expenditure.
  • The model is introduced in the week 5 overview and developed in week 6.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• A newsvendor chooses newspaper stock before daily demand is known.
  • A shop chooses seasonal dress inventory; a canteen prepares meals before evening demand.

docs.title: Proposition
docs.text:
For a fixed integer quantity \(y\) and fixed purchase cost \(c\) and salvage value \(s<c\), newsvendor price sensitivity finds selling prices \(p>c\) for which \(y\) remains optimal. The condition is

\[ F(y-1)\le\frac{p-c}{p-s}\le F(y). \]

The endpoints include ties with neighbouring quantities.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: A higher selling price raises the opportunity cost of unmet demand. The interval identifies how far the price can move before the chosen stock level stops being optimal.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• The condition is for being an optimum, not necessarily the smallest optimum.
  • At the lower boundary, \(y-1\) can tie with \(y\).
  • This analysis holds the demand distribution fixed, as the exercise does.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• The dress solution uses effective unit cost \(c=80+30=110\) and salvage \(s=50\).
  • For \(y=10\), \(F(9)=0.70\) and \(F(10)=0.85\) give \(250\le p\le450\).

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: A nonbasic variable is a variable outside the chosen basis and is set to zero when the associated basic solution is read. For \(m\) independent equations in \(n\) variables, there are \(n-m\) nonbasic variables.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: The method explores another basis by allowing a selected nonbasic variable to enter. The remaining basic values change to maintain the equations.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• A zero value alone does not establish that a variable is nonbasic; basic variables can also be zero.
  • The objective row expresses the effect of changing nonbasic variables.
  • The entering variable becomes basic after a pivot.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• The original decision variables are nonbasic at the initial slack-basis solution.
  • The final two-variable example sets \(s_1=s_2=0\) as its nonbasic variables.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: Nonconvex region modelling represents a union of allowed regions using binary variables that select which region's inequalities are enforced. The selected region must satisfy all its defining inequalities; common constraints remain active for every selection.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: A single system of continuous linear inequalities cannot describe separated allowed regions exactly. Binary switches can exclude the gaps between them.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Use one indicator per region and require exactly one selected region.
  • Relax every inequality belonging only to an unselected region with a valid \(M\).
  • Keep nonnegativity and shared boundaries outside the switches.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• The video region is \(x_1,x_2\ge0\), \(x_1+x_2\le3\), with either \(x_2\le1\) or \(x_2\ge2\).
  • The practice region additionally selects \(x_1\in[0,1]\), \([2,3]\), or \([4,5]\) under \(2x_1+5x_2\le20\).

docs.title: Nonnegativity Constraint
docs.text: This page presents the OR Modelling treatment. See also the treatment in Math IV: Multivariate Calculus. Mastery is recorded separately for each course context.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: A nonnegativity constraint requires a decision variable to satisfy \(x_j\ge0\). It excludes negative quantities while permitting zero. In the course's augmented simplex models, all original and auxiliary variables are nonnegative.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: Production and shipment quantities are normally nonnegative. Variables representing signed quantities need a different domain or a transformation.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Nonnegativity is a constraint, not an automatic consequence of a variable name.
  • With two nonnegative variables, feasible points lie in the first quadrant.
  • Nonnegative continuous variables may still take fractional values.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• \(x_s\ge0\) prevents negative soldier production.
  • \(s_1\ge0\) ensures that a slack variable represents unused rather than exceeded capacity.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
In the course's normal demand approximation, \(D\sim N(\mu,\sigma^2)\) with standard deviation \(\sigma>0\). If \(\Phi\) is the standard normal CDF, then

\[ F(y)=\Phi\!\left(\frac{y-\mu}{\sigma}\right),\qquad y^*=\max\!\left\{0,\mu+\sigma\Phi^{-1}(\beta)\right\}. \]

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: The mean sets the central demand level, while the standard deviation scales the distance to the required quantile. The examples use the normal model as an approximation to practical demand.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Use the standard deviation \(\sigma\), not the variance \(\sigma^2\), in the quantile formula.
  • The order quantity must satisfy \(y\ge0\). Use the normal quantile when it is nonnegative; otherwise the constrained optimum is \(y^*=0\).
  • The untruncated normal distribution allows negative values; the course examples retain that approximation.
  • The normal table gives rounded quantiles.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• Meal demand with \(\mu=100\), \(\sigma=20\) and \(\beta=0.6\) gives about 105.07.
  • For apples, \(\beta=1.8/2.2\approx0.8182\) and the source table approximation \(z\approx0.91\) gives 82.75 kilograms.
