docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
An objective coefficient range is an interval of values for one objective coefficient over which the current optimal basis remains optimal while all other data stay fixed. A report with coefficient \(c_j\), allowable decrease \(d_j\), and allowable increase \(u_j\) gives

\[ c_j-d_j\le c_j^{\mathrm{new}}\le c_j+u_j. \]

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: Within this interval the reported decision vector remains an optimum. Its objective value changes because the same quantity now earns a different unit return.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• For a change \(\Delta c_j\) within the range, the value changes by \(x_j^*\Delta c_j\).
  • At a range endpoint, additional optimal solutions may become available.
  • Separate reported ranges do not justify simultaneous changes automatically.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• The small-pipe profit coefficient 5 has allowable decrease 1 and increase 3, giving \([4,8]\).
  • Changing banana profit by \(-0.03\) with quantity 75 changes total profit by \(-2.25\).

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
The objective function assigns a numerical value to a decision vector. The model specifies whether this value should be maximized or minimized. In an LP it has the form

\[ z=c_1x_1+\cdots+c_nx_n, \]

where the \(c_j\) are given objective coefficients.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: The objective expresses the criterion used to compare feasible choices. Profit maximization and cost minimization are common, but the course also considers distance, time, and flow.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• An objective value is a number; an optimal solution is a vector of decisions.
  • In a profit objective, use revenues minus relevant costs.
  • The direction of optimization determines what constitutes an improvement.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• Giapetto maximizes \(z=3x_s+2x_t\).
  • The pig diet minimizes \(z=0.4x_A+0.8x_B\).

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
For a two-variable linear objective \(z=c_1x_1+c_2x_2\) with at least one nonzero coefficient, an objective line is the set of points giving a fixed value \(z=\bar z\). If \(c_2\ne0\), its slope-intercept form is

\[ x_2=-\frac{c_1}{c_2}x_1+\frac{\bar z}{c_2}. \]

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: Changing the objective value translates the line without changing its slope. This is the geometric basis of the graphical solution method.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• All constant-objective lines for a fixed objective are parallel.
  • If \(c_2<0\), a larger objective value lowers the vertical intercept.
  • When \(c_2=0\), the objective lines are vertical.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: Operations research (OR) uses mathematical models and analytical solution methods to support optimal, or sufficiently good, decisions in practical situations. The decision problem includes an objective, available choices, and restrictions on those choices.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: OR turns a practical planning question into a problem that can be analysed systematically. The usefulness of the answer depends on how well the model represents the situation.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Applications include production, transport, scheduling, maintenance, and inventory management.
  • An optimal model solution must still be checked against the practical situation.
  • Difficult problems may require a heuristic instead of an exact solution method.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• Lecture scheduling allocates teaching activities to times and rooms.
  • A warehouse chooses replenishment quantities and ordering times.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text: • No additional prerequisites.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
For a minimization problem with feasible set \(F\), a feasible vector \(x^*\) is an optimal solution if

\[ f(x^*)\le f(x)\quad\text{for every }x\in F. \]

For maximization the inequality is reversed. The number \(z^*=f(x^*)\) is the optimal value.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: Optimality compares a feasible decision with every allowed alternative. There may be several equally good decisions, even when the optimal value is fixed.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• A model may have no feasible solution or no finite optimum.
  • The optimal value and the vector attaining it are different objects.
  • An optimum is relative to the specified objective, constraints, and input data.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• The manufacturing example has \(x_1^*=2\), \(x_2^*=5\), and \(z^*=12\).
  • The practice LP with objective \(2x_1+2x_2\) has optimum \((3,4)\) and value 14.

docs.title: Proposition
docs.text:
Suppose an optimization problem has a finite optimal value \(z^*\). Let \(z_H\) be the value of a feasible solution and \(z_R\) the finite optimal value of a relaxation with the same objective. Then

\[ z_R\le z^*\le z_H\quad\text{for minimization}, \] \[ z_H\le z^*\le z_R\quad\text{for maximization}. \]

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: The two bounds enclose the unknown optimum. Their difference limits how much the current feasible solution could still be improved.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• For a minimization problem, \(z_H-z^*\le z_H-z_R\).
  • If the feasible and relaxed values coincide, the feasible solution is proven optimal.
  • A feasible solution of a relaxation alone is not generally an opposing bound; its optimal value is needed.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• The routing example gives \(202\le z^*\le214\), so the remaining improvement is at most 12 miles.
  • A 232-mile route is also an upper bound, but 214 is tighter.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
An optimization model specifies decision variables \(x\), an objective function \(f(x)\) to maximize or minimize, and constraints defining the allowed decisions. Writing the feasible set as \(F\), its form is

\[ \min_{x\in F} f(x)\qquad\text{or}\qquad\max_{x\in F} f(x). \]

The coefficients and other given inputs are model parameters.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: The model states what can be chosen, what counts as better, and which choices are allowed. Solving it selects the best allowed decision according to the chosen objective.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• The objective and constraints need not be linear in a general OR model.
  • Some simple models have a closed-form solution; many require an algorithm.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• For \(\min\{x^2+bx+c:x\ge d\}\), the optimum is \(x^*=\max\{-b/2,d\}\).
  • Giapetto chooses soldier and train production to maximize profit under labour limits.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: The OR study cycle moves from a real situation to an assumed representation of it, then to a mathematical model, a solution, validation, and implementation. Validation checks whether the model and its solution adequately represent the practical decision problem.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: A mathematically correct answer can be unsuitable if the modelling assumptions omit an essential feature. Model building and validation therefore belong to the same decision process.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Additional detail may improve realism but also increase data requirements and solution difficulty.
  • The required data must be available or obtainable.
  • Validation can reveal a need to revise assumptions before implementation.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• A route model may initially approximate travel distances by straight lines.
  • Road layout and time-dependent traffic may require a more detailed route model.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
In the constant-demand EOQ setting, the ordering cycle length \(t_0\) is the time between consecutive orders. If each order contains \(y\) units and demand occurs at rate \(D>0\), then

\[ t_0=\frac{y}{D}. \]

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: A batch supports exactly one cycle's demand in the repeating policy. The same identity holds with planned backorders because each batch still covers total demand over a cycle.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Orders per unit time equal \(D/y\).
  • Cycle length and lead time are different: one measures spacing of orders, the other order-to-receipt delay.
  • Convert demand and time consistently.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• Ordering 22 phones at demand two per day gives an 11-day cycle.
  • Ordering 6,000 pencils at demand 100 per day gives a 60-day cycle.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
The overage cost in the newsvendor model is the net loss on one unit ordered but not sold at its regular price:

\[ h=c-s>0, \]

where \(c\) is its unit cost and \(s\) its salvage value. Total expected overage cost at order quantity \(y\) is \(h\mathbb E[(y-D)^+]\).

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: The salvage recovery offsets part of the cost of excess stock. A negative salvage value represents an additional disposal cost.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Only leftover units incur overage loss.
  • Increasing salvage value lowers overage cost.
  • This is a single-period per-unit loss, whereas EOQ holding cost is charged per unit per unit time.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• Newspapers costing 3.50 and salvaged for 1.50 have \(h=2\).
  • Meals costing 2.20 with zero salvage have \(h=2.20\).

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
For three binary decisions \(y_1,y_2,y_3\), requiring an even number of yes decisions is equivalent to

\[ y_1+y_2+y_3=2x,\qquad x\in\{0,1\}. \]

The sum can therefore be 0 or 2, the only even values possible for three binary decisions.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: An auxiliary variable encodes the allowed count. The equality imposes a logical restriction using only linear expressions.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• When \(x=0\), all three decisions are no.
  • When \(x=1\), exactly two decisions are yes.
  • Allowing \(x\) to be continuous would remove the parity restriction.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• \((y_1,y_2,y_3)=(1,1,0)\) is allowed with \(x=1\).
  • \((1,1,1)\) is excluded because it would require \(x=3/2\).

docs.title: Path
docs.text: This page presents the OR Modelling treatment. See also the treatment in Math III: Analysis. Mastery is recorded separately for each course context.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: In the course's terminology, a path is a sequence of distinct edges connecting a starting vertex to an ending vertex, with consecutive edges joined through their shared vertices. For directed edges, traversal respects their directions.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: A path describes a connected route through a network. The course definition requires distinct edges; it does not add a requirement that all visited vertices be distinct.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• The length of a weighted path is the sum of the lengths of the traversed edges.
  • The course convention corresponds to what some texts call a trail.
  • A path whose first and last vertices coincide is called a cycle or tour in the terminology video.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• The highlighted introduction example follows \(A-D-C-E-G\).
  • The shortest-path example gives \(S-B-A-D-E-T\) with length 12.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
For a real number \(u\), its positive part is

\[ u^+=\max\{u,0\}=\begin{cases}u,&u\ge0,\\0,&u<0.\end{cases} \]

In the newsvendor model, \((y-D)^+\) is leftover stock and \((D-y)^+\) is unmet demand.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: The operator keeps a positive excess and replaces a negative excess with zero. It allows the two different demand cases to be expressed in a single formula.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Both leftover and shortage quantities are nonnegative.
  • For a fixed realized demand, at least one of them is zero.
  • For discrete demand, expectations are computed by probability-weighting the positive parts for every demand outcome.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• If \(y=10\) and \(D=7\), leftovers are 3 and unmet demand is zero.
  • If \(y=10\) and \(D=12\), leftovers are zero and unmet demand is 2.

docs.title: Proposition
docs.text:
Let \(y_m=\sqrt{2KD/h}\) and \(TCU_j(y)=Dc_j+KD/y+hy/2\), with \(c_1>c_2\). The price-break indifference quantity \(Q>y_m\) solves

\[ TCU_2(Q)=TCU_1(y_m), \]

or equivalently

\[ Q^2+\frac{2(c_2D-TCU_1(y_m))}{h}Q+\frac{2KD}{h}=0. \]

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: The larger root marks how far the qualifying order threshold can exceed the ordinary EOQ before extra holding costs outweigh the purchasing discount.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• With the worked-example convention that \(q\) qualifies, a threshold \(y_m<q<Q\) favours ordering \(q\).
  • For \(q>Q\), retain \(y_m\); for \(q<y_m\), \(y_m\) already receives the discount.
  • At \(q=Q\), the two candidates tie.
  • Directly comparing candidate costs avoids solving for \(Q\).

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• The snack-bar exercise gives \(Q\approx89.07\) kilograms; its threshold 100 is too high.
  • For the phone example, \(Q\approx39.86\), and threshold 35 lies between \(y_m=22\) and \(Q\).

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
A production-inventory model chooses production \(P_t\) and end-of-period stock \(I_t\) to meet known demands \(d_t\) across periods. With given initial stock \(I_0\), unit production costs \(c_t\), and end-of-period holding costs \(h_t\), the course problem is represented by

\[ \min\sum_{t=1}^T(c_tP_t+h_tI_t),\qquad I_{t-1}+P_t-d_t=I_t,\qquad P_t,I_t\ge0. \]

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: Production in a cheaper month may be stored for a later month. The inventory balance ensures that every unit sold comes from current production or previously held stock.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Nonnegative inventory rules out shortages.
  • The PDF charges 8 per window per month on end-of-month inventory.
  • The six-month exercise does not specify initial stock; taking \(I_0=0\) is an explicit modelling assumption.
  • With positive production and holding costs and no required final stock, surplus final inventory is unnecessary.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• Month 1 requires 100 windows; producing 120 from zero stock leaves 20.
  • Producing a month-3 window in month 2 costs 45 plus 8 holding, compared with 55 in month 3.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: The course's project longest path model uses a directed acyclic activity network with start \(S\) and finish \(T\). Each edge has an activity duration; an outgoing activity may start only after all activities entering its starting vertex finish. Under these precedence rules and without additional resource restrictions, project duration is the length of a longest \(S\)-to-\(T\) path.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: The longest chain of dependent activities determines the earliest possible project completion. The exercise models this chain with binary edge-selection variables.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Maximize the sum of selected activity durations.
  • Use one unit of source-to-sink binary flow with balance at intermediate vertices.
  • Acyclicity matters: in a general cyclic network, flow balance alone could allow unrelated selected cycles.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• In the exercise, \(S-A-D-F-T\) has duration \(5+2+6+4=17\).
  • \(S-B-D-F-T\) has duration \(3+3+6+4=16\).

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
The project selection model chooses complete projects under resource budgets. Let \(y_j=1\) if project \(j\) is selected, \(r_j\) be its return, \(a_{tj}\) its expenditure in year \(t\), and \(B_t\) that year's budget. Then

\[ \max\sum_jr_jy_j,\qquad\sum_ja_{tj}y_j\le B_t\ \text{for every }t,\qquad y_j\in\{0,1\}. \]

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: A project uses resources in each relevant year and contributes its full return only when selected. Fractional project funding is excluded in this model.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• A separate budget constraint is needed for each year.
  • The later development-project example uses one capital budget.
  • Relaxing a binary variable to a fraction supplies a bound but not an implementable partial project.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• The week 2 exercise has five projects and a budget of 25 in each of three years.
  • The development-project example has capital 20 and an optimal return of 3.4 from projects 1, 3, and 4.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: The purchasing cost is the amount paid per inventory unit, multiplied by the quantity purchased. If its constant unit price is \(c\) and all demand is met at constant rate \(D\), the long-run purchasing cost rate is \(cD\).

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: A constant unit price adds the same cost rate to every feasible EOQ policy. Quantity discounts change this because the chosen order size affects the unit price.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• A constant \(cD\) can be omitted when finding the classical EOQ, but retained when reporting full costs.
  • All-unit price breaks require comparing purchasing cost as well as setup and holding costs.
  • Purchasing cost is different from the fixed cost of initiating an order.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• At two phones per day and price 170, purchasing costs are 340 per day.
  • A discounted unit price of 160 reduces that rate to 320 when the order qualifies.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: A pure integer program is an integer linear program in which every decision variable is restricted to integer values. Nonnegativity, upper bounds, and other restrictions remain separate model constraints.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: This model type fits decisions consisting entirely of counts. A linear objective alone does not permit fractional values once integrality has been imposed.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• If there are \(n\) variables, each of the \(n\) original decision variables is integer.
  • Binary integer programs are a special case with the additional bounds 0 and 1.
  • Dropping integrality gives its LP relaxation.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• The bus-scheduling model counts buses beginning each shift.
  • The integer work-order model counts tow bars and stabilizer bars.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: In the course's maximization sensitivity report, the reduced cost of a currently zero-valued variable is the marginal change in the objective when that variable is increased and the other variables adjust through the current basis. If the tableau row is \(z+q_jx_j+\cdots=z_0\), the corresponding reduced cost is \(-q_j\).

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: The number measures the opportunity cost of forcing an unused activity into the plan. A negative value means that a small forced increase reduces profit.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Do not confuse a reported reduced cost with the original objective coefficient.
  • The sign is opposite to the coefficient in the course maximization tableau.
  • The interpretation is local and relies on a feasible basis adjustment.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• Sheets have reported reduced cost -3.3 in the pipes-and-sheets example.
  • Their profit coefficient is 4 and its allowable increase is 3.3 before the current optimal basis can cease to be optimal.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: A relaxation retains a problem's objective and removes or weakens constraints to obtain an easier problem. If \(F\) and \(F_R\) are the original and relaxed feasible sets, then \(F\subseteq F_R\).

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: The larger feasible set gives a benchmark that may be unattainable in the original problem. Its optimum helps assess a feasible solution obtained by another method.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• For minimization, the relaxed optimum is no greater than the original optimum; for maximization, it is no smaller.
  • A relaxed optimum that is also feasible for the original problem is optimal for the original problem.
  • An infeasible relaxed optimizer need not have a strictly better value; equality can occur.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• Ignore the 100-mile refuelling limit in the routing example.
  • Remove integrality restrictions from an integer program while keeping its other constraints.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: For an original directed edge \(i\to j\) with capacity \(c_{ij}\) and assigned flow \(x_{ij}\), its residual capacities are \(c_{ij}-x_{ij}\) in the forward direction and \(x_{ij}\) in the reverse direction. The residual network records these possibilities for increasing or cancelling current flow.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: Reverse residual movement revises an earlier flow assignment. It is essential because a good final routing may require undoing part of an initially chosen path.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• The course draws a connection with two directional residual labels; it must not be interpreted as equal capacity in both directions.
  • Only directions with positive residual capacity can be used by an augmenting path.
  • A forward augmentation decreases forward residual capacity and increases reverse residual capacity by the same amount.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• Capacity 6 and flow 2 on A-B give residual capacities 4 forward and 2 backward.
  • Cancelling one unit changes those residual capacities to 5 forward and 1 backward.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: A right-hand-side sensitivity range is the interval for one constraint's right-hand side over which the current optimal basis remains feasible and optimal, with other parameters fixed. Within this range, its shadow price gives the exact linear change in optimal value.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: The same basis can represent different production quantities as a resource changes. Thus a valid shadow price does not imply an unchanged solution vector.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Use \(b_i-d_i\le b_i^{\mathrm{new}}\le b_i+u_i\) from the report.
  • A slack resource can often be reduced by its unused amount without affecting the current decision.
  • A change beyond the range cannot generally be valued by multiplying the full change by the old shadow price.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• The metal RHS is 960, with allowable increase 240 and decrease 360; the range is 600 to 1,200.
  • Milk availability can fall from 200 to 180 in the ice-cream example without changing its plan or value.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: A rounding heuristic solves an integer program's LP relaxation and converts fractional variable values to nearby integers. The rounded vector is only a candidate: all original constraints must be checked before accepting it as a feasible solution.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: Rounding is simple and may be useful when quantities are large. Coupled constraints can make the nearest rounded decisions infeasible or substantially worse than an integer optimum.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Rounding up can violate resource upper bounds.
  • Rounding down can violate minimum requirements or equalities.
  • Even a feasible rounded solution need not be optimal.
  • The video's numerical rounding illustration has inconsistent written constraints and a plotted feasible region; its claimed optimum is not used here.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• Rounding \((2.6,1.6)\) upward to \((3,2)\) violates \(4x_1+x_2\le12\) because the left-hand side is 14.
  • The nearby vector \((2,2)\) satisfies that capacity inequality, but its objective value alone does not prove optimality.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: Sensitivity analysis examines how changes in model parameters affect an LP's optimal solution and optimal value. The course studies changes to objective coefficients and resource right-hand sides using final simplex tableaux and Excel sensitivity reports.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: Inputs may be estimates, and additional resources may be purchasable. Sensitivity information helps assess whether the current decision remains suitable after an input changes.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• The reported allowable ranges apply to one parameter change at a time.
  • Changing an objective coefficient can preserve the solution vector while changing profit.
  • Changing a right-hand side can change the solution vector even while the same basis and shadow prices remain valid.
  • Outside a valid range, reoptimization may be needed.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• A change in banana ice-cream profit from 0.95 to 0.92 leaves the given production plan optimal.
  • Losing three gallons of cream changes the ice-cream quantities and reduces optimal profit by 3.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
A setup cost is a fixed charge incurred whenever an order is placed, regardless of the order quantity. In the EOQ model it is denoted by \(K\). With demand rate \(D\) and batch size \(y\), its average rate is

\[ \frac{K}{y/D}=\frac{KD}{y}. \]

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: Larger orders spread one fixed charge over more units and reduce ordering frequency. This saving must be balanced against extra holding cost.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• The charge is per order, not per inventory unit.
  • A period with no order incurs no setup in the dynamic lot-size model.
  • Increasing \(K\) increases the classical optimal order size.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• The phone example has setup cost 605 per order.
  • The snack bar pays 50 per order in addition to a per-kilogram purchase price.

docs.title: Shadow Price
docs.text: This page presents the OR Modelling treatment. See also the treatment in Math IV: Multivariate Calculus. Mastery is recorded separately for each course context.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
The shadow price \(y_i^*\) of resource \(i\) is the rate of change of the optimal objective value when its right-hand side \(b_i\) increases slightly. Within the applicable sensitivity range,

\[ z^*(b_i+\Delta)=z^*(b_i)+y_i^*\Delta. \]

For the course's maximization LPs with \(\le\) resource constraints, it equals the coefficient of slack \(s_i\) in the final objective row.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: A shadow price measures the marginal value of more resource under the current model. It can be compared with the cost of acquiring that resource.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• The rate is valid only over its allowable right-hand-side range.
  • An unused resource has zero marginal value in the illustrated resource-allocation setting.
  • A binding constraint does not by itself guarantee a positive shadow price.
  • The tableau sign interpretation must be adjusted if the model or objective convention changes.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• Malt and barley have shadow prices 1, while hops has shadow price 0 in the beer-and-ale example.
  • In the drinks example, an additional unit of sugar is worth 0.5 within the valid range.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
A shortage cost penalizes unmet demand. In the EOQ model with planned shortages, customers wait for replenishment and the parameter \(p\) charges each outstanding unit per unit of waiting time. With maximum backlog \(y-s\), the average shortage cost rate is

\[ p\frac{(y-s)^2}{2y}. \]

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: The penalty permits a trade-off between holding stock and making customers wait. This time-based backlog penalty differs from the single-period lost-margin measure in the newsvendor model.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• The planned-shortage model assumes demand is backordered and later filled.
  • Use the same time unit for \(p\), \(h\), and \(D\).
  • In the newsvendor notation, \(p\) instead denotes selling price; symbols must be interpreted within their model.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• The phone shop compensates waiting customers by 6 per phone per day.
  • The EOQ practice exercise permits planned shortages at 10 per unit per week.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
For nonnegative edge lengths, the course's shortest path algorithm sets \(d(s)=0\) and \(U=\{s\}\). Repeatedly choose an edge \(u-v\) with \(u\in U\), \(v\notin U\) minimizing

\[ d(u)+\ell_{uv}. \]

Set \(d(v)\) equal to this value, record predecessor \(u\), and add \(v\) to \(U\). Stop when the destination is added, or continue to obtain distances to all vertices.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: Vertices enter the settled set in order of their shortest distance from the origin. Predecessors recover the actual route after the distance has been computed.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Compare complete distances from the origin, not just individual edge lengths.
  • Ties can be broken arbitrarily when one shortest path is sufficient.
  • Backtrack from the destination through predecessors and reverse the sequence.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• The worked labels are \(d(B)=2\), \(d(A)=3\), \(d(D)=6\), \(d(C)=7\), \(d(E)=8\), \(d(T)=12\).
  • The predecessor chain \(T,E,D,A,B,S\) recovers the route of length 12.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
A shortest path binary formulation assigns \(x_{ij}=1\) if a directed edge is selected. For the undirected course network, create both directed orientations of each edge. With origin \(s\), destination \(t\), and edge lengths \(\ell_{ij}\), use

\[ \min\sum_{(i,j)}\ell_{ij}x_{ij},\qquad \sum_jx_{ij}-\sum_jx_{ji}=\begin{cases}1,&i=s,\\-1,&i=t,\\0,&\text{otherwise},\end{cases} \qquad x_{ij}\in\{0,1\}. \]

Sums include only existing directed orientations.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: A unit of selected flow connects the origin to the destination. The objective chooses its least-cost route. This is the formulation derived from the video exercise.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• With strictly positive lengths as in the exercise, an optimum contains no unnecessary cycle.
  • If zero-cost edges are allowed, an optimal binary solution may contain removable zero-cost cycles.
  • The balances alone must not be claimed to prohibit every possible cycle.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• The route S-B-A-D-E-T selects its five directed edges and has cost 12.
  • At A on that route, \(x_{BA}=x_{AD}=1\) balances one incoming and one outgoing edge.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: The course's shortest path problem is defined on a connected undirected network with nonnegative edge lengths, a specified origin, and a specified destination. It asks for a path between those vertices whose sum of edge lengths is minimum.

docs.title: Interpretation

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
The Silver-Meal heuristic chooses consecutive periods to cover with each order when the variable unit ordering cost is constant and identical across periods. For an order in period \(i\) covering through \(t\), define

\[ TC(i,t)=K_i+\sum_{j=i+1}^tD_j\sum_{k=i}^{j-1}h_k,\qquad TCU(i,t)=\frac{TC(i,t)}{t-i+1}. \]

Starting at the first uncovered period, extend coverage while average cost decreases, select the first local minimum, order \(\sum_{j=i}^{t^*}D_j\), and restart at \(i=t^*+1\). Stop at the horizon; on a flat tie, selecting the first local minimum is the convention used here.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: The rule compares setup-plus-holding cost per covered period. It is simpler than full dynamic programming but does not guarantee the optimum.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Purchasing cost is omitted from the comparisons because the common unit price gives the same total for every complete demand-covering policy.
  • Add that constant purchasing cost when reporting a total that includes it.
  • At the start or end of the horizon, use only available neighbouring average-cost comparisons.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• The six-period video orders \((32,0,0,20,13,25)\), with setup and holding cost 122.
  • Week 6 practice 4 orders \((9,22,0,0)\) and costs 169 including purchases; the exact DP cost is 152.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: The simplex method solves an LP by moving between basic feasible solutions through basis exchanges. In the course's maximization tableau convention, start with a feasible basis, test the objective row, select an improving entering variable, apply the minimum-ratio test to select a leaving variable, pivot, and repeat until optimality or unboundedness is established.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: Simplex uses the structure of an LP instead of enumerating all possible corners. Algebraic row operations implement movement between feasible corners.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• The elementary starting form uses equality constraints, nonnegative right-hand sides, and nonnegative variables.
  • A slack basis starts the method for \(\le\) constraints with nonnegative right-hand sides.
  • The two-phase method supplies a feasible basis when one is not immediately available.
  • Degenerate pivots can change the basis without moving the decision vector.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• The two-variable example visits \((0,0)\), \((5,0)\), and \((3,4)\), with values 0, 15, and 17.
  • The three-variable example ends at \((0,5,4)\) with value 33.

docs.title: Proposition
docs.text: For a maximization LP with a feasible canonical tableau written as \(z+\sum_{j\in N}q_jx_j=z_0\), if \(q_j\ge0\) for every nonbasic variable, the current basic feasible solution is optimal. Here \(N\) is the nonbasic index set and every variable is nonnegative.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: Every allowed increase of a nonbasic variable then leaves the objective unchanged or reduces it. The tableau therefore certifies that the current value cannot be exceeded.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• The sign test depends on the course objective-row convention.
  • Feasibility and canonical form are required before applying the test.
  • A negative coefficient calls for further simplex analysis; degeneracy means it does not alone prove that a strictly better feasible vector exists.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• \(z+(7/5)s_1+(1/5)s_2=17\) proves \(z\le17\).
  • \(z-(1/2)x_2+(3/2)s_1=15\) still has a negative coefficient to investigate.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: A simplex pivot replaces the leaving basic variable with the entering variable. Divide the selected pivot row by the nonzero pivot element, then subtract appropriate multiples of that normalized row from every other row, including the objective row, so that the pivot column is a unit column.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: These Gauss-Jordan operations preserve the equations while expressing them in terms of a new basis. The updated tableau can be used for the next iteration.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• The pivot element is the intersection of the entering column and leaving row.
  • Update all coefficients and the right-hand side during each row operation.
  • Update the basic-variable label as well as the numerical entries.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• In the initial example, divide \(2x_1+x_2+s_1=10\) by 2.
  • Add three times that normalized row to \(z-3x_1-2x_2=0\) to eliminate \(x_1\) from the objective row.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
A simplex tableau records the variable coefficients, right-hand sides, and basic-variable labels of the current simplex equations. In the course convention, the first row writes the objective as

\[ z+\sum_jq_jx_j=z_0. \]

In proper form, basic-variable columns form unit columns and have zero objective-row coefficients.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: The tableau stores the equations compactly so that each pivot can be performed through row operations. It also makes the current solution and improvement directions easy to read.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Set nonbasic variables to zero and read basic values from the solution column.
  • The objective-row right-hand side is the current objective value.
  • A negative nonbasic coefficient indicates an improving direction for maximization.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• \(z-3x_1-2x_2=0\) gives initial objective coefficients \(-3,-2\).
  • The final main-example row is \(z+(7/5)s_1+(1/5)s_2=17\).

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
For a constraint \(\sum_ja_{ij}x_j\le b_i\), a slack variable \(s_i\) converts it into

\[ \sum_ja_{ij}x_j+s_i=b_i,\qquad s_i\ge0. \]

Thus \(s_i=b_i-\sum_ja_{ij}x_j\) measures the unused allowance in the inequality.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: The equality records both the amount used and the amount left over. This lets simplex work with equalities while preserving the original feasible choices.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• A zero slack means the constraint is binding at that solution.
  • The introduced slack has zero coefficient in the original objective.
  • With nonnegative right-hand sides, slack variables can form an initial feasible basis.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• \(2x_1+x_2\le10\) becomes \(2x_1+x_2+s_1=10\).
  • At \((x_1,x_2)=(3,4)\) this slack equals zero.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: A spanning tree of a connected undirected network contains every original vertex and a subset of its edges that forms a tree. If the network has \(n\) vertices, every spanning tree has \(n-1\) edges.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: All locations remain connected, but enough edges are removed to eliminate every cycle. Different edge selections may produce different spanning trees.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Spanning refers to including all vertices, not all edges.
  • Adding another original edge to a spanning tree creates a cycle.
  • The minimum spanning tree problem compares the total lengths of spanning trees.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• A network with seven vertices needs six edges in each spanning tree.
  • The Euclidean example selects \(1-7\), \(1-4\), \(4-3\), \(3-6\), \(6-2\), and \(6-5\).

docs.title: Standard Normal Distribution
docs.text: This page presents the OR Modelling treatment. See also the treatment in Probability Theory for EOR. Mastery is recorded separately for each course context.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: The standard normal distribution is the normal distribution with mean 0 and variance 1. Its CDF is denoted by \(\Phi(z)=P(Z\le z)\). For \(D\sim N(\mu,\sigma^2)\), the standardized variable \(Z=(D-\mu)/\sigma\) is standard normal.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: The supplied table converts a standard score into a cumulative probability. For inventory decisions, use it in reverse to find the score corresponding to the critical ratio.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• The table entries are left-tail probabilities.
  • A normal demand quantile is obtained by transforming back with \(y=\mu+\sigma z\).
  • Table rounding should be reflected in the reported precision.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• The supplied table gives \(\Phi(0.25)=0.5987\) and \(\Phi(0.26)=0.6026\), bracketing 0.6.
  • It gives \(\Phi(0.91)=0.8186\), close to the apple critical ratio.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
A surplus variable \(S_i\ge0\) transforms a lower-bound constraint into an equality:

\[ \sum_ja_{ij}x_j\ge b_i \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad \sum_ja_{ij}x_j-S_i=b_i,\quad S_i\ge0. \]

It measures the excess of the left-hand side over the required minimum.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: A surplus is subtracted because it represents an amount above the minimum requirement. This differs from the added slack used for an upper-bound constraint.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• The course uses capital \(S_i\) for surplus and lower-case \(s_i\) for slack.
  • A surplus variable alone generally does not produce an initial feasible slack-style basis.
  • An artificial variable may be added for the first simplex phase.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• \(2x_1+x_2\ge4\) becomes \(2x_1+x_2-S_1=4\).
  • At \((x_1,x_2)=(3,0)\), this surplus is 2.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
In task quota assignment, each task is assigned to exactly one agent and agent \(i\) must receive exactly \(q_i\) tasks. For binary assignment variables \(x_{ij}\) and times or costs \(c_{ij}\), the model is

\[ \min\sum_i\sum_jc_{ij}x_{ij},\qquad \sum_ix_{ij}=1,\qquad\sum_jx_{ij}=q_i,\qquad x_{ij}\in\{0,1\}. \]

The quotas sum to the number of tasks.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: Quotas impose a workload distribution while the objective minimizes the combined cost or time. The household exercise assigns two tasks to each person.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• In the later Hungarian-method treatment, duplicate each agent row \(q_i\) times to represent its available task slots.
  • Each task remains assigned exactly once.
  • Minimizing summed execution time is different from minimizing the latest completion time.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• Eve receives marketing and dishwashing; Steven receives cooking and laundry, totalling 18.4 hours.
  • In week 5 practice 3, two identical rows per machine represent its two required jobs.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
The transportation problem chooses shipments \(x_{ij}\ge0\) from plants \(i\) to distribution centres \(j\) to minimize total transport cost. With unit costs \(c_{ij}\), plant capacities \(s_i\), and required deliveries \(d_j\), a formulation is

\[ \min\sum_i\sum_j c_{ij}x_{ij},\qquad \sum_jx_{ij}\le s_i\ \text{for every }i,\qquad \sum_ix_{ij}=d_j\ \text{for every }j. \]

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: Each shipment consumes origin capacity and contributes to one destination's demand. The course example has more total production capacity than required demand, so unused capacity is permitted.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• The decision variables are shipment quantities on routes.
  • Plant capacities are upper bounds rather than mandatory production amounts.
  • For the example with positive transport costs, allowing deliveries above demand cannot improve the optimum.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• The plants have capacities 5,000, 6,000, and 2,500; destination demands total 12,000.
  • The illustrated optimum has transport cost 35,000.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: A tree is a connected undirected network containing no cycles. In the course, a tree can be formed by choosing a subset of the vertices and edges of a larger network.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: A tree connects its selected vertices without redundant loops. This makes it the basic structure for minimum-cost connection problems.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• A finite tree with \(n\) vertices has \(n-1\) edges.
  • There is exactly one path between any two distinct vertices of a tree.
  • A spanning tree additionally includes every vertex of the original network.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• The edges A-B and B-C form a tree on three vertices.
  • A tree on 77 vertices has 76 edges, as reinforced by the final-week statements exercise.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
The two-phase method initializes and solves an LP using artificial variables \(R_i\ge0\). Phase I maximizes

\[ r=-\sum_iR_i \]

subject to the augmented constraints. If its optimum is negative, the original LP is infeasible. If its optimum is zero, restore the original objective, remove artificial variables from the working model, put the objective row in canonical form for the resulting feasible basis, and apply simplex in Phase II.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: The first phase finds a point satisfying the original constraints. The second phase improves the objective from that feasible starting point.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Eliminate basic artificial variables from the initial phase-I objective row before pivoting.
  • The phase-I objective can never exceed zero.
  • A zero-valued artificial variable still in the basis needs basis cleanup before its column is removed; the supplied worked example avoids this case.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• For \(x_1+x_2\le10\) and \(2x_1+3x_2=25\), Phase I finds \((0,25/3)\).
  • Phase II for objective \(3x_1+2x_2\) reaches \((5,5)\) and value 25.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: A maximization LP has an unbounded objective if feasible solutions attain objective values greater than any prescribed finite bound. For minimization, feasible values can be arbitrarily negative. In a feasible maximization tableau, an improving entering column with no strictly positive constraint coefficient certifies unboundedness.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: There is no finite best value: a feasible improvement can continue indefinitely. In a practical model, this can point to a missing restriction.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• An unbounded feasible region can still have a finite optimum for a particular objective.
  • The simplex certificate requires an improving objective coefficient and an unrestricted feasible increase together.
  • Do not confuse unboundedness with infeasibility.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• In week 2 practice 1(c), \(x_1=0\), \(x_2=t\ge0\) satisfies \(3x_1-2x_2\le8\) and gives \(z=t\).
  • In the week 3 example, \(x_1=x_2=t\) is feasible and yields \(2x_1+x_2=3t\).

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
The underage cost in the newsvendor model is the foregone margin on one unit of demand that cannot be served:

\[ b=p-c>0, \]

where \(p\) is selling price and \(c\) is unit cost. Expected underage cost is \(b\mathbb E[(D-y)^+]\).

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: A stockout loses the opportunity to earn the margin, rather than the full selling price. The purchase cost that would have been paid must be subtracted.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Only demand above the available quantity contributes to underage loss.
  • Increasing selling price increases underage cost when unit cost is fixed.
  • The course assumes no additional per-unit stockout penalty beyond the lost margin.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• Newspapers sold for 5 and purchased for 3.50 have \(b=1.50\).
  • Meals sold for 5.50 and costing 2.20 have \(b=3.30\).

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: An undirected network is a network in which edges have no prescribed orientation. An edge joining vertices \(i\) and \(j\) may be traversed in either direction.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: This represents connections whose availability is symmetric. The course uses undirected networks for spanning trees, Euler tours, the Chinese postman problem, and shortest paths.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• The pair \(i-j\) describes one undirected connection.
  • A path can traverse its edges in either direction.
  • Connectedness requires a path between every pair of vertices.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• A two-way road connects two towns.
  • A cable connecting two sites can be selected as part of a spanning tree.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
The course's uniform demand model assumes \(D\) is uniformly distributed on a known interval \([a,u]\), with \(a<u\). Its CDF inside the interval is \(F(y)=(y-a)/(u-a)\), with values 0 below \(a\) and 1 above \(u\). Thus the continuous newsvendor quantity is

\[ y^*=a+(u-a)\beta. \]

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: Demand is spread uniformly across the stated interval. The relevant inventory calculation is a linear interpolation to the critical quantile.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• The distribution is used as an application of probability prerequisites; the course does not develop a general distribution theory.
  • For \(\beta=1/2\), the quantity is the midpoint.
  • The quantile lies within the demand interval.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• For meal demand on \([80,120]\) and \(\beta=0.6\), order 104.
  • For that same interval, \(F(100)=0.5\) and \(F(104)=0.6\).

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
An unrestricted variable \(x_j\) can be replaced everywhere by the difference of two nonnegative variables:

\[ x_j=x_j^+-x_j^-,\qquad x_j^+,x_j^-\ge0. \]

If \(x_j\le0\) is required, use \(x_j=-x_j^-\) with \(x_j^-\ge0\) instead.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: The substitution allows simplex to use nonnegative variables while preserving the original variable's ability to take negative values. Recover the original decision after solving.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Apply the substitution to both the objective and every constraint.
  • The difference representation is not unique; it is not necessary to impose a nonlinear restriction preventing both parts from being positive.
  • The optimal original variable is the difference of the computed parts.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• \(x_2^+=0\) and \(x_2^-=10\) give \(x_2=-10\).
  • The other-model-forms exercise transforms its nonpositive \(x_1\) as \(-x_1^-\).

docs.text: The course's vehicle routing problem asks for a minimum-distance route plan that starts at a depot, visits eight required locations, and returns to the depot. The vehicle can travel at most 100 miles between refuelling stops, and refuelling is possible only at the depot.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: The degree of a vertex in the undirected networks considered in the course is the number of edges incident to it. Parallel edges are counted separately. A vertex has even or odd degree according to the parity of that count.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: Degree counts how many edge ends meet at a vertex. Its parity determines whether a closed traversal can use every incident edge exactly once.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• At a vertex on an Euler tour, arrivals and departures pair the incident edges.
  • Duplicating a path reverses degree parity at its endpoints and preserves it at internal vertices.
  • Odd-degree vertices are the vertices matched in the Chinese postman construction.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• In the introduction network, A has degree 3 and C has degree 5.
  • In the five-vertex Chinese postman example, A, B, D, and E are odd-degree vertices.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
The Weibull demand distribution in the exercise has shape \(k>0\), scale \(\lambda>0\), and nonnegative support. For \(x\ge0\),

\[ F(x)=1-e^{-(x/\lambda)^k},\qquad f(x)=\frac{k}{\lambda}\left(\frac{x}{\lambda}\right)^{k-1}e^{-(x/\lambda)^k}. \]

For the newsvendor critical ratio \(0<\beta<1\), inversion gives

\[ y^*=\lambda[-\ln(1-\beta)]^{1/k}. \]

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: The exercise supplies the density and CDF, so the required task is to solve the CDF equation at the cost-based probability. No broader Weibull theory is needed for this application.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Use the given shape and scale parametrization.
  • The CDF is zero below zero.
  • The scale parameter has the same units as demand.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• Bananas have \(k=2\), \(\lambda=50\), \(b=1.3\), \(h=0.2\), so \(\beta=13/15\).
  • The optimum is \(50\sqrt{-\ln(2/15)}\approx70.97\) kilograms.

docs.title: Proposition
docs.text:
In the course's uncapacitated dynamic lot-size special case, assume no shortages or lead time, nonincreasing marginal production and holding costs, and zero initial inventory. There exists an optimal policy with

\[ y_ix_i=0\qquad(i=1,\ldots,n). \]

Thus a positive order is placed only when starting stock is zero, and it covers the exact demand of one or more consecutive periods.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: The property reduces the number of order quantities that need to be examined. Candidate orders are cumulative demands, rather than every integer quantity.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• The statement guarantees an optimal policy of this form; it need not describe every tied optimum.
  • The special case is not justified for increasing marginal ordering costs, as in the general example.
  • The course handles positive initial stock by subtracting it from successive demands until exhausted.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• In the four-period example, initial stock 15 reduces first-period demand from 76 to 61.
  • The optimal orders \((61,116,0,67)\) cover period 1, periods 2-3, and period 4, at total cost 860.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
The 2-argument arctangent, denoted as \(\text{atan2}\), is a function defined by

\[ \text{atan2}(y,x)=\begin{cases} \displaystyle \,\arctan(y/x),& x>0,\\[2pt] \displaystyle \,\arctan(y/x)+\pi,& x<0 \text{ and }y\geq 0,\\[2pt] \displaystyle \,\arctan(y/x)-\pi,& x<0 \text{ and }y< 0,\\[2pt] \displaystyle \,\pi/2,& x=0 \text{ and }y> 0,\\[2pt] \displaystyle \,-\pi/2,& x=0 \text{ and }y< 0,\\[2pt] \displaystyle \,\text{undefined},&x=0 \text{ and }y= 0. \end{cases} \]

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: The function \(\text{atan2}\) computes the principal argument of the complex number, correctly covering all four quadrants and avoiding division‑by‑zero issues.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• The range of \(\text{atan2}(y, x)\) is \((-\pi, \pi]\), covering all four quadrants.
  • \(\text{atan2}(y, x)\) is continuous for all \((x, y) \neq (0, 0)\), except along the negative real axis where it has a jump discontinuity of \(2\pi\).

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• \(\text{atan2}(1, -1) = 3\pi/4\) (second quadrant).
  • \(\text{atan2}(-1, -1) = -3\pi/4\) (third quadrant, within range \((-\pi, \pi]\)).

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: An Abelian group is a group whose operation is commutative.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: Abelian groups are groups in which order does not matter.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Every Abelian group is a group, but not every group is Abelian.
  • Associativity, identity elements, and inverse elements determine which algebraic structure is present.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• \((\mathbb R,+)\) is an Abelian group.
  • \((\mathbb R,+)\) is a standard example where the operation is ordinary addition.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: The adjugate matrix \(\operatorname{adj}(A)\) is the transpose of the cofactor matrix of a square matrix \(A\).

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: The adjugate packages all cofactors into a matrix that can compute the inverse.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• If \(A\) is nonsingular, then \(A^{-1}=\frac{1}{\det(A)}\operatorname{adj}(A)\).
  • The adjugate is defined for every square matrix, even if the inverse does not exist.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• For \(A=\begin{pmatrix}a&b\\c&d\end{pmatrix}\), \(\operatorname{adj}(A)=\begin{pmatrix}d&-b\\-c&a\end{pmatrix}\).
  • If \(A=I_n\), then \(\operatorname{adj}(A)=I_n\).

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
Aleph null, denoted \(\aleph_0\), is the cardinality of the natural numbers:

\[\aleph_0=\operatorname{card}(\mathbb N).\]

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: It is the standard symbol for countable infinity.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• A set has cardinality \(\aleph_0\) exactly when it is countably infinite.
  • A bijection is the main tool for proving that two sets have the same cardinality.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• \(\mathbb N\), \(\mathbb Z\), and \(\mathbb Q\) all have cardinality \(\aleph_0\).
  • The natural numbers \(\mathbb N\) are the standard example of a countably infinite set.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
If the characteristic polynomial factors as \(c(\lambda-\lambda_i)^{k_i}\) times other factors, then \(k_i\) is the algebraic multiplicity of eigenvalue \(\lambda_i\).

The geometric multiplicity of an eigenvalue \(\lambda\) is the maximal number of linearly independent eigenvectors associated with \(\lambda\).

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: Algebraic multiplicity counts how often an eigenvalue appears as a root of the characteristic polynomial. Geometric multiplicity counts how many independent eigendirections it actually has.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• For every eigenvalue of an \(n\times n\) matrix, \(1\leq gm(\lambda)\leq am(\lambda)\leq n\).
  • A matrix is diagonalizable iff \(gm(\lambda)=am(\lambda)\) for every eigenvalue.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• For \((\lambda-2)^3(\lambda+1)\), eigenvalue \(2\) has algebraic multiplicity \(3\).
  • For \(\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\0&1\end{pmatrix}\), eigenvalue \(1\) has algebraic multiplicity \(2\) but geometric multiplicity \(1\).

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: A field \(\mathbb F\) is algebraically closed if every nonconstant polynomial in \(\mathbb F[x]\) has a root in \(\mathbb F\).

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: An algebraically closed field contains enough elements to solve all polynomial equations with coefficients in that field.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• The complex numbers \(\mathbb C\) are algebraically closed.
  • The real numbers \(\mathbb R\) are not algebraically closed.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• \(x^2+1\) has no root in \(\mathbb R\), but has roots \(\mathrm i\) and \(-\mathrm i\) in \(\mathbb C\).
  • \((\mathbb R,+)\) is a standard example where the operation is ordinary addition.

docs.title: Theorem
docs.text: For nonzero vectors \(x,y\in\mathbb R^n\), the angle \(\theta\) between them satisfies \(x\cdot y=\|x\|\|y\|\cos\theta\).

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: The inner product determines whether two vectors point in similar, opposite, or perpendicular directions.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• If \(x\cdot y>0\), the angle is acute.
  • If \(x\cdot y=0\), the angle is right and the vectors are orthogonal.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• \((1,0)\) and \((0,1)\) have angle \(\pi/2\).
  • \((1,0)\) and \((1,1)\) have a positive inner product, so their angle is acute.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: The argument of a complex number \(z\), denoted \(\arg z\), is the angle between the positive real axis and the line joining the origin and \(z\). It is a multivalued function due to the periodicity of the angle in the polar coordinate system. The principal argument, denoted as \(\operatorname{Arg} z\), is the unique value of the argument that lies in the interval \((-\pi, \pi].\)

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: For a complex number \(z\), if \(\varphi\) is a polar angle, then \(\varphi + 2\pi k\) also represents a valid polar angle for any integer \(k\).

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Each complex number has a unique principal argument.
  • The principal argument of the complex number \(a+\mathrm i b\) is \(\text{atan2}(b,a)\), where \(\text{atan2}\) is the 2-argument arctangent.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• \(\operatorname{Arg} \mathrm i=\pi /2\).
  • \(\operatorname{Arg}(1-\mathrm i)=-\pi/4\).

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
A binary operation \(\star\) on \(A\) is associative if

\[(a\star b)\star c=a\star(b\star c)\]

for all \(a,b,c\in A\).

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: Associativity means that parentheses do not affect the result of repeated applications of the operation.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Associativity is required in semigroups, monoids, and groups.
  • Associativity, identity elements, and inverse elements determine which algebraic structure is present.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• Addition and multiplication of real numbers are associative. Subtraction is not associative.
  • \((\mathbb R,+)\) is a standard example where the operation is ordinary addition.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: The augmented matrix of a linear system \(Ax=b\) is the matrix formed by adjoining the right-hand side vector \(b\) to the coefficient matrix \(A\), often written \((A\mid b)\).

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: An augmented matrix contains all numerical information needed to solve a linear system.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Elementary row operations on the augmented matrix correspond to elementary operations on the equations.
  • Gauss-Jordan elimination is performed on augmented matrices.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• For \(2x+y=3\), \(x-y=1\), the augmented matrix is \(\begin{pmatrix}2&1&3\\1&-1&1\end{pmatrix}\).
  • The vertical bar in \((A\mid b)\) is visual; the augmented matrix is still a matrix.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: A basis of a vector space \(V\) is a collection of vectors that is linearly independent and spans \(V\).

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: A basis is a minimal generating collection and a non-redundant coordinate system for the vector space.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Every vector in \(V\) can be written uniquely as a linear combination of basis vectors.
  • Any two bases of a finite-dimensional vector space have the same length.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• The standard basis of \(\mathbb R^2\) is \(((1,0),(0,1))\).
  • In \(\mathbb R^2\), vectors such as \((1,0)\) and \((0,1)\) illustrate the concept concretely.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
A block matrix is a matrix viewed as being partitioned into smaller matrices called blocks or submatrices.

A block diagonal matrix is a square block matrix of the form

\[ \begin{pmatrix} A_1&0&\cdots&0\\ 0&A_2&\cdots&0\\ \vdots&\vdots&\ddots&\vdots\\ 0&0&\cdots&A_k \end{pmatrix}, \]

where \(A_1,\ldots,A_k\) are square matrices.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: Block notation lets us calculate with large matrices by treating compatible submatrices as entries. Block diagonal matrices represent independent components that do not interact across blocks.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Compatible block matrices can be added and multiplied block-by-block using the usual matrix rules.
  • If \(A\) is block diagonal with diagonal blocks \(A_1,\ldots,A_k\), then
\[ \det(A)=\det(A_1)\det(A_2)\cdots\det(A_k). \]

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• \(\begin{pmatrix}A_{11}&A_{12}\\A_{21}&A_{22}\end{pmatrix}\) is a matrix written in four blocks.
  • \(\begin{pmatrix}A_1&0\\0&A_2\end{pmatrix}\) is block diagonal.

docs.title: Theorem
docs.text: Cantor's diagonal argument shows that there is no bijection between \(\mathbb N\) and the interval \([0,1]\).

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: If a list claimed to contain every binary expansion in \([0,1]\), one can construct a new sequence by flipping the diagonal entries. This new sequence differs from the \(i\)th listed sequence in its \(i\)th digit, so it cannot be on the list.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• The interval \([0,1]\) is uncountable.
  • The real numbers have strictly larger cardinality than the natural numbers.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• From a list \(s_1,s_2,s_3,\ldots\), define \(s^*\) by making its \(i\)th digit different from the \(i\)th digit of \(s_i\).
  • The natural numbers \(\mathbb N\) are the standard example of a countably infinite set.

docs.title: Theorem
docs.text:
Cantor's theorem states that for every set \(A\),

\[\operatorname{card}(A)<\operatorname{card}(2^A),\]

where \(2^A\) is the power set of \(A\).

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: No function from a set to its power set can be surjective. Thus the power set is always strictly larger than the original set.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• There is an infinite staircase of larger and larger infinities: \(A,2^A,2^{2^A},\ldots\).
  • A bijection is the main tool for proving that two sets have the same cardinality.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• For \(A=\mathbb N\), the power set \(2^{\mathbb N}\) has larger cardinality than \(\mathbb N\).
  • The natural numbers \(\mathbb N\) are the standard example of a countably infinite set.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
Two sets \(A\) and \(B\) have the same cardinality, written

\[ \operatorname{card}(A)=\operatorname{card}(B), \]

if there exists a bijection \(f\colon A\to B\text{.}\)

The empty set has cardinality \(0\text{.}\) A set \(A\) has finite cardinality \(n\) if it has the same cardinality as \(\{1,2,\ldots,n\}\text{.}\)

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: Cardinality measures the size of a set through one-to-one correspondence. For finite sets this reproduces ordinary counting; for infinite sets it provides a precise way to compare sizes.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Having equal cardinality is an equivalence relation on sets.
  • A finite set with \(n\) distinct elements has cardinality \(n\text{.}\)
  • Infinite sets can have the same cardinality even when one is a proper subset of the other.
  • Cantor's theorem shows that every set has strictly smaller cardinality than its power set.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• \(\{1,2,3\}\) and \(\{a,b,c\}\) have the same cardinality.
  • \(\mathbb N\) and the even natural numbers have the same cardinality because \(n\mapsto 2n\) is a bijection.
  • \(\mathbb N\), \(\mathbb Z\), and \(\mathbb Q\) are countably infinite, whereas \(\mathbb R\) is uncountable.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
The Cartesian product of two sets \(A\) and \(B\) is the set of all ordered pairs whose first component comes from \(A\) and whose second component comes from \(B\):

\[ A \times B = \{(a,b) : a \in A,\ b \in B\}. \]

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: A Cartesian product lists every possible pairing of an element of \(A\) with an element of \(B\).

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• If \(A\) and \(B\) are finite, then \(\operatorname{card}(A\times B)=\operatorname{card}(A)\operatorname{card}(B)\).
  • Cartesian products are used to define binary operations, since a binary operation on \(A\) is a function from \(A\times A\) to \(A\).

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• If \(A=\{1,2\}\) and \(B=\{x,y\}\), then \(A\times B=\{(1,x),(1,y),(2,x),(2,y)\}\).
  • The set \(\mathbb R^2\) can be understood as \(\mathbb R\times\mathbb R\), the set of all ordered pairs of real numbers.

docs.title: Cauchy-Schwarz Inequality
docs.text: This page presents the Math II: Linear Algebra treatment. See also the treatment in Probability Distributions. Mastery is recorded separately for each course context.

docs.title: Theorem
docs.text: For vectors \(x\) and \(y\) in an inner product space, the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality states \(|x\cdot y|\leq\|x\|\|y\|\).

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: The inner product of two vectors cannot exceed the product of their lengths in absolute value.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Cauchy-Schwarz justifies the formula for the angle between vectors.
  • It can be used to prove the triangle inequality.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• For orthogonal vectors, the left side is \(0\).
  • For \(x=y\), equality holds.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: For a square matrix \(A\), the characteristic polynomial is \(\det(A-\lambda I)\), viewed as a polynomial in \(\lambda\). The equation \(\det(A-\lambda I)=0\) is called the characteristic equation.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: The characteristic polynomial packages the eigenvalue problem into a polynomial equation.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• The eigenvalues of \(A\) are exactly the roots of the characteristic polynomial, equivalently the solutions of the characteristic equation.
  • For an \(n\times n\) matrix, the characteristic polynomial has degree \(n\).

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• For \(A=\begin{pmatrix}a&0\\0&b\end{pmatrix}\), the characteristic polynomial is \((a-\lambda)(b-\lambda)\).
  • For \(I_n\), the characteristic polynomial is \((1-\lambda)^n\).

docs.title: Theorem
docs.text:
For a square matrix \(A\), let \(A_{ij}\) be the matrix obtained by deleting row \(i\) and column \(j\). The number \(\det(A_{ij})\) is the minor of entry \((i,j)\), and

\[ C_{ij}=(-1)^{i+j}\det(A_{ij}) \]

is the corresponding cofactor.

The determinant can be computed by expanding along any row or column:

\[ \det(A)=\sum_k a_{ik}C_{ik} \]

for expansion along row \(i\), or

\[ \det(A)=\sum_k a_{kj}C_{kj} \]

for expansion along column \(j\).

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: Cofactor expansion reduces the determinant of an \(n\times n\) matrix to determinants of smaller matrices.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Cofactor expansion can be performed along any row or column.
  • Choosing a row or column with many zeros makes the computation shorter.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• For a \(3\times3\) matrix, expanding along the first row gives three \(2\times2\) determinants.
  • For a diagonal matrix, expanding along sparse rows quickly gives the product of diagonal entries.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
Let \(A\subseteq U\text{,}\) where \(U\) is a fixed universal set. The complement of \(A\) relative to \(U\) is

\[ A^{\complement}=U\setminus A=\{x\in U:x\notin A\}. \]

Background recalled in Math II

Math II: Linear Algebra recalls complements in Week 1 as prior set-theory language. The operation is the difference set \(U\setminus A\) once the universal set \(U\) has been fixed.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: The complement contains everything in the chosen universe that does not belong to the set. It therefore depends on which universal set is being used.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• \((A^{\complement})^{\complement}=A\text{.}\)
  • \(U^{\complement}=\varnothing\) and \(\varnothing^{\complement}=U\text{.}\)

  • De Morgan's laws:

    \[ (A\cup B)^{\complement}=A^{\complement}\cap B^{\complement},\qquad (A\cap B)^{\complement}=A^{\complement}\cup B^{\complement}. \]

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• If \(U=\{1,2,3,4\}\) and \(A=\{1,3\}\text{,}\) then \(A^{\complement}=\{2,4\}\text{.}\)
  • If \(U=\mathbb R\) and \(A=[0,\infty)\text{,}\) then \(A^{\complement}=(-\infty,0)\text{.}\)

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: Given a complex number \(z=a+\mathrm{i}b\) where \(a,b\in\mathbb{R}\), the absolute value or modulus of \(z\) is denoted as \(|z|\) is a real number and is calculated by \(|z| = \sqrt{a^2 + b^2}.\)

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: The absolute value of a complex number is simply its distance from the origin on the complex plane​.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• While it is true that \(|z| = \sqrt{z^2}\) when \(z\) is real number, it does not hold whenever \(z\) is a non-real complex number, i.e., \(|z| \neq \sqrt{z^2}\) for \(z\in (\mathbb C\setminus \mathbb R)\).
  • Complex numbers extend the real numbers by adding a solution of \(x^2=-1\).

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• \(|1+\mathrm i|=\sqrt 2\).
  • \(|z|=1\) represents a unit circle in the complex plane.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: Given two complex numbers \(z=a+\mathrm{i}b\) and \(w=c+\mathrm{i}d\) where \(a,b,c,d\in\mathbb{R}\), the sum of complex numbers \(z\) and \(w\) is defined as \(z+w=(a+c)+\mathrm{i}(b+d).\)

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: Adding complex numbers is like adding two vectors: you simply add their real parts together and their imaginary parts together.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• The addition identity for complex numbers is \(0_\mathbb{C} = 0 + 0\mathrm{i},\) which is the real number \(0.\)
  • Complex addition has commutativity: \(z_1 + z_2 = z_2 + z_1.\)
  • Complex addition has associativity: \((z_1 + z_2) + z_3 = z_1 + (z_2 + z_3)\).

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• \((2+\mathrm{i}) + (3+4\mathrm{i}) = 5+5\mathrm{i}\).
  • \((1-\mathrm i)+(-1+\mathrm i) = 0_{\mathbb{C}}=0\).

docs.title: Theorem
docs.text: If \(P\) is a polynomial in one variable with real coefficients, and \(a + \mathrm i b\) is a root of \(P\) with \(a\) and \(b\) being real numbers, then its complex conjugate \(a − \mathrm i b\) is also a root of \(P\).

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: Complex roots of real polynomials come in pairs.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• If the degree of a real polynomial is odd, it must have at least one real root.
  • Any real square matrix of odd degree has at least one real eigenvalue.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• For \(z=3+4\mathrm i\), the real part is \(3\), the imaginary part is \(4\), and \(|z|=5\).
  • For \(z=1+\mathrm i\) and \(w=2-\mathrm i\), ordinary complex arithmetic gives examples of the definition in use.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: Given a complex number \(z=a+\mathrm{i}b\) where \(a,b\in\mathbb{R}\), the conjugate of the complex number \(z\) is defined as \(\overline{z}=a-\mathrm{i}b.\)

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: The conjugate of a complex number retains the original real part while inverting the sign of the imaginary part.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• We have \(\overline{z + w} = \overline{z} + \overline{w},\) \(\overline{-z} = -\overline{z},\) and \(\overline{zw} = \overline{z} \cdot \overline{w}.\)
  • \(z\) and \(\overline z\) are symmetric about the real axis.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• \(\overline{1+\mathrm i}=1-\mathrm i\).
  • \(\overline{-2-3\mathrm i}=-2+3\mathrm i\).

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: For any two complex numbers \(z\) and \(w\) (where \(w \neq 0\)), the quotient of complex numbers \(z/w\) is defined as \(z/w = z \cdot w^{-1} = \dfrac{z\overline{w}}{|w|^2}.\)

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: To divide one complex number by another, you multiply the numerator and denominator by the conjugate of the denominator, which turns the denominator into a real number you can divide by.

docs.title: Key Results

• \(|z/w|=|z|/|w|\).
  • \(\overline{z/w}=\overline z /\overline w\).

docs.title: Examples

docs.text:
Let \(z\in\mathbb{C}\). The complex exponential function \(\mathrm{e}^z\) is defined as

\[ \mathrm{e}^z=\sum_{n=0}^\infty\frac{z^n}{n!}=1+z+\frac{z^2}{2!}+\frac{z^3}{3!}+\cdots, \]

where the power functions \(z^n\)'s are defined according to De Moivre's formula.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: The complex exponential is defined based on the Taylor series of the real exponential, extending its definition using powers of complex numbers.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text: • The series converges for all \(z \in \mathbb{C}\) (infinite radius of convergence).

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • \(\displaystyle \mathrm e^{\mathrm i}=1+\mathrm i-\frac{1}{2!}-\frac{\mathrm i}{3!}+\frac{1}{4!}+\frac{\mathrm i}{5!}+\cdots\)

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: Let \(z\neq 0\) and \(w\) be complex numbers. The complex exponential \(z^w\) is defined as \(e^{w \log z}\), where the complex logarithm \(\log z\) is a multivalued function. The principal value of the complex exponentiation \(z^w\) is \(e^{w \operatorname{Log}z}\), where \(\operatorname{Log}z\) denotes the principal value of the complex logarithm.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: Raising a complex number to a complex power is done by first taking the logarithm of the base, then using that result as the exponent for the ordinary exponential function.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text: • Complex exponentiation is multivalued.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• \[\displaystyle \mathrm{i}^{1/2}= \left(\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}(\pi/2+2\pi k)}\right)^{1/2}= \mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}\left(\pi k+\pi/4\right)}=\left\{\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}+\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}\mathrm{i},-\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}-\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}\mathrm{i}\right\}.\]
  • \(\displaystyle \mathrm{i}^\mathrm{i} = \left(\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}(\pi/2+2\pi k) }\right)^\mathrm{i} = \mathrm{e}^{-\pi/2-2k\pi}\in\mathbb{R},\) where \(k\in\mathbb{Z}.\)

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: A complex logarithm of a nonzero complex number \(z\), defined to be any complex number \(w\) for which \(e^{w}=z\). Such a number \(w\) is denoted by \(\log z\). If \(z\) is given in polar form as \(z=re^{i\varphi}\), where \(r>0\) and \(\varphi\) are real numbers, then \(\ln r+\mathrm i \varphi\) is one logarithm of \(z\), and all the complex logarithms of \(z\) are exactly the numbers of the form \(\ln r+\mathrm i\left(\varphi +2\pi k\right)\) for integers \(k.\) For each nonzero complex number \(z\), the principal value of the complex logarithm \(\operatorname{Log} z\) is the logarithm whose imaginary part lies in the interval \((-\pi ,\pi].\)

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: The complex logarithm is a multivalued function since the complex exponential function is not bijective.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text: • \(\operatorname{Log} (zw)\neq \operatorname{Log}z+\operatorname{Log}w\).

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• \(\log 1=2\pi\mathrm i k\) while \(\operatorname{Log} 1=0.\)
  • \(\log (-1)=\mathrm i (\pi+2\pi k)\) while \(\operatorname{Log} (-1)=\mathrm \pi i.\)

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: Given two complex numbers \(z=a+\mathrm{i}b\) and \(w=c+\mathrm{i}d\) where \(a,b,c,d\in\mathbb{R}\), the product of complex numbers \(z\) and \(w\) is defined as \(zw = (a+\mathrm{i}b)(c+\mathrm{i}d) = (ac-bd) + \mathrm{i}(ad+bc).\)

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: Multiplying two complex numbers is similar to multiplying two binomials.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• The multiplicative identity for complex numbers is \(1_\mathbb{C} = 1 + 0\mathrm{i},\) which is the real number \(1.\)
  • Complex multiplication has commutativity, associativity, and distributivity over complex addition.
  • In polar form, complex multiplication combines stretching, because \(|zw|=|z|\,|w|\), with rotation, because arguments add modulo \(2\pi\).

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• \((1+2\mathrm{i})(2-\mathrm{i})=4+3\mathrm{i}=(2-\mathrm{i})(1+2\mathrm{i})\).
  • \((3+4\mathrm{i})1_\mathbb{C}=(3+4\mathrm{i})(1+0\mathrm{i})=3+4\mathrm{i}\).

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: A complex number is of the form \(a + \mathrm{i}b\), where \(a\) and \(b\) are real numbers, and \(\mathrm{i}\) is the imaginary unit. The number \(a\) is the real part of the complex number \(a + \mathrm{i}b\) and is denoted by \(a = \operatorname{Re}(a+\mathrm{i}b)=\Re(a+\mathrm{i}b)\). Similarly, \(b\) is the imaginary part and is represented as \(b = \operatorname{Im}(a+\mathrm{i}b)=\Im(a+\mathrm{i}b).\) If the real part of a complex number \(a+\mathrm{i}b\) is zero, we term the number \(0+\mathrm{i}b\) as a purely imaginary number. The set of all complex numbers is denoted by \(\mathbb{C}\text{.}\)

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: Essentially, a complex number is an ordered pair of two real numbers.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Complex numbers do not have trichotomy, e.g., we cannot say \(1-\mathrm{i}> 0\) or \(1-\mathrm{i} < 0.\)
  • Complex numbers extend the real numbers by adding a solution of \(x^2=-1\).

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• \(2-3\mathrm i\) is a complex number.
  • Any real number is a special complex number, but not every complex number is real, i.e., \(\mathbb R\subset \mathbb C\),

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: The complex plane or \(\boldsymbol{z}\)-plane is the plane formed by the complex numbers, with a Cartesian coordinate system such that the horizontal \(x\)-axis, called the real axis, is formed by the real numbers, and the vertical \(y\)-axis, called the imaginary axis, is formed by the purely imaginary numbers. The form \(a+\mathrm i b\) is called the Cartesian form of a complex number.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: The complex plane can be seen as the Cartesian plane \(\mathbb R^2\) equipped with a number of additional structures (e.g., complex multiplication).

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Each complex number \(a+\mathrm i b\) corresponds to unique coordinates \((a,b).\)
  • In the Cartesian coordinate system, the addition of complex numbers can be visualized as vector addition.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• \(1+\mathrm i\) and \(2-\mathrm i\) are elements in the complex plane \(\mathbb C\).
  • For \(z=3+4\mathrm i\), the real part is \(3\), the imaginary part is \(4\), and \(|z|=5\).

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: The polar form of a complex number describes it using its distance from the origin and the angle it makes with the positive real axis.

docs.title: Key Results

docs.text:

  • The complex number \(3+4\mathrm i\) has polar coordinates \((5, \operatorname{atan2}(4,3))\).
