docs.title: Theorem
docs.text: Let \(X_1,X_2,\ldots\) be independent and identically distributed random variables with finite expectation \(\mu\), and let \(\bar X_n\) be their sample mean. The weak law of large numbers states that \(\bar X_n\) converges in probability to \(\mu\).

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: The weak law says that averages stabilize as the sample size grows. Individual observations may be random, but their average becomes predictable.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• The sample mean converges in probability to the common mean under standard finite-variance assumptions.
  • Chebyshev's inequality gives a common proof when the variance is finite.
  • The law justifies using large-sample averages to estimate expectations.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• The proportion of heads in many independent fair coin tosses becomes close to one half with high probability.
  • The average demand over many similar days becomes close to expected demand.
  • The average of repeated independent measurement errors becomes close to the true mean error.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
Let \((\boldsymbol{X},d)\) be a metric space and let \(\boldsymbol{E}\subseteq \boldsymbol{X}\). A point \(\boldsymbol{x}\in \boldsymbol{X}\) is called an accumulation point (or cluster point, limit point) of \(\boldsymbol{E}\) if every metric ball around \(\boldsymbol{x}\) contains a point of \(\boldsymbol{E}\) different from \(\boldsymbol{x}\), i.e.,

\[ \forall \varepsilon>0,\quad \left(\boldsymbol{B}_d(\boldsymbol{x},\varepsilon)\setminus\{\boldsymbol{x}\}\right)\cap \boldsymbol{S}\neq\varnothing. \]

Let \((\boldsymbol{X},d)\) be a metric space and let \((\boldsymbol{x}_n)_{n\in\mathbb{N}}\) be a sequence in \(\boldsymbol{X}\). A point \(\boldsymbol{x}\in \boldsymbol{X}\) is called an accumulation point (or cluster point) of \((\boldsymbol{x}_n)\) if, for every \(\varepsilon>0\), there exist infinitely many \(n\in\mathbb{N}\) such that \(\boldsymbol{x}_n\in \boldsymbol{B}_d(\boldsymbol{x},\varepsilon)\), i.e.,

\[ \forall \varepsilon>0,\quad \left|\{n\in\mathbb{N}\colon \boldsymbol{x}_n\in \boldsymbol{B}_d(\boldsymbol{x},\varepsilon)\}\right|=\infty. \]

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
An accumulation point of a set is a location you can approach arbitrarily closely using other points from the set.

For a sequence, it is a value that the sequence visits infinitely often, no matter how tight a neighborhood you pick.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text: • A limit point can be characterized as an adherent point that is not an isolated point.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• For \(E=\{1,\,1/2,\,1/3,\, \dots,\}\), the only accumulation point is \(0\). Each point \(1/n\) is isolated.
  • The sequence \(a_n=(−1)^n\) has accumulation points 1 and -1. It does not converge.
  • Consider the sequence \((a_n)_{n=1}^\infty\) that is defined by \(a_n=\sin n\). We can show that any number \(A\in[-1,1]\) is an accumulation point of this sequence.

docs.title: Adherent Point and Closure of a Set
Definition
docs.text: Let \((\boldsymbol{X},d)\) be a metric space and let \(\boldsymbol{E}\) be a subset of \(\boldsymbol{X}\). A point \(\boldsymbol{x}_0\) in \(\boldsymbol{X}\) is termed an adherent point of \(\boldsymbol{E}\) if, for every \(\varepsilon > 0\), the ball \(\boldsymbol{B}(\boldsymbol{x}_0, \varepsilon)\) intersects \(\boldsymbol{E}\) nonemptily. The set of all adherent points of \(\boldsymbol{E}\) constitutes the closure of \(\boldsymbol{E}\), denoted as \(\overline{\boldsymbol{E}}\) or \(\mathrm{cl}\boldsymbol{E}\).

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
An adherent point of a set is one that you can get arbitrarily close to from inside the set.

The closure is the original set together with all its adherent points, meaning everything you can touch or approach.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• We have \(\overline{\boldsymbol{E}} = \mathrm{int}\boldsymbol{E} \cup \partial \boldsymbol{E} = \boldsymbol{E} \cup \partial \boldsymbol{E} = \boldsymbol{X} \setminus \mathrm{ext}\boldsymbol{E}.\)
  • A set is closed if and only if it contains all its adherent points.
  • The closure of a set \(\boldsymbol{E}\) is the intersection of all closed sets which contain \(\boldsymbol{E}\), or equivalently, the smallest closed set that contains \(\boldsymbol{E}\).

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• The closure of \((0,1)\) in \(\mathbb{R}\) is \([0,1]\). The endpoints \(0\) and \(1\) are adherent points even though they are not in the open interval.
  • If \(E = \{1/n \colon n \in \mathbb{N}^+\}\) in \(\mathbb{R}\), the closure is \(E \cup {0}\). Zero is an adherent point approached by the sequence.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
Let \(n,\,k \in\mathbb N^+\), let \(\boldsymbol A\in\mathbb R^{k\times n}\) be a \(k\times n\) real-valued matrix, and let \(\boldsymbol b\in\mathbb R^k\) be a column vector of real numbers. An affine transformation \(\boldsymbol f\colon \mathbb R^n\to \mathbb R^k\) is a function that can be represented as \(\boldsymbol f(\boldsymbol x)=\boldsymbol A \boldsymbol x+ \boldsymbol b.\) In the terminology of this Math III page, such affine functions are called linear functions. In particular, a linear real-valued function \(f\colon \mathbb R^n\to \mathbb R\) has the general expression:

\[ f(x_1,\,x_2,\,\dots,\,x_n)=a_1x_1+a_2x_2+\cdots+a_nx_n+b. \]

The term linear map/transformation, as used in linear algebra and on the Linear Transformation page, requires the additional condition \(\boldsymbol b=\boldsymbol 0\). Thus an affine function with a nonzero constant term is not a linear map.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: If one argument of an affine transformation is increased by \(c\) units, the function value changes by a constant multiple of \(c\) units.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text: • The graph of a linear real-valued function on \(\mathbb R^n\) is a hyperplane of dimension \(n\).

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• \(f(x,y) = x + 2y - 1\) is linear.
  • \(g(x,y) = x + xy\) and \(h(x,y) = 2^x + \sin y\) are nonlinear.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
Consider two functions \(f\colon \mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R}\) and \(g\colon \mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R}\text{.}\) Let \(a\in[-\infty,+\infty]\).

  • Assume that \(g\) is nonnegative in a punctured neighbourhood of \(a\text{.}\) We say that \(f(x)\) is big-\(\boldsymbol{O}\) of \(g(x)\) as \(x\) tends to \(a\text{,}\) and write \(f(x)=O(g(x))\) as \(x\to a\text{,}\) if there exist constants \(M>0\) and \(\delta>0\) such that \(|f(x)| \le M g(x)\text{,}\) for \(0<|x-a|<\delta\text{.}\)
  • Assume that \(g\) is strictly positive in a punctured neighbourhood of \(a\text{.}\) We say that \(f(x)\) is little-\(\boldsymbol{o}\) of \(g(x)\) as \(x\) tends to \(a\text{,}\) and write \(f(x)=o(g(x))\) as \(x\to a\text{,}\) if \(\displaystyle \lim\limits_{x\to a}\frac{f(x)}{g(x)}=0\text{.}\)

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: • Big-\(O\) means if \(g\) goes to zero, \(f\) goes to zero too; little-\(o\) means \(f\) goes to zero faster than \(g\) does.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• The little-\(o\) notation makes a stronger assertion than the big-\(O\) notation: every function that is little-\(o\) of \(g\) is also big-\(O\) of \(g\text{,}\) but not all functions that are big-\(O\) of \(g\) are little-\(o\) of \(g\text{.}\)
  • If \(f(x)\) and \(g(x)\) are asymptotically equivalent as \(x\) tends to \(a\text{,}\) i.e., \(f(x)\sim g(x)\) as \(x\to a\text{,}\) then we have \(f(x)=O(g(x))\) and \(g(x)=O(f(x))\text{,}\) as \(x\to a\text{.}\)

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• As \(x\to 0\), \(x^2\) is both \(O(x)\) and \(o(x)\) since \(\displaystyle \lim\limits_{x \to 0}\frac{x^2}{x} = 0\).
  • As \(x\to 0\), \(\sin (x^2)\) is \(O(x^2)\) but not \(o(x^2)\) since \(\displaystyle \lim\limits_{x \to 0}\frac{\sin(x^2)}{x^2} = 1\).
  • In the following graph, we have \(g(x)=o(f(x))\) and \(g(x)=o(h(x))\) as \(x\to 0\):

docs.title: Theorem
docs.text:
Each bounded sequence in the Euclidean space \((\mathbb{R}^n,d_2)\) has a convergent subsequence.

Equivalently, a subset \(\boldsymbol{E}\) of the Euclidean space is sequentially compact if and only if it is both closed and bounded.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
Even if a sequence wanders around without settling down, as long as it stays within a bounded region you can always pick out a subsequence that eventually homes in on some point.

In Euclidean space, closedness and boundedness guarantee enough crowding to force a convergent tail.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• The limit of a convergent subsequence is an accumulation point of the original sequence.
  • In \(\mathbb{R}^n\), every Cauchy sequence is bounded, so by Bolzano–Weierstrass theorem it has a convergent subsequence. A Cauchy sequence with a convergent subsequence must itself converge. This gives another proof that \(\mathbb{R}^n\) is complete.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• The sequence \(x_n = (-1)^n\) in \(\mathbb{R}\) is bounded between \(-1\) and \(1\). It does not converge, but it has two convergent subsequences: the even terms \(x_{2n}=1\) converge to \(1\), and the odd terms \(x_{2n-1}=-1\) converge to \(-1\).
  • The sequence \(x_n = 1/n\) in \(\mathbb{R}\) is bounded in \([0,1]\). It already converges to \(0\), so every subsequence also converges to \(0\).

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: For a metric space \((\boldsymbol{X},d)\text{,}\) and a subset \(\boldsymbol{E} \subseteq \boldsymbol{X}\text{,}\) a point \(\boldsymbol{x}_0\) is a boundary point of \(\boldsymbol{E}\) if it's neither an interior nor an exterior point of \(\boldsymbol{E}\text{.}\) We denote the set of boundary points of \(\boldsymbol{E}\) as \(\partial \boldsymbol{E}\text{.}\)

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: The boundary is the dividing line between inside and outside.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• A boundary point \(\boldsymbol{x}_0\) of \(\boldsymbol{E}\) may or may not be in \(\boldsymbol{E}\text{.}\)
  • For a boundary point \(\boldsymbol{x}_0\) of \(\boldsymbol{E}\text{,}\) any balls centered at \(\boldsymbol{x}_0\) will contain points both inside and outside \(\boldsymbol{E}\text{.}\)

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• The boundary of \((0,1)\) is \(\{0,1\}\). Every neighborhood around \(0\) contains points in \((0,1)\) and points not in \((0,1)\).
  • The boundary of \(\mathbb{Q}\) in \(\mathbb{R}\) is all of \(\mathbb{R}\).

docs.title: Bounded Set in a Metric Space
Definition
docs.text: Given a metric space \((\boldsymbol{X},d_{\boldsymbol{X}})\text{,}\) a set \(\boldsymbol{E}\subseteq \boldsymbol{X}\) is termed bounded if there exists \(M>0\) such that the ball \(\boldsymbol{B}_{(\boldsymbol{X},d_{\boldsymbol{X}})} (\boldsymbol{x},M)\) contains \(\boldsymbol{E}\text{.}\) Here, \(\boldsymbol{x}\) can be any point in \(\boldsymbol{X}\) (usually chosen to be the origin or a particular point in \(\boldsymbol{E}\)).

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: A bounded set is one that fits entirely inside some large enough ball.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• A set is bounded if and only if \(\displaystyle \sup_{\boldsymbol x,\boldsymbol y\in \boldsymbol E} d_{\boldsymbol{X}}(\boldsymbol x,\boldsymbol y)\) is finite.
  • Any subset of a bounded set is bounded.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• A unit sphere \(\{(x,y,z)\in\mathbb R^3\colon x^2+y^2+z^2=1\}\) is bounded.
  • A parabola curve \(\{(x,y)\in\mathbb R^2\colon y=x^2\}\) is unbounded.

docs.title: Cauchy Sequence in a Metric Space
Definition
docs.text: For a sequence of points \((\boldsymbol{x}_i)_{i=1}^\infty\) in a metric space \((\boldsymbol{X},d)\), it is termed a Cauchy sequence if, for every \(\varepsilon > 0\), there exists an integer \(N\geq 1\) such that the distance \(d(\boldsymbol{x}_j,\boldsymbol{x}_k)<\varepsilon\) for all \(j, k \geq N\).

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: It is the same idea as a Cauchy sequence of real numbers, but with the absolute value replaced by a general metric.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text: • While all convergent sequences are Cauchy, not every Cauchy sequence converges because a sequence can cluster together (Cauchy property) around a limit that does not exist within the current space.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • The sequence \(a_n=\left(1+\dfrac{1}{n}\right)^n\) is a Cauchy sequence in \((\mathbb Q, d)\), but it does not converge to any point in this space.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
For a metric space \((\boldsymbol{X},d)\), a point \(\boldsymbol{x}_0\) in \(\boldsymbol{X}\), and \(r > 0\), the closed metric ball \(\overline{\boldsymbol{B}}_{(\boldsymbol{X},d)}(\boldsymbol{x}_0,r)\) in \(\boldsymbol{X}\), centered at \(\boldsymbol{x}_0\) with radius \(r\) in metric \(d\), is defined as the following set:

\[ \overline{\boldsymbol{B}}_{(\boldsymbol{X},d)}(\boldsymbol{x}_0,r) = \{\boldsymbol{x} \in \boldsymbol{X} \colon d(\boldsymbol{x}, \boldsymbol{x}_0) \leq r\}. \]

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: A closed metric ball is the set of all points whose distance from the center is less than or equal to the radius.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• The closed metric ball is a closed set.
  • Under the Euclidean metric or equivalent metrics, the closed metric ball is the closure of the corresponding open metric ball.
  • In a general metric space, we do not have \(\overline{\boldsymbol{B}}_{(\boldsymbol{X},d)}(\boldsymbol{x}_0,\varepsilon)=\overline{\boldsymbol{B}_{(\boldsymbol{X},d)}(\boldsymbol{x}_0,\varepsilon)}\).

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • In \(\mathbb{R}^2\) with the usual distance, \(\overline{\boldsymbol B}((0,0),1)\) is the closed disc of radius \(1\) centered at the origin. Points with \(x^2 + y^2 \leq 1\) are elements of this ball.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: Consider a space \(\boldsymbol{X}\) in which open sets are defined. A subset \(\boldsymbol{E}\) of \(\boldsymbol{X}\) is called compact if every open cover of \(\boldsymbol{E}\) has a finite subcover.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: No matter how you try to cover a compact set with open patches, you only ever need finitely many of them to do the job.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• The set \(\boldsymbol{E}\subseteq \mathbb R ^n\) is compact if and only if it is both closed and bounded.
  • Let \(\boldsymbol{E} \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n\text{,}\) \(\boldsymbol{f} \colon \boldsymbol{E} \to \mathbb{R}^k\) be a function, and \(\boldsymbol{X} \subseteq \boldsymbol{E}\) be a compact set. If \(\boldsymbol{f}\) is continuous on \(\boldsymbol{X}\text{,}\) then the image \(\boldsymbol{f}(\boldsymbol{X})\) is also compact. This result is known as continuity preserves compactness.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• The closed unit ball \(\{x\in \mathbb R^n\colon \|x\|\leq 1\}\) is compact.
  • Any finite set in any metric space is compact. You can always pick one open set for each point; finitely many suffice.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: A metric space \((\boldsymbol{X}, d)\) is termed complete if each Cauchy sequence contained within converges in \((\boldsymbol{X}, d)\). When a complete normed vector space is encountered, it's also referred to as a Banach space.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: A complete metric space is one with no “missing points”: every sequence that looks like it should converge actually lands inside the space.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text: • Every Cauchy sequence converges in the completion of the space.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• The Euclidean space \(\mathbb R^n\) is a complete normed vector space.
  • The \(n\)-dimensional real coordinate space equipped with the discrete metric is not complete.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: Consider a space \(\boldsymbol{X}\) in which openness is defined. A subset \(\boldsymbol{E} \subseteq \boldsymbol{X}\) is called disconnected if \(\boldsymbol{E}\) possesses a disjoint open cover \(\{\boldsymbol{V},\boldsymbol{W}\}\) (i.e., \(\boldsymbol{V}\cap\boldsymbol{W}=\varnothing\) and \(\boldsymbol{E} \subseteq \boldsymbol{V} \cup \boldsymbol{W}\)) such that both \(\boldsymbol{E} \cap \boldsymbol{V}\) and \(\boldsymbol{E} \cap \boldsymbol{W}\) are nonempty. If \(\boldsymbol{E}\) is nonempty and not disconnected, it is connected.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
A set is disconnected if you can split it into two nonempty open pieces that do not touch each other.

A set is connected if it comes in one piece without such a split.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• The only type of connected subsets of \(\mathbb R\) is interval.
  • Consider metric spaces \((\boldsymbol{X},d_{\boldsymbol{X}})\) and \((\boldsymbol{Y},d_{\boldsymbol{Y}})\text{.}\) Let \(\boldsymbol{f}:\boldsymbol{X}\to\boldsymbol{Y}\) be a continuous function, and let \(\boldsymbol{E}\) be a connected subset of \(\boldsymbol{X}\text{.}\) Then \(\boldsymbol{f}(\boldsymbol{E})\) is a connected subset of \(\boldsymbol{Y}\text{.}\) This result is known as continuity preserves connectedness.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• Any singleton set is connected.
  • \(\mathbb Q\) is a disconnected subset of \(\mathbb R\).
  • In a discrete metric space, any set with at least two points is disconnected because each singleton is open.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: Consider two metric spaces \((\boldsymbol{X},d_{\boldsymbol{X}})\) and \((\boldsymbol{Y},d_{\boldsymbol{Y}})\text{,}\) and a function \(\boldsymbol{f}\colon \boldsymbol{E}\to\boldsymbol{Y}\) where \(\boldsymbol{E}\subseteq\boldsymbol{X}\text{.}\) Let \(\boldsymbol{x}_0\in\boldsymbol{X}\text{.}\) Assume there exists an \(r>0\) such that \(\boldsymbol{B}_{(\boldsymbol{X},d_{\boldsymbol{X}})}(\boldsymbol{x}_0,r)\subseteq \boldsymbol{E}\text{.}\) We say that \(\boldsymbol{f}\) is continuous at \(\boldsymbol{x}=\boldsymbol{x}_0\) if, for any \(\varepsilon > 0\text{,}\) there exists a \(0<\delta \leq r\) such that whenever \(d_{\boldsymbol{X}}(\boldsymbol{x},\boldsymbol{x}_0)<\delta\text{,}\) we have \(d_{\boldsymbol{Y}}(\boldsymbol{f}(\boldsymbol{x}),\boldsymbol{f}(\boldsymbol{x}_0))<\varepsilon\text{.}\)

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: A function is continuous at a point if you can make the outputs as close as you want to the value at that point by taking inputs sufficiently close to it.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• If one path approaching the point has a different limit, then the function's limit at that point does not exist, and therefore the function is not continuous at that point.
  • A vector-valued function is continuous if and only if each of its component functions is continuous.
  • Most properties of real-valued functions of one real variable are preserved under continuity. In particular, continuity is preserved under addition, subtraction, multiplication, division (where the denominator is nonzero), as well as taking the maximum, minimum, and composition of functions.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • \(f(x,y)=x^2+y^2\) on \(\mathbb{R}^2\). At \((0,0)\), if you want \(f\) within \(\varepsilon\) of \(0\), choose \(\delta=\sqrt{\varepsilon}\). Then \(\sqrt{x^2+y^2}<\delta\) gives \(x^2+y^2<\varepsilon\).

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: Given a metric space \((\boldsymbol{X}, d)\), a sequence \((\boldsymbol{x}_{i})_{i=1}^\infty\) and a point \(\boldsymbol{x}\) in \(\boldsymbol{X}\), the sequence is said to converge to \(\boldsymbol{x}\) under metric \(\boldsymbol{d}\) if \(\displaystyle \lim_{i\to\infty}d(\boldsymbol{x}_i, \boldsymbol{x}) = 0\).

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: This is just like convergent sequences of real numbers, but with a general notion of distance.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text: • A convergent sequence in a metric space must be a Cauchy sequence.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• The sequence \((\boldsymbol{x}_{i})_{i=1}^\infty\) where \(\boldsymbol{x}_i = (1/i, 1/i)\) in \(\mathbb{R}^2\) converges to \((0,0)\) under the Euclidean metric \(d_2\).

docs.title: Theorem
docs.text:
Consider a power series \(\displaystyle f(x)=\sum_{n=0}^\infty c_n (x-a)^n\) with a radius of convergence \(R > 0\text{.}\) For any chosen \(r\) such that \(0 < r < R\):

  • The series converges pointwise on the open interval \((a-R, a+R)\text{.}\)
  • It converges uniformly on the closed interval \([a-r, a+r]\text{.}\)
  • The limit function \(f\) is differentiable on \((a-R, a+R)\text{.}\)
  • The derivative series \(\displaystyle \sum_{n=1}^\infty nc_n (x-a)^{n-1}\) converges uniformly to the derivative, \(f'\text{,}\) on \([a-r, a+r]\text{.}\)

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: The derivative of a power series within its radius of convergence can be found by differentiating each term individually, and the resulting series converges to the correct derivative.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Term-by-term differentiation is valid inside the radius of convergence.
  • Locally (on \([a-r,a+r]\)), a power series behaves like a polynomial: it is smooth and uniformly controlled.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• The series \(\displaystyle \sum_{n=0}^\infty n(-2)^n (x-3)^n\) with \(R = 1/2\) centered at \(a = 3\text{,}\) converges pointwise on \((5/2, 7/2)\) and uniformly on any closed interval within it.
  • The series \(\displaystyle \sum_{n=0}^\infty 2^{n^2} (x+2)^n\) with \(R = 0\) centered at \(a = -2\text{,}\) converges solely at its center \(x = -2\text{.}\)
  • The series \(\displaystyle \sum_{n=0}^\infty 2^{-n^2} (x+2)^n\) with \(R = +\infty\) centered at \(a = -2\text{,}\) converges pointwise over the entire real line \(\mathbb{R}\text{.}\) Uniform convergence for this series over \(\mathbb{R}\) needs further analysis.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
Consider a (topological) space \(\boldsymbol{X}\text{.}\) Let \(\boldsymbol{E}\) be a subset of \(\boldsymbol{X}\text{,}\) and let \(\boldsymbol{\mathcal{C}}=\{\boldsymbol{G}_i\colon i\in I\}\) be a collection of subsets \(\boldsymbol{G}_i\) of \(\boldsymbol{X}\) indexed by an arbitrary index set \(I\text{.}\) The collection \(\boldsymbol{\mathcal{C}}\) is called a cover of \(\boldsymbol{E}\) if \(\displaystyle \boldsymbol{E} \subseteq \bigcup_{i\in I} \boldsymbol{G}_i\text{.}\)

  • An open cover is a cover where each "patch" \(\boldsymbol{G}_i\) is open.
  • A finite cover consists of a collection \(\{\boldsymbol{G}_i\colon i\in I\}\) where \(I\) is finite. A cover is called a countable cover when \(I\) is a countable set, e.g., \(\mathbb{N}\text{.}\)
  • A subcover is a cover that is a subset of another cover.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
A cover is just a collection of sets that together contain the set you care about.

Think of it as laying patches over the set so every point is under at least one patch.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text: • Any set \(\boldsymbol E\subseteq \boldsymbol X\) is covered by the space \(\boldsymbol X\). So covers always exist.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• The set \((0,1)\) in \(\mathbb R\) can be covered by the collection of open sets \(\{(1/n,1−1/n)\colon n≥3\}\). This is an infinite open cover.
  • The set \(\{1,2,3\}\) is covered by the three singletons \(\{1\}\), \(\{2\}\), \(\{3\}\). That is a finite cover.
  • The set of rational numbers \(\mathbb Q\) in \(\mathbb R\) can be covered by open intervals centered at each rational with radius \(1\). That's a countable cover because \(\mathbb Q\) is countable.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
Consider a subset \(\boldsymbol{E} \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n\) and a function \(\boldsymbol{f}\colon \boldsymbol{E}\to\mathbb{R}^k\). Let \(\boldsymbol{x}_0\) be an interior point of \(\boldsymbol{E}\) and \(\boldsymbol{v}\) be a unit vector in \(\mathbb{R}^n\) (note: some authors only require \(\boldsymbol{v}\) to be a nonzero vector). If the limit

\[ \lim_{t\to 0^+}\frac{\boldsymbol{f}(\boldsymbol{x}_0+t\boldsymbol{v})-\boldsymbol{f}(\boldsymbol{x}_0)}{t} \]

exists, then \(\boldsymbol{f}\) is said to be differentiable in the direction \(\boldsymbol{v}\) at \(\boldsymbol{x}=\boldsymbol{x}_0\). This limit is termed the directional derivative and is denoted by \(\mathrm{D}_{\boldsymbol{v}} \boldsymbol{f}(\boldsymbol{x}_0)\).

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
The directional derivative measures the instantaneous rate of change of a function as you move from a point in a specific direction.

It generalizes the one-sided derivative to functions of several variables by looking at how the function changes along a straight line in that direction.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• The directional derivative, \(\mathrm{D}_{\boldsymbol{v}}\boldsymbol{f}(\boldsymbol{x}_0)\), is equal to the total derivative at \(\boldsymbol v\), \(\mathrm{D} \boldsymbol{f}_{\boldsymbol{x}_0}(\boldsymbol{v})\).
  • A function is totally differentiable at a point implies that this function is directionally differentiable in any direction. The converse is incorrect.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • For the function \(\boldsymbol{f}(x,y)=(x^2,y^2)\), consider \(\boldsymbol{x}_0=(1,2)\) and \(\boldsymbol{v}=(3/5,4/5)\). We have \(\displaystyle \mathrm{D}_{\boldsymbol{v}}\boldsymbol{f}(\boldsymbol{x}_0) =\left(\frac{6}{5},\frac{16}{5}\right)\).

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
Consider the space \(\mathbb{R}^n\) with its elements \(\boldsymbol{x}\) and \(\boldsymbol{y}\). We define a discrete metric \(d_{\text{disc}}\) as:

\[ d_{\text{disc}}(\boldsymbol{x},\boldsymbol{y}) = \begin{cases} \displaystyle \;1, & \text{if } \boldsymbol{x} \neq \boldsymbol{y}, \\[2pt] \displaystyle \;0, & \text{if } \boldsymbol{x} = \boldsymbol{y}. \end{cases} \]

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
The discrete metric is the simplest possible distance: distinct points are always exactly 1 unit apart, and a point is 0 units from itself.

It treats every pair of different points as equally far.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text: • The discrete metric is not strongly equivalent to any of the \(p\)-metrics.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • \(d_{\text{disc}}(2,5)=1\) since \(2\neq 5\).

docs.title: Theorem
docs.text:
Let \((\boldsymbol{X},d_{\boldsymbol{X}})\) and \((\boldsymbol{Y},d_{\boldsymbol{Y}})\) be metric spaces, let \(\boldsymbol{x}_0\in\boldsymbol{X}\) be an arbitrary point in the space, and let \(\boldsymbol{f}\colon \boldsymbol{X}\to\boldsymbol{Y}\) be a function. The following statements are equivalent:

  • \(\boldsymbol{f}\) is continuous.
  • For any convergent sequence \((\boldsymbol{x}_i)_{i=1}^\infty\) in \((\boldsymbol{X},d_{\boldsymbol{X}})\), converging to \(\boldsymbol{x}_0\), its image under \(\boldsymbol{f}\), \(\boldsymbol{f}(\boldsymbol{x}_i)_{i=1}^\infty\), also converges to \(\boldsymbol{f}(\boldsymbol{x}_0)\).
  • The preimage of any open set in \((\boldsymbol{Y},d_{\boldsymbol{Y}})\) is open in \((\boldsymbol{X},d_{\boldsymbol{X}})\).
  • The preimage of any closed set in \((\boldsymbol{Y},d_{\boldsymbol{Y}})\) is closed in \((\boldsymbol{X},d_{\boldsymbol{X}})\).

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: A function is continuous if and only if the preimage operation preserves openness and closedness.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text: • In metric spaces, the sequential condition is often the easiest to work with when proving discontinuity. To show \(f\) is not continuous at a point, find one sequence converging to that point whose image does not converge to the function value.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• A continuous function \(f\) might map an open set \(V\) to a non-open set \(f(V)\). For example, let \(V=(0,1)\) with \(f(x)=1\) for all \(x\in\mathbb{R}\). Then \(f(V)=\{1\}\) isn't open under usual metrics.
  • A continuous function \(f\) might map a closed set \(F\) to a non-closed set \(f(F)\). For example, let \(F=[1,+\infty)\) and \(f(x)=1/x\) for all \(x>0\). Then \(f(F)=(0,1]\) isn't closed under usual metrics.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
Two norms \(\|\cdot\|_p\) and \(\|\cdot\|_q\) on a vector space \(\boldsymbol{V}\) are termed equivalent if there exist constants \(a, b > 0\) such that for every \(\boldsymbol{v} \in \boldsymbol{V}\), we have:

\[ a \|\boldsymbol{v}\|_p \leq \|\boldsymbol{v}\|_q \leq b \|\boldsymbol{v}\|_p. \]

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: Equivalent norms are different ways of measuring length that are comparable up to fixed scaling factors.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text: • Any two norms \(\|\cdot\|_p\) and \(\|\cdot\|_q\) on a finite-dimensional vector space \(\boldsymbol{V}\) are equivalent.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • The Euclidean norm and the taxicab norm are equivalent.

docs.title: Euclidean Space
docs.text: This page presents the Math III: Analysis treatment. See also the treatment in Math II: Linear Algebra. Mastery is recorded separately for each course context.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: Let \(\boldsymbol V\) be a real vector space with \(\dim \boldsymbol V<\infty\). If \(V\) has an inner product \(\left\langle\cdot.\cdot\right\rangle\colon \boldsymbol V\times \boldsymbol V\to\mathbb R\), then \((\boldsymbol V,\left\langle\cdot.\cdot\right\rangle)\) is a Euclidean space. In practice, the real coordinate space \(\mathbb R^n\) equipped with the standard inner product denotes the \(n\)-dimensional Euclidean space.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: A Euclidean space is a real finite-dimensional inner product space.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text: • In a Euclidean space \(\mathbb{R}^n\), the inner product induces a norm given by \(\displaystyle \|\boldsymbol x\| = \sqrt{\langle \boldsymbol x,\boldsymbol x\rangle} = \sqrt{\sum_{i=1}^n x_i^2}.\) The metric induced by this norm is defined as \(\displaystyle d(\boldsymbol x,\boldsymbol y) = \|\boldsymbol x-\boldsymbol y\| = \sqrt{\sum_{i=1}^n (x_i - y_i)^2},\) which is precisely the Euclidean distance.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• The coordinate plane \(\mathbb{R}^2\) with the usual distance formula \(\sqrt{(x_1-x_2)^2+(y_1-y_2)^2}\) is a Euclidean space.
  • A sheet of flat paper in the real world is not truly Euclidean. According to general relativity, the presence of mass bends the surrounding space, so physical space is curved rather than perfectly Euclidean.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: For a metric space \((\boldsymbol{X},d)\text{,}\) and a subset \(\boldsymbol{E} \subseteq \boldsymbol{X}\text{,}\) a point \(\boldsymbol{x}_0\) is an exterior point of \(\boldsymbol{E}\) if \(\boldsymbol{B}(\boldsymbol{x}_0,\varepsilon) \cap \boldsymbol{E} = \varnothing\) for some \(\varepsilon > 0\text{.}\) We denote the set of exterior points of \(\boldsymbol{E}\) as \(\mathrm{ext} \boldsymbol{E}\text{.}\)

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: An exterior point is one that has a ball around it completely missing the set.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text: • An exterior point \(\boldsymbol{x}_0\) of \(\boldsymbol{E}\) can never be in \(\boldsymbol{E}\text{.}\)

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• For \(E = (0,1) \subseteq \mathbb{R}\), the point \(x = 2\) is an exterior point. A small ball around \(2\), say \((1.9,2.1)\), avoids \((0,1)\).
  • For \(E = \{(x,y)\in\mathbb R^2\colon x^2 + y^2 \leq 1\}\), the point \((3,0)\) is an exterior point. A small disc around it stays entirely outside the unit disc.

docs.title: Theorem
docs.text: Let \(\boldsymbol{E} \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n\text{,}\) \(f \colon \boldsymbol{E} \to \mathbb{R}\) be a function, and \(\boldsymbol{X} \subseteq \boldsymbol{E}\) be a compact set. If \(f\) is continuous on \(\boldsymbol{X}\text{,}\) then \(f\) attains both its maximum and minimum on \(\boldsymbol{X}\text{.}\)

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: A continuous function on a compact set cannot sneak off to infinity or skip its highest and lowest values. It must actually hit both a maximum and a minimum somewhere inside that set.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• If the domain is not compact, the conclusion may fail. For example, \(f(x)=1/x\) on \((0,1)\) is continuous but has no maximum (it blows up) and no minimum (it approaches 0 but never reaches it).
  • This theorem is used to prove existence of solutions in optimization problems.
  • Together with the intermediate value theorem, it gives a complete picture of the range of a continuous function on a connected compact set (a closed interval in \(\mathbb R\)).

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • The function \(f(x,y)=x+y\) on the closed unit disc \(\{(x,y)\in\mathbb R^2\colon x^2+y^2\leq 1\}\) attains maximum \(\sqrt{2}\)​ at \((1/\sqrt{2},1/\sqrt{2})\) and minimum \(-\sqrt{2}\)​ at \((-1/\sqrt{2},-1/\sqrt{2})\).

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
Consider a function \(\boldsymbol f\colon \boldsymbol X \to\boldsymbol Y\) where \(\boldsymbol X\) is set in an \(n\)-dimensional space (e.g., \(\mathbb R^n\)) and \(\boldsymbol Y\) in an \(k\)-dimensional space (e.g., \(\mathbb R^k\)). We have the following terminologies:

  • it is called a univariate function (also known as single variable function, function of one variable) if \(n=1\);
  • it is called a bivariate function (also known as function of two variables) if \(n=2\);
  • it is called a multivariable function (also known as multivariate function, function of several variables) if \(n\geq 2\);
  • it is called a real-valued function if its codomain is a subset of \(\mathbb R\);
  • it is called a vector-valued function if \(k\geq 2\).

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: A function is classified by how many numbers go in and how many come out.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text: • A multivalued function is neither a multivariable function nor a vector-valued function.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• \(f(x,y) = x^2 + y^2\) from \(\mathbb{R}^2\) to \(\mathbb{R}\) is a bivariate real valued function.
  • \(\boldsymbol{F}(x,y) = (x+y, x-y, xy)\) from \(\mathbb{R}^2\) to \(\mathbb{R}^3\) is a multivariable vector valued function.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
Let \(\boldsymbol{E}\subseteq \mathbb{R}^n\), and let \(f \colon \boldsymbol{E} \to \mathbb{R}\) be a real-valued function. If \(\boldsymbol{x}_0\) is an interior point of \(\boldsymbol{E}\), the gradient \(\nabla f (\boldsymbol{x}_0)\) of \(f\) at \(\boldsymbol{x}=\boldsymbol{x}_0\) is given as the \(n\)-dimensional column vector:

\[ \nabla f (\boldsymbol{x}_0) = \left(\frac{\partial f}{\partial x_1}(\boldsymbol{x}_0),\, \frac{\partial f}{\partial x_2}(\boldsymbol{x}_0),\, \ldots,\, \frac{\partial f}{\partial x_n}(\boldsymbol{x}_0)\right)^\intercal. \]

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
When \( abla f ( oldsymbol{x}_0)= oldsymbol{0}\), we say that \( oldsymbol{x}_0\) is a stationary point of \(f\) (possibly a local extremum point).

When \( abla f ( oldsymbol{x}_0) eq oldsymbol{0}\), the gradient offers two insights: the maximum value of \(\mathrm{D}_{ oldsymbol{u}}f( oldsymbol{x}_0)\) and the direction \( oldsymbol{u}\) where this maximum occurs.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• The gradient can be perceived as a vector whose dot product with any unit vector \(\boldsymbol{v}\) equals the directional derivative of \(f\) at \(\boldsymbol{x}=\boldsymbol{x}_0\) along \(\boldsymbol{v}\), i.e.,
\[ \nabla f (\boldsymbol{x}_0) \cdot \boldsymbol{v} = \mathrm{D}_{\boldsymbol{v}}f(\boldsymbol{x}_0). \]

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• Let \(f(x,y) = e^{x+y}\). Then \(\displaystyle \nabla f(x,y) = \begin{pmatrix} e^{x+y} \\ e^{x+y} \end{pmatrix}\).
  • Let \(f(x,y) = x^2 y + y^3\). Then \(\nabla f(x,y) = \begin{pmatrix} 2xy \\ x^2 + 3y^2 \end{pmatrix}\).

docs.title: Theorem
docs.text: Let \(\boldsymbol{E}\) be a subset of the Euclidean space \(\mathbb{R}^n\text{.}\) The set \(\boldsymbol{E}\) is compact if and only if it is both closed and bounded.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: A set in Euclidean space is compact exactly when it contains all its limit points and stays within some finite distance from the origin. Closedness keeps the boundary in, boundedness keeps it from running off to infinity.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• The continuous image of a compact set is compact. This yields the extreme value theorem.
  • Any closed subset of a compact set in \(\mathbb R^n\) is itself compact.
  • Finite unions of compact sets are compact. Arbitrary intersections of compact sets are compact.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• A closed metric ball \(\overline{\boldsymbol{B}}(\boldsymbol{x}_0,r) = \{\boldsymbol{x} \in \boldsymbol{X} \colon d_2(\boldsymbol{x}, \boldsymbol{x}_0) \leq r\}\) in the Euclidean space is closed and bounded, so compact.
  • Any finite set \(\{\boldsymbol x_1,\dots,\boldsymbol x_k\}\subset \mathbb R^n\) is closed (finite sets are closed) and bounded, so compact.

docs.title: Theorem
docs.text: Let \(a < b\) be real numbers, and consider a function \(f\colon [a, b] \to \mathbb{R}\) that is continuous on \([a, b]\text{.}\) Then, \(f\) is uniformly continuous on \([a, b]\text{.}\)

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
• A continuous function on a closed interval can’t "escape" or behave wildly near the edges because the interval includes its endpoints.
  • This prevents sudden jumps or unbounded growth, ensuring that the function's small changes near one point apply uniformly across the whole interval.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• This theorem has a generalized version if \([a,b]\) is replaced by a compact set.
  • This theorem does not imply that uniform continuity holds only on closed intervals.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• The function \(f(x)=\dfrac{x^2+\sin x}{\mathrm e^x}\) is uniformly continuous on any closed interval since we know it is continuous everywhere.
  • The function \(g(x)=x\) is uniformly continuous on \((0,1)\) though \((0,1)\) is not a closed interval. This does not contradict with the theorem since the "closed interval" condition is sufficient but not necessary.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
Let \(n,\,k \in\mathbb N^+\) and \(m\in \mathbb Z\). A function \(\boldsymbol f\colon \mathbb R^n\to \mathbb R^k\) is homogeneous of degree \(\boldsymbol m\) if

\[ \boldsymbol f(cx_1,\,cx_2,\,\dots,\,cx_n)=c^m \boldsymbol f(x_1,\,x_2,\,\dots,\,x_n) \]

for every \((x_1,\,x_2,\,\dots,\,x_n)\) and \(c\neq 0\).

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: If each of the homogeneous function's arguments is multiplied by the same scalar, then the function's value is multiplied by some power of this scalar.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• If \(f\) is homogeneous of degree \(m\) and differentiable, then each partial derivative is homogeneous of degree \(m-1\).
  • Homogeneity is preserved by addition, multiplication and composition.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• \(f(x,y) = x^2 + y^2 + xy\) is homogeneous as \(f(cx, cy) = c^2 f(x,y)\).
  • \(g(x,y) = xy + x\) is said to be inhomogeneous.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: A polynomial on \(\mathbb R^n\) is called homogeneous of degree \(\boldsymbol k\) if all of its non-zero terms have degree \(k\). Such a polynomial is also called a (algebraic) form.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
A homogeneous polynomial is one where every term has the same total degree.

Scaling all variables by a factor scales the polynomial by that factor raised to that degree.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• The sum of two homogeneous polynomials of the same degree is homogeneous of that degree.
  • The product of a homogeneous polynomial of degree \(k\) and one of degree \(\ell\) is homogeneous of degree \(k+\ell\).

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• \(P(x) = 2x^5\) is a homogeneous polynomial of degree 5.
  • \(P(x,y) = x^2 + xy + y^2\) is homogeneous of degree 2. Each term has total degree 2.

docs.text: This page presents the Math III: Analysis treatment. See also the treatment in Math II: Linear Algebra. Mastery is recorded separately for each course context.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: A hyperplane of a vector space \(\boldsymbol{V}\) is a particular type of subspace characterized by its dimensionality, which is precisely one less than that of \(\boldsymbol{V}\).

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: A hyperplane of an \(n\)-dimensional space \(\boldsymbol{V}\) is a subspace of dimension \(n-1\).

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text: • In \(\mathbb{R}^n\), a hyperplane divides the space into two half-spaces.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• The \(xy\)-plane is a hyperplane of \(\mathbb{R}^3\).
  • A hyperplane in \(\mathbb{R}^n\) (or any finite-dimensional vector space) can be described as \(H=\{x\in\mathbb R^n\colon \boldsymbol a\cdot \boldsymbol x=c\}\), where \(\boldsymbol{a} \in \mathbb{R}^n \setminus {\boldsymbol{0}}\) and \(c \in \mathbb{R}\).

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
Let \(\boldsymbol{X}\) and \(\boldsymbol{Y}\) be two sets in metric spaces, and let \(\boldsymbol{f}\colon \boldsymbol{X}\to\boldsymbol{Y}\) be a function. Let \(\boldsymbol{C}\) be a subset of the domain \(\boldsymbol{X}\), the image of \(\boldsymbol{C}\) under \(\boldsymbol{f}\) is defined as:

\[ \boldsymbol{f}(\boldsymbol{C})=\{\boldsymbol{y}\in\boldsymbol{Y}\colon \text{there exists some } \boldsymbol{x}\in\boldsymbol{C} \text{ such that } \boldsymbol{y}=\boldsymbol{f}(\boldsymbol{x})\}. \]

Let \(\boldsymbol{V}\) be a subset of the codomain \(\boldsymbol{Y}\), the preimage of \(\boldsymbol{V}\) under \(\boldsymbol{f}\) includes all points in the domain that give results in \(\boldsymbol{V}\):

\[ \boldsymbol{f}^{-1}(\boldsymbol{V})=\{\boldsymbol{x}\in\boldsymbol{X}\colon\boldsymbol{f}(\boldsymbol{x})\in\boldsymbol{V}\}. \]

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
Image is the set of all outputs you actually get from the function when you put in points from a specific set.

Preimage is the set of all inputs that the function sends into a chosen target set.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• \(\boldsymbol{V}\) only needs to be a part of the codomain of \(\boldsymbol{f}\). This means there might be some \(\boldsymbol{y}\) in \(\boldsymbol{V}\) that doesn't match any \(\boldsymbol{x}\) in the domain \(\boldsymbol{X}\).
  • We have \(\boldsymbol{C} \subseteq \boldsymbol{f}^{-1}(\boldsymbol{f}(\boldsymbol{C}))\) and \(\boldsymbol{f}(\boldsymbol{f}^{-1}(\boldsymbol{V})) \subseteq \boldsymbol{V}\).

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• Let \(f\colon\mathbb{R}^2\to\mathbb{R}\) be \(f(x,y)=x+y\). Image of the unit square \([0,1]\times[0,1]\) under \(f\) is \([0,2]\). Preimage of \(\{0\}\) under \(f\) is the line \(y=-x\).
  • Let \(f\colon \mathbb{R}^2\to\mathbb{R}\) be \(f(x,y)=x\). Image of the disc \(\{(x,y)\in\mathbb R^2\colon x^2+y^2 \leq 1\}\) under \(f\) is \([-1,1]\). Preimage of \([2,3]\) under \(f\) is the vertical strip \([2,3]\times\mathbb{R}\).

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: Consider a sequence of functions \((f_n)_{n=1}^\infty\) from \(X\) to \(\mathbb{R}\text{.}\) If the sequence of partial sums \(\displaystyle S_N(x) = \sum_{n=1}^N f_n(x)\) converges to \(f\colon X \to \mathbb{R}\) pointwise or uniformly on \(X\) as \(N \to \infty\text{,}\) then we say the infinite series \(\displaystyle \sum_{n=1}^\infty f_n\) converges pointwise/uniformly to \(\boldsymbol{f}\) on \(\boldsymbol{X}\text{,}\) denoted as \(\displaystyle f(x) = \sum_{n=1}^\infty f_n(x)\text{.}\)

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: The infinite sum of functions is defined by its partial sums, and if these partial sums converge to a function, we say the series itself converges to that function.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• If \(f_n\)'s are (continuously) differentiable, \(\displaystyle \sum_{n=1}^\infty f_n \rightarrow f\text{,}\) and \(\displaystyle \sum_{n=1}^\infty f'_n\rightrightarrows g\) on \((a,b)\text{,}\) then \(f\) is (continuously) differentiable on \((a, b)\) with \(f' = g\text{,}\) i.e.,
\[ \sum_{n=1}^\infty f'_n(x_0)=\left(\sum_{n=1}^\infty f_n\right)'(x_0),\quad x_0\in(a,b). \]
  • If \(f_n\)'s are Riemann integrable, and the series \(\displaystyle \sum_{n=1}^\infty f_n\) converges uniformly on \(X\text{,}\) then the series is Riemann integrable, and
\[ \int_X \left(\sum_{n=1}^\infty f_n(x)\right) \, \mathrm{d}x = \sum_{n=1}^\infty \int_X f_n(x) \, \mathrm{d}x. \]

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• The infinite series \(\displaystyle \sum_{n=0}^\infty\dfrac{x^n}{n!}\) converges uniformly on \(\mathbb R\).
  • The infinite series \(\displaystyle 1+x+x^2+x^3+\cdots\) converges uniformly on \((-1,1)\).

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: For a metric space \((\boldsymbol{X},d)\text{,}\) and a subset \(\boldsymbol{E} \subseteq \boldsymbol{X}\text{,}\) a point \(\boldsymbol{x}_0\) is an interior point of \(\boldsymbol{E}\) if there exists some \(\varepsilon > 0\) such that \(\boldsymbol{B}(\boldsymbol{x}_0,\varepsilon) \subseteq \boldsymbol{E}\text{.}\) We denote the set of interior points of \(\boldsymbol{E}\) as \(\mathrm{int} \boldsymbol{E}\text{.}\)

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: An interior point is one that has a little ball around it completely contained in the set.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• An interior point \(\boldsymbol{x}_0\) of \(\boldsymbol{E}\) is always in \(\boldsymbol{E}\) since balls centered at \(\boldsymbol{x}_0\) include \(\boldsymbol{x}_0\text{.}\)
  • The interior of \(\boldsymbol{E}\) is the largest open subset of \(\boldsymbol{E}\).

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• For \(E = (0,1) \subseteq \mathbb{R}\), every point in \((0,1)\) is interior. Pick a small enough interval around any point and it stays inside \((0,1)\).
  • For \(E = \{1,2,3\} \subseteq \mathbb{R}\), no point is interior. Any ball around \(1\) contains numbers other than \(1,2,3\).

docs.title: Theorem
docs.text: Let \(f\colon \mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{R}\) be a continuous real-valued function. Let \(\boldsymbol{E}\) be any connected subset of \(\mathbb{R}^n\text{,}\) and let \(\boldsymbol{a}\) and \(\boldsymbol{b}\) be any two points in \(\boldsymbol{E}\text{.}\) If \(y\) is a real number between \(f(\boldsymbol{a})\) and \(f(\boldsymbol{b})\text{,}\) then there exists a \(\boldsymbol{c} \in \boldsymbol{E}\) such that \(f(\boldsymbol{c}) = y\text{.}\)

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: A continuous function on a connected set cannot skip values: if it takes two different numbers, it must also take every number in between.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Continuous image of a connected set is connected.
  • If \(\boldsymbol{E}\) is path‑connected, the theorem can be proved by composing \(f\) with a path and applying the one‑dimensional intermediate value theorem.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• Let \(\boldsymbol{E}\) be the closed unit disk in \(\mathbb R^2\) and \(f(x,y)=x^2+y^2\)​. The image is \([0,1]\) which is also a connected set.
  • Let \(\boldsymbol{E}\) be the unit sphere in \(\mathbb R^3\) and \(f(x,y,z)=z\) (height). The image is \([−1,1]\).

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
Let \(\boldsymbol{f}\colon \boldsymbol{X} \to \mathbb R\) be a real-valued function defined on a set \(\boldsymbol{X}\subseteq \mathbb R^n\). A level set is defined as the preimage of a singleton set \(\{k\}\), i.e.,

\[ L_k(f)=f^{-1}(\{k\})=\{(x_1,x_2,\ldots,x_n)\in\mathbb{R}^n\colon f(x_1,x_2,\ldots,x_n)=k\}. \]

When the number of independent variables is two, a level set is called a level curve, also known as contour line.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: A level curve is the set of all real-valued solutions of an equation in two variables \(x_1\) and \(x_2\).

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text: • Different level sets for distinct values are disjoint, and the union over all possible values covers the entire domain where the function is defined.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• Let \(f\colon \mathbb R^2\to\mathbb R\) be \(f(x,y)=x^2+y^2\). Level sets are circles centered at the origin for \(k>0\), a single point \((0,0)\) for \(k=0\), and empty for \(k<0\).
  • Let \(f\colon \mathbb R^2\to\mathbb R\) be \(f(x,y)=x+y\). Level sets are straight lines of slope \(−1\): \(x+y=k\). All level sets are parallel lines.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
Let \((a_n)_{n=0}^{\infty}\) be a sequence. For each \(N\in\mathbb{N}\text{,}\) consider the supremum and infimum of the terms from \(a_N\) onward: \(\displaystyle s_N = \sup_{n\geq N} a_n\) and \(\displaystyle i_N = \inf_{n\geq N} a_n\text{.}\) The limit superior and limit inferior of \((a_n)_{n=0}^{\infty}\) are defined as:

\[ \begin{aligned} \limsup_{n\to \infty}a_n &:= \lim_{N\to\infty} s_N = \inf_{N\geq 0} s_N=\inf_{N\geq 0}\sup_{n\geq N} a_n, \\ \liminf_{n\to \infty}a_n &:= \lim_{N\to\infty} i_N = \sup_{N\geq 0} i_N=\sup_{N\geq 0}\inf_{n\geq N} a_n. \end{aligned} \]

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: The limit superior and limit inferior describe the largest and smallest "long-run" accumulation points of a sequence, essentially capturing its eventual upper and lower bounds.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• The limit superior and limit inferior of a sequence always exist.
  • A sequence converges if and only if its \(\limsup\) and \(\liminf\) are equal and finite; otherwise, it's divergent.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• For \(a_n = (-1)^n\): \(\limsup\limits_{n\to \infty}a_n = 1\text{,}\) \(\liminf\limits_{n\to \infty}a_n = -1\text{.}\)
  • For \(a_n = 1/2^n\): \(\limsup\limits_{n\to \infty}a_n = \liminf\limits_{n\to \infty}a_n = 0\text{.}\)

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
Let \(n,\,k \in\mathbb N^+\). A function \(\boldsymbol{f}\colon \mathbb{R}^n\to \mathbb{R}^k\) is termed a linear transformation/map if it is a homogeneous linear function, i.e., a function that can be represented as \(\boldsymbol f(\boldsymbol x)=\boldsymbol A \boldsymbol x,\) where \(\boldsymbol A\in\mathbb R^{k\times n}\) is a \(k\times n\) real-valued matrix. In particular, a linear transformation from \(\mathbb R^n\) to \(\mathbb R\) is a homogeneous polynomial on \(\mathbb R^n\) with terms all of degree one, i.e., it has the general expression

\[ f(x_1,\,x_2,\,\dots,\,x_n)=a_1x_1+a_2x_2+\cdots+a_nx_n. \]

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
A linear transformation upholds vector addition and scalar multiplication, e.g., for any \(\boldsymbol{x}, \boldsymbol{y} \in \mathbb{R}^n\) and \(c \in \mathbb{R}\), it holds:

\[ \boldsymbol{f}(\boldsymbol{x}+\boldsymbol{y}) = \boldsymbol{f}(\boldsymbol{x}) + \boldsymbol{f}(\boldsymbol{y}), \quad \boldsymbol{f}(c\boldsymbol{x}) = c\boldsymbol{f}(\boldsymbol{x}), \]

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• The graph of a linear transformation from \(\mathbb R^n\) to \(\mathbb R\) is a hyperplane of dimension \(n\) that goes through the origin.
  • Level sets of linear transformations from \(\mathbb{R}^n\) to \(\mathbb{R}\) are a collection of parallel hyperplanes.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• \(f(x,y)=x+y\) is a linear transformation.
  • \(f(x,y,z)=x-y+2z+1\) is not a linear transformation.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
The maximum norm of \(\boldsymbol x=(x_1,x_2,\ldots,x_n)\) in an \(n\)-dimensional real coordinate space \(\mathbb R^n\) with fixed Cartesian coordinate system is:

\[ \|\boldsymbol x\|_\infty=\max_{1\leq i\leq n}|x_i|. \]

Correspondingly, the Chebyshev distance between \(\boldsymbol x=(x_1,x_2,\ldots,x_n)\) and \(\boldsymbol y=(y_1,y_2,\ldots,y_n)\) is calculated as:

\[ d_\infty(\boldsymbol x,\boldsymbol y)=\max_{1\leq i\leq n}|x_i-y_i|. \]

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: The maximum norm is the limiting case of the \(p\)-norm when \(p\to+\infty\).

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• The closed unit ball in the maximum norm is an axis-aligned hypercube
\[ \overline{\boldsymbol B}_{d_\infty}(\boldsymbol 0,1)=[-1,1]^n. \]

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
A metric space \((\boldsymbol{X}, d)\) consists of a set of points \(\boldsymbol{X}\) and a distance function (or metric) \(d\colon \boldsymbol{X} \times \boldsymbol{X} \to [0,+\infty)\) that maps pairs of points to nonnegative real values. The metric adheres to the following properties:

  1. Non-negativity: \(d(\boldsymbol{x},\boldsymbol{y}) \geq 0\) for any \(\boldsymbol{x}, \boldsymbol{y} \in \boldsymbol{X}\text{.}\)
  2. Identity of indiscernibles: \(d(\boldsymbol{x},\boldsymbol{y}) = 0\) if and only if \(\boldsymbol{x}=\boldsymbol{y}\text{.}\)
  3. Symmetry: \(d(\boldsymbol{x},\boldsymbol{y}) = d(\boldsymbol{y},\boldsymbol{x})\) for any \(\boldsymbol{x}, \boldsymbol{y} \in \boldsymbol{X}\text{.}\)
  4. Triangle inequality: \(d(\boldsymbol{x},\boldsymbol{z}) \leq d(\boldsymbol{x},\boldsymbol{y}) + d(\boldsymbol{y},\boldsymbol{z})\) for any \(\boldsymbol{x}, \boldsymbol{y}, \boldsymbol{z} \in \boldsymbol{X}\text{.}\)

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: A metric space is just a set of points with a clear and reasonable rule for measuring the distance between any two of them.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Metrics are always nonnegative. The only point at a zero distance from a point \(\boldsymbol{x}\) is \(\boldsymbol{x}\) itself.
  • Metrics are symmetric and adhere to the triangle inequality.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• The Euclidean distance in \(\mathbb{R}^n\) is defined as \(\displaystyle d(\boldsymbol{x}, \boldsymbol{y}) = \left(\sum_{i=1}^n (x_i - y_i)^2\right)^{1/2}\text{.}\)
  • The complex numbers \(\mathbb{C}\) with the distance function (based on modulus) \(d(z,w) = |z-w|\) form a metric space.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
A monomial on \(\mathbb R^n\) is a function from \(\mathbb R^n\) to \(\mathbb R\) is a product of real coefficients and variables raised to nonnegative integer powers, i.e., a monomial has the general expression

\[ f(x_1,x_2,\dots,x_n) = a x_1^{k_1} x_2^{k_2} \cdots x_n^{k_n}, \]

with constant \(a \in \mathbb{R}\) and exponents \(k_1,\, \dots,\, k_n \in \mathbb{N}\). The total degree of a monomial on \(\mathbb R^n\) is the sum of the exponents of all variables appearing in that monomial, i.e., \(k_1+\cdots+k_n\).

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
A monomial is a simple expression made by multiplying a constant with each variable raised to a whole number power.

Its total degree is the sum of those powers, telling you how many factors of variables appear in total.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• The product of two monomials is again a monomial. The exponents add componentwise, and the constant multiplies.
  • Every monomial is a homogeneous function whose degree equals its total degree.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• \(f(x,y)=-2x^2y\)  is a monomial with exponents \(k_1=2\), \(k_2=1\), total degree \(3\).
  • The monomial \(f(x,y)=x^4\) has \(k_1=4\), \(k_2=0\), total degree \(4\).

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
A norm on a vector space \(\boldsymbol{V}\) over the scalar field \(\mathbb{F}\) (commonly \(\mathbb{R}\)) is a function \(\|\cdot\|\colon \boldsymbol{V}\to[0,+\infty)\) that adheres to the following criteria:

  1. Non-negativity and definiteness: For any \(\boldsymbol{x} \in \boldsymbol{V}\), \(\|\boldsymbol{x}\| \geq 0\), and \(\|\boldsymbol{x}\| = 0\) if and only if \(\boldsymbol{x} = \boldsymbol{0}\).
  2. Positive homogeneity: For any scalar \(c \in \mathbb{F}\) and any \(\boldsymbol{x} \in \boldsymbol{V}\), \(\|c\boldsymbol{x}\| = |c|\cdot\|\boldsymbol{x}\|\).
  3. Triangle inequality: For any \(\boldsymbol{x}, \boldsymbol{y} \in \boldsymbol{V}\): \(\|\boldsymbol{x} + \boldsymbol{y}\| \leq \|\boldsymbol{x}\| + \|\boldsymbol{y}\|\).

A normed vector space \((\boldsymbol{V}, \|\cdot\|)\) is a vector space \(\boldsymbol{V}\) over the scalar field \(\mathbb{F}\) (commonly \(\mathbb{R}\)), equipped with a norm \(\|\cdot\|\).

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
A norm is a rule that assigns a length to every vector in a consistent way.

A normed vector space is just a vector space where every vector has such a length, and scaling or adding vectors behaves as you would expect.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text: • Given a normed vector space \((\boldsymbol{V}, \|\cdot\|)\), one can define the metric as \(d(\boldsymbol{x},\boldsymbol{y}) = \|\boldsymbol{x} - \boldsymbol{y}\|,\) making \((\boldsymbol{V}, d)\) inherently a metric space.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• The real line \(\mathbb{R}\) with the absolute-value norm forms a normed vector space over \(\mathbb{R}\).
  • The plane \(\mathbb{R}^2\) with the Euclidean norm is similarly a normed vector space. Using the taxicab norm, \(\mathbb{R}^2\) remains a normed vector space.

docs.title: Theorem
docs.text: Let \((f_n)_{n=1}^\infty\) be a sequence of bounded functions on \(X\). We say the series \(\displaystyle \sum_{n=1}^\infty f_n(x)\) is normally convergent if the series of uniform norms of the terms of the series converges, i.e., \(\displaystyle \sum_{n=1}^\infty \|f_n\|_\infty<+\infty.\)

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: Normal convergence means the functions are so well controlled that their worst-case contributions are summable.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Normal convergence implies uniform absolute convergence, which in turn implies uniform convergence, which in turn implies pointwise convergence, i.e.,
\[ \sum_{n=1}^\infty \|f_n\|_\infty<+\infty\;\implies\; \sum_{n=1}^\infty |f_n(x)|\rightrightarrows f\;\implies\; \sum_{n=1}^\infty f_n(x)\rightrightarrows f\;\implies\; \sum_{n=1}^\infty f_n(x)\to f. \]

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Uniform absolute convergence does not imply normal convergence. Consider $\(f(x)=\begin{cases} \displaystyle \, 1/n, &x=n,\\[2pt] \displaystyle \, 0, &x\neq n.\end{cases}\)$Then the series \(\displaystyle \sum_{n=1}^\infty |f_n(x)|\) is uniformly convergent, however the series of uniform norms is the harmonic series and thus diverges.

docs.title: Open and Closed Sets in a Metric Space
Definition
docs.text:
For a metric space \((\boldsymbol{X},d)\) and its subset \(\boldsymbol{E}\):

  • \(\boldsymbol{E}\) is closed if it includes all of its boundary points, i.e., \(\partial \boldsymbol{E} \subseteq \boldsymbol{E}\).
  • \(\boldsymbol{E}\) is open if it doesn't include any of its boundary points, i.e., \(\partial \boldsymbol{E} \cap \boldsymbol{E} = \varnothing\).
  • \(\boldsymbol{E}\) is neither open nor closed if it includes some but not all of its boundary points.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: Open sets keep their boundaries out. Closed sets keep their boundaries in. Sets that include some boundary points but not others are neither open nor closed.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• A set \(\boldsymbol{E}\) is open if and only if \(\boldsymbol{E} = \mathrm{int}\boldsymbol{E}\).
  • A set \(\boldsymbol F\) is closed if and only if every convergent sequence \((\boldsymbol{x}_i)_{i=1}^{\infty}\) within \(\boldsymbol{F}\) converges to a limiting point lying in \(\boldsymbol{F}\).
  • A set \(\boldsymbol{E}\) is open if and only if its complement \(\boldsymbol{E}^\complement=\boldsymbol{X}\setminus \boldsymbol{E}\) is closed.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• The open metric ball \(\boldsymbol{B}(\boldsymbol{x}_0, \varepsilon)\) is open.
  • \(\varnothing\) is both open and closed. It has no boundary points to include or exclude.
  • Under the discrete metric, every set is both open and closed. Each singleton set has a ball containing only itself.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
For a metric space \((\boldsymbol{X},d)\), a point \(\boldsymbol{x}_0\) in \(\boldsymbol{X}\), and \(r > 0\), the open metric ball \(\boldsymbol{B}_{(\boldsymbol{X},d)}(\boldsymbol{x}_0,r)\) in \(\boldsymbol{X}\), centered at \(\boldsymbol{x}_0\) with radius \(r\) in metric \(d\), is defined as the following set:

\[ \boldsymbol{B}_{(\boldsymbol{X},d)}(\boldsymbol{x}_0,r) = \{\boldsymbol{x} \in \boldsymbol{X} \colon d(\boldsymbol{x}, \boldsymbol{x}_0) < r\}. \]

If the context is clear, we'll abbreviate this as \(\boldsymbol{B}_d(\boldsymbol{x}_0,r)\) or simply \(\boldsymbol{B}(\boldsymbol{x}_0,r).\)

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
An open metric ball is the set of all points whose distance from the center is strictly less than the radius.

It is the basic building block for defining open sets and continuity in metric spaces.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Open balls are open sets.
  • A subset of a metric space is open if and only if it can be written as a union of open balls.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• In \(\mathbb{R}^2\) with the usual distance, \(\boldsymbol B((0,0),1)\) is the open disc of radius \(1\) centered at the origin. Points with \(x^2 + y^2 < 1\) are elements of this ball.
  • In \(\mathbb{R}^2\) with \(d_1\), \(\boldsymbol B((0,0),1)\) is a diamond shape with vertices at \((\pm1,0)\) and \((0,\pm1)\).
  • In any set with the discrete metric, \(\boldsymbol B(\boldsymbol x,1) = \{\boldsymbol x\}\) and \(\boldsymbol B(\boldsymbol x,0.5) = \{\boldsymbol x\}\), but \(\boldsymbol B(\boldsymbol x,2)\) is the whole space.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
Let \(\boldsymbol{x}=(x_1,x_2, \ldots,x_n)\in\mathbb{R}^n\). For \(p\in[1,+\infty]\), the \(\boldsymbol{p}\)-norm, denoted \(\|\cdot\|_p\), is defined on \(\mathbb{R}^n\) by:

\[ \|\boldsymbol{x}\|_p = \left(\sum_{i=1}^n |x_i|^p\right)^{\frac{1}{p}}. \]

Correspondingly, the \(p\)-metric \(d_p\) is defined as

\[ d_p(\boldsymbol x,\boldsymbol y)=\left(\sum_{i=1}^n |x_i-y_i|^p\right)^{\frac{1}{p}}. \]

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: The \(p\)-norm is a way of measuring the size of a vector by raising each coordinate's absolute value to the \(p\)-th power, summing them, and taking the \(p\)-th root.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text: • The smallest permissible value for \(p\) in the \(p\)-norm is \(1\).

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• The Euclidean distance \(d_2\) is a particular \(p\)-metric when \(p=2\).
  • The taxicab distance \(d_1\) is a particular \(p\)-metric when \(p=1\).
  • The maximum norm \(\|\cdot\|_\infty\) is a particular \(p\)-norm when \(p=+\infty\).

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
Let \(\boldsymbol{E} \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n\) and consider a function \(\boldsymbol{f} \colon \boldsymbol{E} \to \mathbb{R}^k\). For an interior point \(\boldsymbol{x}_0\) of \(\boldsymbol{E}\) and an integer \(1 \leq j \leq n\), the partial derivative of \(\boldsymbol{f}\) with respect to the \(x_j\)-variable at \(\boldsymbol{x} = \boldsymbol{x}_0\), denoted by \(\displaystyle \frac{\partial \boldsymbol{f}}{\partial x_j}(\boldsymbol{x}_0)\), is given by

\[ \frac{\partial \boldsymbol{f}}{\partial x_j}(\boldsymbol{x}_0) = \lim_{{t\to0}} \frac{\boldsymbol{f}(\boldsymbol{x}_0 + t\boldsymbol{e}_j) - \boldsymbol{f}(\boldsymbol{x}_0)}{t} = \left.\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}\boldsymbol{f}(\boldsymbol{x}_0 + t\boldsymbol{e}_j)\,\right|_{t=0}, \]

where \(\boldsymbol{e}_j\) represents the unit vector in the positive direction of the \(j\)-th coordinate, provided the limit exists.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
The partial derivative measures how the function changes when you nudge only one coordinate while keeping all others fixed.

It is like taking an ordinary derivative in the direction of that coordinate axis.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• The partial derivative \(\displaystyle \frac{\partial \boldsymbol{f}}{\partial x_j}(\boldsymbol{x}_0)\) exists if and only if both \(\mathrm{D}_{\boldsymbol{e}_j}\boldsymbol{f}(\boldsymbol{x}_0)\) and \(\mathrm{D}_{-\boldsymbol{e}_j}\boldsymbol{f}(\boldsymbol{x}_0)\) exist and are negatives of each other. In such a scenario, we have \(\displaystyle \frac{\partial \boldsymbol{f}}{\partial x_j}(\boldsymbol{x}_0)=\mathrm{D}_{\boldsymbol{e}_j}\boldsymbol{f}(\boldsymbol{x}_0).\)
  • For vector \(\displaystyle \boldsymbol{v} = (v_1,\,\ldots,\,v_n)= \sum_{j=1}^n v_j\boldsymbol{e}_j\), we have \(\displaystyle \mathrm{D}_{\boldsymbol{v}}\boldsymbol{f}(\boldsymbol{x}_0) = \sum_{j=1}^n v_j \frac{\partial }{\partial x_j}\boldsymbol{f}(\boldsymbol{x}_0).\)
  • If all the partial derivatives are both existent within a neighborhood and continuous at the center, then \(\boldsymbol{f}\) is totally differentiable at this point.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • The partial derivative of \(f(x,y) = 3x^2y^2 + 4xy^3 + 7y\) with respect to the first variable is \(\dfrac{\partial }{\partial x}f(x,y) = 6xy^2 + 4y^3.\)

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: In the metric space \((\boldsymbol{X}, d_{\boldsymbol{X}})\text{,}\) a subset \(\boldsymbol{E}\) is termed path-connected if, for any two distinct points \(\boldsymbol{a}, \boldsymbol{b} \in \boldsymbol{E}\text{,}\) a path \(\boldsymbol{p}\colon [0,1] \to \boldsymbol{E}\) exists such that \(\boldsymbol{p}(0) = \boldsymbol{a}\) and \(\boldsymbol{p}(1) = \boldsymbol{b}\text{.}\)

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: You can walk from any point to any other point in a path-connected set without ever leaving the set.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text: • In the metric space \((\boldsymbol{X}, d_{\boldsymbol{X}})\text{,}\) any path-connected subset of \(\boldsymbol{X}\) is connected.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• The topologist's sine curve is connected but not path-connected:
\[ \{(0,0)\}\cup \{(x,\sin (1/x)) \colon x\in (0,+\infty)\}. \]

- The collection of line segments joining the origin to points \((1, 1/n)\) for all positive integers \(n\), together with the point \((1,0)\) is also connected but not path-connected.

docs.title: Path
docs.text: This page presents the Math III: Analysis treatment. See also the treatment in OR Modelling. Mastery is recorded separately for each course context.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: In a metric space \((\boldsymbol{X}, d_{\boldsymbol{X}})\), a path is a continuous function \(\boldsymbol{p}\colon [0,1] \to \boldsymbol{X}\). If for two points \(\boldsymbol{a}, \boldsymbol{b} \in \boldsymbol{X}\), the path \(\boldsymbol{p}\) satisfies \(\boldsymbol{p}(0) = \boldsymbol{a}\) and \(\boldsymbol{p}(1) = \boldsymbol{b}\), it is termed as a path from \(\boldsymbol{a}\) to \(\boldsymbol{b}\).

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
A path is a continuous journey from one point to another within the space.

It is like drawing a curve without lifting your pencil, with the curve entirely contained in the space.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• If \(\boldsymbol p\) is a path from \(\boldsymbol a\) to \(\boldsymbol b\) and \(\boldsymbol q\) is a path from \(\boldsymbol b\) to \(\boldsymbol c\), then it is possible to construct a path from \(\boldsymbol a\) to \(\boldsymbol c\) using \(\boldsymbol p\) and \(\boldsymbol q\). This is called the concatenation.
  • For any path \(\boldsymbol p\) from \(\boldsymbol a\) to \(\boldsymbol b\), the reverse path \(\boldsymbol p(1−t)\) is a path from \(\boldsymbol b\) to \(\boldsymbol a\).

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• In Euclidean space, the function \(p(t)=(1−t)a+tb\) is a path from \(a\) to \(b\).
  • The function \(p(t)=(\cos⁡(2\pi t),\sin(⁡2\pi t))\) is a path from \((1,0)\) back to itself (a loop).

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: Let \((f_n)_{n=1}^{\infty}\) be a sequence of functions \(f_n\colon X_n\to \mathbb{R}\) and \(f\colon X \rightarrow \mathbb{R}\) be another function. We say that \((f_n)_{n=1}^{\infty}\) converges pointwise to \(\boldsymbol{f}\) on \(\boldsymbol{X}\) and write \(f_n\to f\text{,}\) if for every \(x \in X\text{,}\) \(\displaystyle \lim _{n \rightarrow \infty} f_n(x) = f(x)\text{.}\)

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: Pointwise convergence means that for each fixed point, the function values get closer to a limit as the index goes to infinity.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Pointwise convergence guarantees that the limit exists at each individual point.
  • Pointwise convergence does not preserve boundedness, limits/continuity, differentiability, or integrals.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• \(f_n(x) = \dfrac{n}{nx + 1}\) converges pointwise to \(f(x)=1/x\text{.}\)
  • \(f_n(x)=\dfrac{x^2}{\sqrt{x^2+1 / n}}\) converges pointwise to \(f(x)=|x|.\)

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: A polynomial on \(\mathbb R^n\) is a real-valued function that is a finite sum of monomials on \(\mathbb R^n\). The degree of a polynomial on \(\mathbb R^n\) is is defined as the maximum, over all its monomials, of the  total degree of each monomial.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
A polynomial in several variables is a finite combination of monomials added together.

Its degree is the highest total degree among all the monomials that appear with nonzero coefficient.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• The degree of the sum of two polynomials is at most the maximum of their degrees. The degree of the product of two polynomials is the sum of their degrees.
  • Polynomials are infinitely differentiable. All partial derivatives of all orders exist and are themselves polynomials (or zero).

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• \(f(x,y) = x^2 + 2xy + y^2 + x + 1\) is a polynomial of degree 2. Its highest total degree comes from \(x^2\), \(xy\), and \(y^2\), all degree 2.
  • \(f(x,y) = x^3 + xy + y^2\) has degree 3 from the \(x^3\) term.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: Let \(a \in \mathbb{R}\text{.}\) A power series centered at \(\boldsymbol{a}\) is expressed as \(\displaystyle\sum_{n=0}^\infty c_n (x-a)^n\text{,}\) where \((c_n)_{n=0}^\infty\) is a sequence of real numbers, independent of \(x\text{.}\) We refer to \(c_n\) as the \(\boldsymbol{n}\)-th coefficient of the power series.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: A power series is an infinite sum of power functions.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text: • This is the formal definition of power series since it is not discussed whether such a series is convergent or divergent for different \(x\text{.}\)

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• Any polynomial is a special case of a power series, since the coefficients \(c_n\) are allowed to be zero.
  • \(1+x+\dfrac{x^2}{2}+\dfrac{x^3}{6}+\cdots\) is a power series.

docs.title: Quadratic Form
docs.text: This page presents the Math III: Analysis treatment. See also the treatment in Math II: Linear Algebra. Mastery is recorded separately for each course context.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
A quadratic form is a polynomial from \(\mathbb R^n\) to \(\mathbb R\) with terms all of degree two, i.e., a quadratic on \(\mathbb R^n\) has the general expression:

\[ f(\boldsymbol x) = \boldsymbol{x}^\intercal \boldsymbol{A}\boldsymbol{x}= \sum_{i,j=1,\,i\leq j}^{n} a_{ij} x_i x_j. \]

where \(\boldsymbol{x}=(x_1\,x_2,\,\dots,\,x_n)^\intercal\) and \(\boldsymbol A=(a_{ij})_{1\leq i,j\leq n}\) is any nonzero \(n\times n\) matrix.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
A quadratic form is a polynomial where every term has exactly two variables multiplied together, possibly the same variable squared.

It can always be written using a symmetric matrix that encodes all the coefficients.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text: • For any quadratic form, the associated matrix is not unique. However, there always exists a unique symmetric matrix \(\overline {\boldsymbol A}=(\boldsymbol A+\boldsymbol A^\intercal)/2\) where \(\boldsymbol A\) is any associated matrix of the quadratic form.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• \(f(x,y) = x^2 + y^2\) is a quadratic form. Both terms are squares, degree two.
  • \(f(x,y) = 3x^2 + 4xy + 5y^2\) is a quadratic form. It includes a square term, a cross term, and another square term.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: For a given power series \(\displaystyle \sum_{n=0}^\infty c_n (x-a)^n\text{,}\) its radius of convergence \(R\) is a nonnegative real number or \(+\infty\) such that the series converges if \(|x-a|<R\) and diverges if \(|x-a|>R\text{.}\) The interval of convergence is the set of all values of \(x\) for which the series converges.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: The radius of convergence tells you how far from the center point a power series will reliably converge.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text: • The convergence of \(\displaystyle \sum_{n=0}^\infty c_n (x-a)^n\) at \(x=a-R\) and \(x=a+R\) is to be determined case-by-case.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• The series \(\displaystyle \sum_{n=0}^\infty n(-2)^n (x-3)^n\) with \(R = 1/2\) centered at \(a = 3\), converges pointwise on \(\left(5/2, 7/2\right)\) and uniformly on any closed interval within it. Its convergence interval is \(\left(5/2, 7/2\right)\) since the series diverges at both endpoints.
  • The series \(\displaystyle \sum_{n=0}^\infty 2^{n^2} (x+2)^n\) with \(R = 0\) centered at \(a = -2\), converges solely at its center \(x = -2.\)

docs.title: Proposition
docs.text:
Consider the series \(\displaystyle \sum_{n=1}^\infty a_n\) where \(a_n\in\mathbb{R}\text{.}\) Let \(\displaystyle L=\lim_{n \to \infty} \left| \dfrac{a_{n+1}}{a_n} \right|\text{,}\) then:

  • If \(L < 1\text{,}\) the series converges. Moreover, \(\displaystyle \sum_{n=1}^\infty |a_n|\) also converges.
  • If \(L > 1\text{,}\) the series diverges.
  • If \(L = 1\) or the limit does not exist, the test is inconclusive.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: The ratio test states that a series converges if the limit of the ratio of consecutive terms is less than 1, and diverges if it is greater than 1.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text: • For the power series \(\displaystyle \sum_{n=0}^\infty c_n (x - a)^n\text{,}\) the radius of convergence \(R\) can be found using \(\displaystyle R = \lim_{n \to \infty} \left| \dfrac{c_{n}}{c_{n+1}} \right|\) if the limit exists or tends to infinity.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• \(\displaystyle \sum_{n=1}^\infty \frac{n}{\mathrm{e}^n}\) is convergent since \(\displaystyle L=\lim_{n \to \infty} \left| \dfrac{(n+1)/\mathrm{e}^{n+1}}{n/\mathrm{e}^n} \right| =\dfrac{1}{\mathrm{e}}<1\text{.}\)
  • \(\displaystyle \sum_{n=1}^\infty \frac{2^n}{n}\) diverges since \(\displaystyle L=\lim_{n \to \infty} \left| \dfrac{2^{n+1}/(n+1)}{2^n/n} \right| =2>1\text{.}\)
  • When \(L=1\text{,}\) both convergent and divergent series exist, e.g., \(\displaystyle \sum_{n=1}^\infty \frac{1}{n}\) diverges while \(\displaystyle \sum_{n=1}^\infty \frac{1}{n^2}\) converges.
  • \(\displaystyle \sum_{n=0}^\infty \frac{x^n}{n!}\) converges for all \(x\in\mathbb{R}\) since \(\displaystyle R=\lim_{n \to \infty} \left| \dfrac{(n+1)!}{n!} \right|=+\infty\text{.}\)
  • \(\displaystyle \sum_{n=0}^\infty 2^n(x-3)^n\) converges for \(|x-3|<1/2\) since \(\displaystyle R=\lim_{n \to \infty} \left| \dfrac{2^{n}}{2^{n+1}} \right|=\dfrac{1}{2}\text{.}\)
  • \(\displaystyle \sum_{n=0}^\infty n!(x+1)^n\) diverges for all \(x\) except \(x=-1\) since \(\displaystyle R=\lim_{n \to \infty} \left| \dfrac{n!} {(n+1)!}\right|=0\text{.}\)

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
Let \(f\colon E \to \mathbb{R}\) be a function where \(E \subseteq \mathbb{R}\text{.}\) We say:

  • \(f\) is real analytic at \(\boldsymbol{x=a}\) if \(a\) is an interior point of \(E\) and there exists a power series \(\displaystyle \sum_{n=0}^\infty c_n (x-a)^n\) centered at \(a\) and an open interval \((a-r, a+r) \subseteq E\) (for some \(r > 0\)) where this series converges to \(f\text{.}\)
  • \(f\) is real analytic on \(\boldsymbol{E}\) if \(E\) is an open set and \(f\) is real analytic at every point \(a \in E\text{.}\)

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: A function is real analytic at a point if it can be represented by a power series that matches the function exactly in a small interval around that point.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• The convergence type here is not limited, but if we consider a closed subinterval of \((a-r,a+r)\text{,}\) then it is the uniform convergence.
  • Sums, products, and compositions of real analytic functions are also real analytic.
  • A real analytic function is always infinitely differentiable, and all of its higher-order derivatives are real analytic.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• Almost all common functions are real analytic.
  • Most piecewise functions are not real analytic, though they can be even infinitely differentiable. For instance, the following function is a particular non-analytic but infinitely differentiable function.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: The real coordinate space of dimension \(n\), denoted \(\mathbb {R} ^{n}\), is the set of all ordered \(n\)-tuples of real numbers.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
Real coordinate space is just the collection of all points with \(n\) real coordinates.

It is the standard space used for doing multivariable calculus and linear algebra.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text: • With component-wise addition and scalar multiplication, the real coordinate space is a real vector space.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Special cases are called the real line \(\mathbb R^1\), the real coordinate plane \(\mathbb R^2\), and the real coordinate three-dimensional space \(\mathbb R^3\).

docs.title: Proposition
docs.text:
Consider the series \(\displaystyle \sum_{n=1}^\infty a_n\) where \(a_n \in \mathbb{R}\text{.}\) Let \(\displaystyle L = \limsup_{n \to \infty} \sqrt[n]{|a_n|}\), then:

  • If \(L < 1\text{,}\) the series converges. Moreover, \(\displaystyle \sum_{n=1}^\infty |a_n|\) also converges.
  • If \(L > 1\text{,}\) the series diverges.
  • If \(L = 1\text{,}\) the test is inconclusive.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: The root test determines convergence by comparing the limit of the \(n\)-th root of the terms' absolute values to 1.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• One of the differences between the ratio test and the root test is that the limit in the ratio test may not exist, while the limit in the root test always exists.
  • The radius of convergence of a power series \(\displaystyle \sum_{n=0}^\infty c_n (x-a)^n\) is given by
\[ R=\frac{1}{\limsup\limits_{n\to\infty} |c_n|^{1/n}}. \]

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• \(\displaystyle \sum_{n=1}^\infty \frac{n}{\mathrm{e}^n}\) is convergent since \(\displaystyle L=\limsup_{n \to \infty} \sqrt[n]{\left| \frac{n}{\mathrm{e}^n} \right|} = \frac{1}{\mathrm{e}}<1\text{.}\)
  • \(\displaystyle \sum_{n=1}^\infty \frac{2^n}{n}\) diverges since \(\displaystyle L=\limsup_{n \to \infty} \sqrt[n]{\left|\frac{2^n}{n} \right|} = 2>1\text{.}\)
  • When \(L=1\text{,}\) both convergent and divergent series exist, e.g., \(\displaystyle \sum_{n=1}^\infty \frac{1}{n}\) diverges while \(\displaystyle \sum_{n=1}^\infty \frac{1}{n^2}\) converges.
  • \(\displaystyle \sum_{n=0}^\infty n(-2)^n (x-3)^n\) is convergent for \(|x-3|<\dfrac{1}{2}\) since \(R = \dfrac{1}{\limsup\limits_{n \to\infty}|n\left(-2\right)^{n}|^{1/n}} = \dfrac{1}{2}\text{.}\)
  • \(\displaystyle \sum_{n=0}^\infty 2^{n^2} (x+2)^n\) is divergent except at \(x=-2\) since \(R= \dfrac{1}{\limsup\limits_{n \rightarrow \infty}|2^{n^{2}}|^{1/n}}= 0\text{.}\)

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: Let \((\boldsymbol{X},d_{\boldsymbol{X}})\) be a metric space. A subset \(\boldsymbol{E}\) of \(\boldsymbol{X}\) is termed sequentially compact if for every sequence \((\boldsymbol{x}_i)_{i=1}^\infty\) with each \(\boldsymbol{x}_i \in \boldsymbol{E}\text{,}\) there exists a convergent subsequence \((\boldsymbol{x}_{i_j})_{j=1}^\infty\) that converges to a point \(\boldsymbol{x} \in \boldsymbol{E}\text{.}\)

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
A set is sequentially compact if every infinite sequence drawn from it has a subsequence that converges to a point still inside the set.

It captures the idea that the set is "closed under taking limits of subsequences."

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text: • In any metric space, a set is compact if and only if it is sequentially compact. This gives two equivalent ways to think about compactness: open covers or convergent subsequences.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• The closed unit ball \(\{x\in \mathbb R^n\colon \|x\|\leq 1\}\) is sequentially compact. This fails in infinite dimensions.
  • Any finite set in any metric space is compact.
