docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
Let \(\boldsymbol{X}\) be a metric space. The metrics \(d_p\) and \(d_q\) on \(\boldsymbol{X}\) are termed strongly equivalent, denoted \(d_p\approx d_q\), if positive constants \(a\) and \(b\) exist such that for any \(\boldsymbol{x},\boldsymbol{y} \in \boldsymbol{X}\),

\[ a \cdot d_p(\boldsymbol{x},\boldsymbol{y}) \leq d_q(\boldsymbol{x},\boldsymbol{y}) \leq b \cdot d_p(\boldsymbol{x},\boldsymbol{y}). \]

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: Equivalent metrics measure distances in different scales but agree on which points are close or far apart.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• The strong equivalence relation possesses symmetry (\(d_p\approx d_q\) if and only if \(d_q\approx d_p\)), reflexivity (\(d_p\approx d_p\)) and transitivity (if \(d_p\approx d_q\) and \(d_q\approx d_r\), then \(d_p\approx d_r\)).
  • Strongly equivalent metrics induce the same notion of convergence.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• Any two \(p\)-metrics on \(\mathbb R^n\) are strongly equivalent.
  • The discrete metric, \(d_{\text{disc}}\), is not strongly equivalent to any of the \(p\)-metrics.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
The taxicab distance between points \(\boldsymbol x=(x_1,x_2,\ldots,x_n)\) and \(\boldsymbol y=(y_1,y_2,\ldots,y_n)\) in an \(n\)-dimensional real coordinate space \(\mathbb R^n\) with fixed Cartesian coordinate system is:

\[ d_1(\boldsymbol x,\boldsymbol y)=\sum_{i=1}^{n}|y_i-x_i|. \]

The taxicab norm, or known as \(\ell^1\) norm, of \(\boldsymbol x=(x_1,x_2,\ldots,x_n)\) is calculated as:

\[ \|\boldsymbol x\|_1=\sum_{i=1}^{n}|x_i|. \]

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: The taxicab distance represents the distance a taxi would travel between two points when restricted to cardinal directions (north, south, east, west) without moving diagonally or in any other curved path.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text: • The closed unit ball in the taxicab norm is an \(n\)-dimensional cross-polytope, e.g., a diamond in \(\mathbb R^2\) and a regular octahedron in \(\mathbb R^3\).

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
The polynomial that emerges from Taylor's theorem is termed the \(\boldsymbol{k}\)-th order Taylor polynomial for the function \(f\) at \(x=a\):

\[ P_{k}(x) = f(a) + f^{\prime}(a)(x-a) + \cdots + \frac{f^{(k)}(a)}{k !}(x-a)^{k}. \]

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
• The \(k\)-th order Taylor polynomial of \(f\) captures the initial \(k+1\) terms of its Taylor series (given existence) centered at the same point.
  • This polynomial stands out as the unique asymptotic best fit for the function \(f\text{.}\)

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• The \(k\)-th order Taylor polynomial and the function \(f\) share the same derivatives up to the \(k\)-th order.
  • One can write a Taylor polynomial for a function just from its first few derivatives, but the full Taylor series exists if the function is smooth, and the full series converges to the function only if it's real analytic.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• The 3rd order Taylor polynomial of \(\sin x\) around \(x=0\) is \(P_3(x) = x - \dfrac{x^3}{3!}\).
  • The 1st order Taylor polynomial of \(1/x\) around \(x = 1\) is \(P_1(x)=2-x\).

docs.title: Taylor Series
docs.text: This page presents the Math III: Analysis treatment. See also the treatment in Probability Distributions. Mastery is recorded separately for each course context.

docs.title: Proposition
docs.text:
Let \(a\) be an interior point of \(E\subseteq \mathbb{R}\text{,}\) and let \(f\colon E\to\mathbb{R}\) be real analytic at \(x=a\text{.}\) Then \(f\) has the power series expansion around \(x=a\):

\[ f(x) = \sum_{n=0}^\infty \frac{f^{(n)}(a)}{n!} (x-a)^n \quad \text{for all } x \in (a-r,a+r), \]

known as the Taylor series of \(f\) around \(x=a\text{.}\)

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: If a function is so smooth that it behaves exactly like an infinite polynomial near a point, then that polynomial is built entirely from its derivatives at that point.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• The Taylor series centered at the origin is called the Maclaurin series.
  • For any smooth function you can write down its Taylor series, but that series is guaranteed to converge to the function only if the function is real analytic.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• The Taylor series of the natural exponential function at the origin:
\[ \displaystyle \mathrm{e}^x = \sum_{n=0}^\infty \frac{x^n}{n!} = 1 + x + \dfrac{x^2}{2!} + \dfrac{x^3}{3!} + \cdots. \]
  • The generalized binomial expansion at the origin:
\[ \displaystyle (x+1)^r = \sum_{i=0}^\infty \binom{r}{i} x^i = 1 + rx + \frac{r(r-1)}{2}x^2 + \frac{r(r-1)(r-2)}{6}x^3 + \cdots. \]

docs.title: Theorem
docs.text:
Let \(k \geq 1\) be an integer and assume that the function \(f\colon \mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R}\) is \(k\)-times differentiable (not necessarily real analytic) at \(x=a\text{.}\) There exists a function \(\displaystyle h_k \colon \mathbb{R} \to\mathbb{R}\) such that \(\displaystyle \lim_{x\to a} h_k(x) = 0\) and

\[ f(x) = f(a) + f'(a)(x-a) + \cdots + \frac{f^{(k)}(a)}{k !}(x-a)^k + R_k(x) \]

where \(R_k(x)= h_k(x)(x-a)^k\) is called the Peano form of the remainder.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: One can approximate a smooth function near a point using a polynomial, and the error term behaves like \((x−a)^k\) multiplied by something that tends to \(0\) as \(x\) approaches \(a\).

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Using the little-\(o\) notation, the statement in Taylor's theorem reads as \(R_k(x)=o((x-a)^k)\text{,}\) as \(x\to a\text{.}\) In this case, we have the \(k\)-th order Taylor expansion:
\[ f(x) = f(a) + f'(a)(x-a) + \cdots + \frac{f^{(k)}(a)}{k !}(x-a)^{k} + o((x-a)^{k}). \]

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• \(\mathrm e^x=1+x+\dfrac{x^2}{2}+h_2(x)x^2\), where \(\displaystyle h_2(x)=\sum_{n=3}^\infty \dfrac{x^{n-2}}{n!}\).
  • \(\dfrac{1}{1-x}=1+x+x^2+h_2(x) x^2\), where \(\displaystyle h_2(x)=\sum_{n=3}^\infty x^{n-2}\), for \(|x|<1\).

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: Two metrics \(d_p\) and \(d_q\) on a space \(\boldsymbol{X}\) are termed (topologically) equivalent if they produce identical topology (the set of open subsets of \(\boldsymbol{X}\)) on \(\boldsymbol{X}\), i.e., a subset \(\boldsymbol{E} \subseteq \boldsymbol{X}\) is open with respect to \(d_p\) if and only if it's open under \(d_q\). This relationship is expressed as \(d_p \sim d_q.\)

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
Two metrics are topologically equivalent if they determine the same collection of open sets.

They may measure distances differently, but they agree on which points are close enough to be in the same open set.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text: • If two metrics are strongly equivalent, then they are topologically equivalent.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• The metric \(d_{\tan}(x,y)=|\tan x-\tan y|\) is topologically equivalent to the absolute value metric on \(\mathbb R\), but they are not strongly equivalent.
  • The discrete metric is not topologically equivalent to any \(p\)-metrics.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
A topology on a set \(\boldsymbol{X}\), often denoted by \(\boldsymbol{\tau}\), is a collection of subsets of \(\boldsymbol{X}\) that satisfies the following properties:

  1. Both the empty set and the entire set \(\boldsymbol{X}\) belong to \(\boldsymbol{\tau}\).
  2. Any union of elements in \(\boldsymbol{\tau}\) also belongs to \(\boldsymbol{\tau}\).
  3. The intersection of any finite number of elements in \(\boldsymbol{\tau}\) remains in \(\boldsymbol{\tau}\).

The pair \((\boldsymbol{X},\boldsymbol \tau)\) is called a topological space.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
A topology is a collection of open sets that tells you which points are close to which without using a distance.

It is the most general setting for studying continuity and convergence.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text: • Metric spaces are topological spaces. Every metric space induces a topology where open sets are unions of open metric balls.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • The trivial topology is the topology with the least possible number of open sets, namely the empty set and the entire space, i.e., \(\boldsymbol{\tau}=\{\varnothing, \boldsymbol X\}\).

docs.title: Total Derivative as a Linear Transformation
Definition
docs.text:
Let \(\boldsymbol{E}\subseteq \mathbb{R}^n\), let \(\boldsymbol{f}\colon \boldsymbol{E}\to\mathbb{R}^k\) be a function, let \(\boldsymbol{x}_0\in\mathrm{int}\boldsymbol{E}\), and let \(\boldsymbol{L}\colon \mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}^k\) be a linear transformation. We say that \(\boldsymbol{f}\) is (totally) differentiable at \(\boldsymbol{x}=\boldsymbol{x}_{\boldsymbol{0}}\) with (total) derivative \(\boldsymbol{L}\) if:

\[ \lim_{\substack{\boldsymbol{x}\to\boldsymbol{x}_0}}\frac{\|\boldsymbol{f}(\boldsymbol{x})-(\boldsymbol{f}(\boldsymbol{x}_0)+\boldsymbol{L}(\boldsymbol{x}-\boldsymbol{x}_0))\|}{\|\boldsymbol{x}-\boldsymbol{x}_0\|}=0. \]

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
Total differentiability means the function can be approximated near the point by a linear transformation, with the error shrinking to zero faster than the distance to the point.

It is the multidimensional version of the Newton's approximation, which is an equivalent formulation of differentiability.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• For the function \(\boldsymbol{f}\colon \mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}^k\) at \(\boldsymbol{x}=\boldsymbol{x}_0\), its derivative, \(\mathrm{D} \boldsymbol{f}_{\boldsymbol{x}_0}\), is a \(k\times n\) matrix or an equivalent linear transformation from \(\mathbb{R}^n\) to \(\mathbb{R}^k\).
  • \(\mathrm{D} \boldsymbol{f}_{\boldsymbol{x}_0}(\boldsymbol{h})\), where \(\boldsymbol{h}\) is an infinitesimal vector, provides an approximation of the shift in \(\boldsymbol{f}\) (a vector in \(\mathbb{R}^k\)) arising from the change \(\boldsymbol{h}\) in \(\boldsymbol{x}\) around \(\boldsymbol{x}=\boldsymbol{x}_0\) (a vector in \(\mathbb{R}^n\)).

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• The function \(\boldsymbol{f}(x,y) = (x^2,y^2)\) is differentiable at \(\boldsymbol{x}=(1,2)\) with the derivative \(\boldsymbol{L}(x,y) = (2x,4y)\).
  • The function \(f(x,y) = \sin(x^2+y)\) is differentiable at \((x,y)=(0,0)\) and the derivative is \(L(x,y)=y\).

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: Consider metric spaces \((\boldsymbol{X},d_{\boldsymbol{X}})\) and \((\boldsymbol{Y},d_{\boldsymbol{Y}})\), and a function \(\boldsymbol{f}\colon \boldsymbol{X}\to\boldsymbol{Y}\). We say \(\boldsymbol{f}\) is uniformly continuous on \(\boldsymbol{X}\) if, for any \(\varepsilon > 0\), there exists a \(\delta > 0\) such that for all \(\boldsymbol{x}_1,\boldsymbol{x}_2\in\boldsymbol{X}\) with \(d_{\boldsymbol{X}}(\boldsymbol{x}_1,\boldsymbol{x}_2)<\delta\), it holds that \(d_{\boldsymbol{Y}}(\boldsymbol{f}(\boldsymbol{x}_1),\boldsymbol{f}(\boldsymbol{x}_2))<\varepsilon\).

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: This is the general definition of uniform continuity where the metric functions are allowed to be potentially different metrics on possibly different spaces.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text: • Any continuous function defined on a compact set is uniformly continuous.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• Every constant function is uniformly continuous regardless of the metrics.
  • Every function from a discrete space is uniformly continuous.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: A function \(f\colon X \to \mathbb{R}\) is said to be uniformly continuous if, for every \(\varepsilon >0\text{,}\) there exists a \(\delta >0\) such that for all pairs of points \(x_1, x_2\in X\) with \(|x_1-x_2|<\delta\text{,}\) it holds that \(|f(x_1)-f(x_2)|<\varepsilon\text{.}\)

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: Uniform continuity means one fixed rule for “how small is small” works everywhere, while ordinary continuity may need different rules at different points.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Every uniformly continuous function is continuous, the converse doesn't necessarily hold.
  • \(f\) is uniformly continuous on \(X\) if and only if given two equivalent sequences \((x_n)_{n=1}^\infty\) and \((y_n)_{n=1}^\infty\) in \(X\text{,}\) sequences \((f(x_n))_{n=1}^\infty\) and \((f(y_n))_{n=1}^\infty\) are also equivalent.
  • A continuous function \(f\) is uniformly continuous on \((a, b)\) if and only if the right limit \(\displaystyle f(a^+)\) and the left limit \(\displaystyle f(b^-)\) both exist and are finite. In other words, continuous functions can fail to be uniformly continuous if they are unbounded on a bounded domain.
  • A differentiable function \(f\) is uniformly continuous on \((a,b)\) if \(f'\) is bounded. In other words, continuous functions can fail to be uniformly continuous if their slopes become unbounded on an infinite domain.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• The function \(f(x)=1/x\) is uniformly continuous on \((1,2)\), but not uniformly continuous on \((0,1)\).
  • The function \(g(x)=\sin x\) is uniformly continuous on any interval in this domain.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: Let \((f_n)_{n=1}^\infty\) be a sequence of functions defined on \(X \subseteq \mathbb{R}\) and \(f\colon X \rightarrow \mathbb{R}\) be another function. We say that \((f_n)_{n=1}^\infty\) converges uniformly to \(\boldsymbol{f}\) on \(\boldsymbol{X}\) and write \(f_n\rightrightarrows f\text{,}\) if for every \(\varepsilon > 0\text{,}\) there exists a positive integer \(N\) such that for all \(n > N\text{,}\) the inequality \(|f_n(x) - f(x) | < \varepsilon\) holds for all \(x \in X\text{.}\)

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: Uniform convergence means that the function values get close to the limit at the same speed for all points, not one point at a time.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Uniform convergence implies pointwise convergence.
  • Uniform convergence preserves boundedness, limits/continuity (uniform limit theorem), differentiability, and integrals.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• The function \(f_n(x) = x/n\) converges uniformly on \(\mathbb R\) to \(f(x)=0\text{.}\)
  • The function \(f_n(x) = \dfrac{n}{nx + 1}\) on \([0,1]\) converges pointwise, but not uniformly, to \(f(x)=1/x\text{.}\)

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
The uniform norm \(\|f\|_\infty\) of a bounded functions \(f\colon X \to \mathbb{R}\) is defined as:

\[ \|f\|_\infty = \sup_{x \in X} |f(x)|. \]

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: The uniform norm is the supremum of the absolute value of the function over its entire domain.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• A sequence of functions \((f_n)_{n=1}^\infty\) converges uniformly to a function \(f\) on \(X\) if and only if:
\[ \lim_{n \to \infty} \|f_n - f\|_\infty = 0. \]

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• For the function \(f\colon (0,+\infty) \to \mathbb{R}\) defined by \(f(x) = \mathrm{e}^{-x}\), we have \(\|f\|_\infty = 1.\)
  • For the function \(g\colon \mathbb R \to \mathbb{R}\) defined by \(g(x) = \sin x\), we have \(\|g\|_\infty = 1.\)

docs.title: Union and Intersection of Closed Sets
Proposition
docs.text: For a metric space \((\boldsymbol{X},d)\) and a collection of closed subsets \((\boldsymbol{E}_i)_{i=1}^\infty\) of \(\boldsymbol{X}\), the countable intersection \(\displaystyle\bigcap_{i=1}^\infty \boldsymbol{E}_i\) and the finite union \(\displaystyle \bigcup_{i=1}^k \boldsymbol{E}_i\) are also closed.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
Closed sets are preserved under finite unions and arbitrary intersections.

Infinite unions can break closedness.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Both \(X\) and \(\varnothing\) are always closed (and also open).
  • In fact any intersection of closed sets, not just countably many, is closed. This holds for uncountable families as well.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• In \(\mathbb{R}\), \(\displaystyle \bigcap_{n=1}^\infty [-1/n, 1/n] = {0}\) is closed. Shrinking closed intervals collapse to a single closed point.
  • In \(\mathbb{R}\), \(\displaystyle \bigcup_{n=1}^\infty [0, 1-1/n] = [0,1)\) is not closed. It is missing the endpoint \(1\).

docs.title: Union and Intersection of Open Sets
Proposition
docs.text: For a metric space \((\boldsymbol{X},d)\) and a collection of open subsets \((\boldsymbol{E}_i)_{i=1}^\infty\) of \(\boldsymbol{X}\), the countable union \(\displaystyle\bigcup_{i=1}^\infty \boldsymbol{E}_i\) and the finite intersection \(\displaystyle \bigcap_{i=1}^k \boldsymbol{E}_i\) are also open.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
Open sets are preserved under finite intersections and arbitrary unions.

Infinite intersections can break openness.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Both \(X\) and \(\varnothing\) are always open (and also closed).
  • In fact any union of open sets, not just countably many, is open. This holds for uncountable families as well.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• In \(\mathbb{R}\), \(\displaystyle \bigcup_{n=1}^\infty (0, 1-1/n) = (0,1)\) is open. Even though each interval misses the right endpoint, the union still does not include 1.
  • In \(\mathbb{R}\), \(\displaystyle \bigcap_{n=1}^\infty (-1/n, 1+1/n) = [0,1]\) is closed. The intersection includes the endpoints 0 and 1, which are not interior points.

docs.title: Theorem
docs.text: For a continuous function \(f\colon [a, b] \to \mathbb{R}\) and any \(\varepsilon > 0\text{,}\) there exists a polynomial \(P\colon [a, b]\to\mathbb{R}\) such that \(\|P-f\|_\infty < \varepsilon\text{.}\)

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: Any continuous function on a closed interval can be approximated as closely as desired by a polynomial.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text: • Polynomials are dense in \(C^0([a,b])\) with respect to the uniform norm.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• Any polynomial can be "approximated" by itself accurately.
  • Continuous functions, e.g., \(f(x)=\mathrm e^x\), over the entirety of \(\mathbb{R}\) aren't always uniformly approximable by polynomials.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
The Weierstrass function is defined as

\[ f(x) = \sum_{n=1}^\infty a^n \cos(b^n x) \]

where \(0<a<1\) and \(ab>1\text{.}\)

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
The Weierstrass function is one of the most famous examples of continuous but nowhere differentiable functions. In the original paper, this function is defined as \(\displaystyle \sum_{n=1}^\infty a^n \cos(b^n \pi x)\) where  \(0<a<1\text{,}\) \(b\) is a positive odd number, and \(ab>1+\dfrac{3\pi}{2}\text{.}\)

The Weierstrass function is based on the earlier Riemann function \(\displaystyle \sum_{n=1}^\infty \dfrac{\sin(n^2 x)}{n^2}\text{,}\) which has also been called the Weierstrass function in some textbooks.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• The Weierstrass function is continuous everywhere as long as \(0<a<1\text{.}\)
  • The Weierstrass function is nowhere differentiable if \(ab>1\text{.}\)

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • \(\displaystyle f(x) = \sum_{n=1}^\infty \frac{1}{2^n} \cos(3^n x)\) is a particular Weierstrass function.

docs.title: Theorem
docs.text: Suppose \((f_n)_{n=1}^\infty\) is a sequence of bounded functions on \(X\) such that the series \(\displaystyle \sum_{n=1}^\infty \|f_n\|_\infty\) converges. Then, the series \(\displaystyle \sum_{n=1}^\infty f_n(x)\rightrightarrows f\text{.}\)

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: Since each function is uniformly small and their sizes add up to a finite number, the whole series converges uniformly.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• The limit function \(f\) is also bounded on \(X\).
  • Due to the uniform limit theorem, if each \(f_n\) is continuous, then the limit function \(f\) is continuous.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• The series \(\displaystyle f(x) = \sum_{n=1}^\infty \frac{1}{2^n} \cos(3^n x)\) is convergent due to the Weierstrass \(M\)-test:
\[ \sum_{n=1}^\infty \left| \frac{1}{2^n} \cos(3^n x) \right| \leq \sum_{n=1}^\infty \frac{1}{2^n} = 1. \]

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
For an inequality constraint written as \(g_i(x)\le b_i\), the constraint is binding at a feasible point \(x^\ast\) if

\[ g_i(x^\ast)=b_i. \]

It is nonbinding or slack at \(x^\ast\) if

\[ g_i(x^\ast)<b_i. \]

The same idea applies to constraints written in other equivalent sign conventions.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: A binding constraint is tight at the chosen point. A nonbinding constraint still has room left and does not directly limit the current choice.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Only binding inequality constraints can carry nonzero multipliers in standard Kuhn-Tucker conditions.
  • The set of binding constraints is often called the active set.
  • Changing a nonbinding constraint slightly usually does not change the optimum locally.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• If \(x\le 10\) and the optimum has \(x=10\), the constraint is binding.
  • If \(x+y\le 5\) and the chosen point is \((1,2)\), the constraint is nonbinding because \(1+2<5\).

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
For an equality-constrained problem with Lagrangian \(L(x,\lambda)\) and constraint Jacobian \(Dg(x^\ast)\), the bordered Hessian matrix is the block matrix

\[ \begin{pmatrix} 0 & Dg(x^\ast)\\ Dg(x^\ast)^\top & H_xL(x^\ast,\lambda^\ast) \end{pmatrix}, \]

with the exact block orientation depending on whether gradients are written as rows or columns.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: The bordered Hessian packages the constraint linearization and the objective curvature into one matrix for second-order constrained tests.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• The zero block corresponds to the multiplier variables.
  • The Hessian block is taken with respect to the choice variables.
  • Determinants of selected bordered submatrices are used in bordered matrix tests.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• For one constraint \(g(x,y)=0\), a common bordered Hessian has first row and column built from \(g_x\) and \(g_y\).
  • For two equality constraints in three variables, the bordered Hessian has a \(2\) by \(2\) zero block and a \(3\) by \(3\) Hessian block.

docs.title: Theorem
docs.text:
Let \(Q(x)=x^\top Ax\) with \(A\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n}\) symmetric, and let the independent linear constraint set be \(Bx=0\) with \(B\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}\) and \(\operatorname{rank}(B)=m\). The bordered matrix is

\[ H= \begin{pmatrix} 0_m & B\\ B^\top & A \end{pmatrix}. \]

Ignore the first \(2m\) leading principal minors. For \(k=2m+1,\ldots,m+n\):

  • If \((-1)^m\det(H_k)>0\) for all relevant \(k\), then \(Q\) is positive definite on the constraint set.
  • If \((-1)^{k-m}\det(H_k)>0\) for all relevant \(k\), then \(Q\) is negative definite on the constraint set.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: The bordered matrix test checks curvature after linear constraints remove some directions. It is the constrained version of reading definiteness from determinant signs.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Definiteness on the whole space can change after restricting to a constraint set.
  • For positive definiteness, all relevant signs match \((-1)^m\).
  • For negative definiteness, relevant signs alternate and the full determinant has sign \((-1)^n\).

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• The form \(x_1^2-x_2^2\) is indefinite on \(\mathbb{R}^2\) but positive on the line \(x_1=2x_2\).
  • When \(n=3\) and \(m=1\), inspect \(\det(H_3)\) and \(\det(H_4)\) after ignoring the first two leading minors.

docs.title: Theorem
docs.text:
Let \(I\subseteq\mathbb{R}\) be an interval and let \(\gamma\colon I\to\mathbb{R}^n\) be a differentiable curve. Its velocity at \(t_0\) is

\[ \gamma'(t_0)= \begin{pmatrix} \gamma_1'(t_0)\\ \vdots\\ \gamma_n'(t_0) \end{pmatrix}. \]

If \(f\colon B\to\mathbb{R}\) is differentiable at \(\gamma(t_0)\in B\), then

\[ \frac{d}{dt}(f\circ\gamma)(t_0) =Df(\gamma(t_0))\gamma'(t_0) =\nabla f(\gamma(t_0))^\top\gamma'(t_0). \]

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: A curve describes motion through a multivariable state space. The chain rule says the value changes by combining the system's velocity with the local sensitivity of the value function.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• The derivative of \(f(\gamma(t))\) is the total derivative of \(f\) applied to the velocity of \(\gamma\).
  • If the velocity is a unit vector, the formula is a directional derivative.
  • The curve case is the one-dimensional input version of the multivariable chain rule.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• If \(f(x,y)=x^2+y^2\) and \(\gamma(t)=(t,2t)\), then \((f\circ\gamma)'(t)=10t\).
  • If \(f(x,y)=xy\) and \(\gamma(t)=(e^t,t^2)\), then \((f\circ\gamma)'(t)=e^t(t^2+2t)\).

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
For an inequality constraint written as \(c_i(x)\le 0\) with multiplier \(\lambda_i\ge 0\), complementary slackness is the condition

\[ \lambda_i c_i(x^\ast)=0. \]

Equivalently, either the constraint is binding or its multiplier is zero.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: Complementary slackness says that a constraint can matter through its multiplier only when it is actually tight.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• If \(c_i(x^\ast)<0\), then \(\lambda_i=0\).
  • If \(\lambda_i>0\), then \(c_i(x^\ast)=0\).
  • The condition is part of the Kuhn-Tucker system for inequality-constrained optimization.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• If \(x\le 4\) is written as \(x-4\le 0\) and the optimum has \(x=3\), then the multiplier must be \(0\).
  • If a multiplier for \(x\le 4\) is positive, then the optimum must satisfy \(x=4\).

docs.title: Convex and Concave Functions on \(\mathbb R^n\)
Definition
docs.text:
Let \(C\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be convex. A function \(f\colon C\to\mathbb R\) is convex if for all \(x,y\in C\) and all \(\lambda\in[0,1]\),

\[ f(\lambda x+(1-\lambda)y) \le \lambda f(x)+(1-\lambda)f(y). \]

It is concave if the inequality is reversed.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: A convex function lies below the straight interpolation of its values. A concave function lies above that interpolation.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• For convex functions, every local minimum is a global minimum.
  • For concave functions, every local maximum is a global maximum.
  • Strict convexity or strict concavity usually gives uniqueness of the corresponding optimum when it exists.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• The function \(f(x,y)=x^2+y^2\) is convex on \(\mathbb R^2\).
  • The function \(u(x,y)=\log x+\log y\) is concave on \((0,\infty)^2\).

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
A set \(C\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) is convex if for every \(x,y\in C\) and every \(\lambda\in[0,1]\),

\[ \lambda x+(1-\lambda)y\in C. \]

Equivalently, the whole line segment between any two points of \(C\) lies inside \(C\).

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: A convex set has no inward gaps when viewed along straight lines. Moving directly between two feasible points stays feasible.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Intersections of convex sets are convex.
  • Open balls, closed balls, half-spaces, and affine subspaces are convex.
  • A feasible region described by linear equality and weak linear inequality constraints is convex.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• The set \(\{(x,y):x+y\le 1\}\) is convex because it is a half-space.
  • The unit disk \(\{(x,y):x^2+y^2\le 1\}\) is convex, but the unit circle \(\{(x,y):x^2+y^2=1\}\) is not.

docs.title: Theorem
docs.text:
In a parametric problem, the value function is the optimized objective value

\[ F(\alpha)=f(\gamma(\alpha);\alpha), \]

where \(\gamma(\alpha)\) is an optimizer. For equality constraints, define

\[ L(x,\mu;\alpha)=f(x;\alpha)+\sum_j\mu_jh_j(x;\alpha). \]

If smooth optimizer and multiplier functions satisfy the first-order conditions, then

\[ \frac{\partial F}{\partial\alpha_\ell}(\alpha) = \frac{\partial L}{\partial\alpha_\ell}(x,\mu;\alpha) \bigg|_{(x,\mu)=(\gamma(\alpha),\widetilde\mu(\alpha))}. \]

For mixed constraints, the same formula holds with the Lagrangian including the binding inequalities and equality constraints, provided the relevant bordered Hessian is nonsingular and the active set is smooth. In the special equality case \(h_j(x;\alpha)=\alpha_j-\widetilde h_j(x)\) with \(f\) independent of \(\alpha\), the multiplier is the shadow price:

\[ \frac{\partial F}{\partial\alpha_j}(\alpha)=\widetilde\mu_j(\alpha). \]

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: The envelope theorem computes how the best attainable value changes when a parameter changes. It avoids separately differentiating every movement of the optimizer.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• The value function records the optimum as a function of parameters.
  • The envelope derivative is the direct parameter derivative of the Lagrangian at the optimal solution.
  • A shadow price is the marginal value of relaxing a constraint in the stated equality-constraint setup.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• For \(f(x;\alpha)=\alpha x-x^2\), the envelope derivative is \(x^\ast(\alpha)\).
  • In utility maximization with income as a parameter, the multiplier on the budget equation measures marginal utility of income.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
In an equation system \(F(x,y)=0\), the variables in \(x\) are called exogenous variables if they are treated as freely chosen inputs. The variables in \(y\) are called endogenous variables if the equation system is used to solve for them as functions of \(x\).

When possible, the implicit function theorem gives a local function \(g\) such that

\[ F(x,g(x))=0. \]

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: Exogenous variables are the knobs set from outside the system. Endogenous variables are the quantities the system determines in response.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• The distinction depends on how the equation system is being used, not only on the symbols.
  • The implicit function theorem requires the partial Jacobian with respect to the endogenous variables to be invertible in the square case.
  • Comparative statics studies how endogenous variables change when exogenous variables are perturbed.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• In \(x+y=10\), if \(x\) is chosen externally, then \(y=10-x\) is endogenous.
  • In supply and demand equilibrium, a tax can be exogenous while price and quantity are endogenous equilibrium variables.

docs.title: Theorem
docs.text:
Let \(A\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be open, and let \(f,g_i,h_j\) be continuously differentiable on \(A\). For minimization, write the inequalities as \(g_i(x)\le0\); for maximization, write them as \(g_i(x)\ge0\). With equalities \(h_j(x)=0\), define the generalized Lagrangian

\[ \Lambda(x,\lambda_0,\lambda,\mu) = \lambda_0 f(x)+\sum_i\lambda_i g_i(x)+\sum_j\mu_j h_j(x). \]

If \(x^\ast\) is a local constrained optimum, then there exist multipliers with \(\lambda_0\in\{0,1\}\), \(\lambda_i\ge0\), and \((\lambda_0,\lambda,\mu)\neq0\) such that stationarity, feasibility, and complementary slackness hold.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: This method avoids a separate regularity check by adding a multiplier on the objective itself. The extra case captures points where the active constraints are degenerate.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• If \(\lambda_0=1\), the regular first-order necessary conditions are recovered.
  • If \(\lambda_0=0\), the condition signals linear dependence among active constraint gradients.
  • The method keeps nonregular feasible points inside the theorem.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• For a regular optimum, choosing \(\lambda_0=1\) gives the usual Lagrangian conditions.
  • If active constraint gradients are linearly dependent, a solution may appear with \(\lambda_0=0\) and nonzero constraint multipliers.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
Let \(A\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\), let \(f\colon A\to\mathbb{R}\), and let \(x^\ast\in A\).

  • \(f(x^\ast)\) is a global maximum if \(f(x^\ast)\ge f(x)\) for all \(x\in A\).
  • \(f(x^\ast)\) is a global minimum if \(f(x^\ast)\le f(x)\) for all \(x\in A\).

The extremum is strict if the inequality is strict for all \(x\in A\setminus\{x^\ast\}\).

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: A global extremum compares the candidate with every feasible point. Strictness means there is no other feasible point with the same optimal value.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• A strict global maximum or minimum has a unique optimizer.
  • A continuous function on a compact feasible set attains both a global maximum and a global minimum.
  • A global extremum is automatically local when neighbourhoods inside the feasible set are considered.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• For \(f(x,y)=-(x^2+y^2)\) on \(\mathbb{R}^2\), \((0,0)\) is a strict global maximizer.
  • For \(f(x,y)=x^2\) on \(\mathbb{R}^2\), every point with \(x=0\) is a global minimizer.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
Let \(f\colon E\subseteq\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R\) be a scalar-valued function whose second-order partial derivatives exist at \(x_0\in E\). The Hessian matrix of \(f\) at \(x_0\) is

\[ H_f(x_0)= \begin{pmatrix} \frac{\partial^2 f}{\partial x_1^2}(x_0) & \cdots & \frac{\partial^2 f}{\partial x_1\partial x_n}(x_0)\\ \vdots & \ddots & \vdots\\ \frac{\partial^2 f}{\partial x_n\partial x_1}(x_0) & \cdots & \frac{\partial^2 f}{\partial x_n^2}(x_0) \end{pmatrix}. \]

The entry in row \(i\) and column \(j\) is the second partial derivative with respect to \(x_i\) and \(x_j\).

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: The Hessian collects all second-order bending information of a scalar function at one point. It is the multivariable analogue of the second derivative in one-variable calculus.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• If \(f\) is \(C^2\) near \(x_0\), then the Hessian is symmetric.
  • At a critical point, a positive definite Hessian gives a strict local minimum.
  • At a critical point, a negative definite Hessian gives a strict local maximum.
  • At a critical point, an indefinite Hessian gives a saddle point.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• For \(f(x,y)=x^2+2xy+3y^2\), the Hessian is \(\begin{pmatrix}2&2\\2&6\end{pmatrix}\) at every point.
  • For \(f(x,y)=x^3+2xy^2-y^3\), the Hessian at \((1,1)\) is \(\begin{pmatrix}6&4\\4&-2\end{pmatrix}\).

docs.title: Hessian Test for Convexity and Concavity
Theorem
docs.text:
Let \(C\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be convex and open, and let \(f\colon C\to\mathbb R\) be twice continuously differentiable.

Then \(f\) is convex on \(C\) if and only if \(H_f(x)\) is positive semidefinite for every \(x\in C\).

The function \(f\) is concave on \(C\) if and only if \(H_f(x)\) is negative semidefinite for every \(x\in C\).

If \(H_f(x)\) is positive definite for every \(x\in C\), then \(f\) is strictly convex. If \(H_f(x)\) is negative definite for every \(x\in C\), then \(f\) is strictly concave.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: The Hessian test turns the geometric question of bending upward or downward into a matrix definiteness check at every point of the domain.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Positive semidefinite Hessian everywhere is equivalent to convexity under the stated smoothness and convex-domain assumptions.
  • Negative semidefinite Hessian everywhere is equivalent to concavity under the same assumptions.
  • Positive definiteness everywhere is sufficient for strict convexity, but not necessary in every case.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• For \(f(x,y)=x^2+y^2\), \(H_f=2I\), so \(f\) is strictly convex.
  • For \(f(x,y)=-(x^2+y^2)\), \(H_f=-2I\), so \(f\) is strictly concave.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
A higher-order partial derivative is obtained by differentiating a partial derivative again with respect to one or more variables. For example, for \(f\colon A\subseteq\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R\),

\[ f_{x_i x_j x_k}(a)= \frac{\partial}{\partial x_i} \left( \frac{\partial}{\partial x_j} \left( \frac{\partial f}{\partial x_k} \right) \right)(a) \]

is a third-order partial derivative, when all indicated derivatives exist.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: Higher-order partial derivatives measure how earlier rates of change themselves change as one moves in chosen coordinate directions.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Second-order partial derivatives form the Hessian matrix when they exist.
  • Third-order partial derivatives can be arranged in a three-dimensional array.
  • Continuity assumptions are usually needed before changing the order of differentiation.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• For \(f(x,y)=x^2y^3\), \(f_{xy}=6xy^2\) and \(f_{xyy}=12xy\).
  • For \(f(x,y,z)=xyz^2\), \(f_{xyz}=2z\) and \(f_{xzz}=2y\).

docs.title: Theorem
docs.text:
Let \(f\) have continuous partial derivatives up to order \(k\) on an open neighbourhood of \(a\). Then any two \(k\)th-order partial derivatives that differentiate with respect to the same variables the same number of times are equal at \(a\).

For third-order derivatives this means, for example,

\[ f_{xyz}(a)=f_{xzy}(a)=f_{yxz}(a)=f_{yzx}(a)=f_{zxy}(a)=f_{zyx}(a) \]

whenever the required third-order partial derivatives are continuous near \(a\).

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: When the function is smooth enough, only the number of times each direction is used matters, not the order in which the differentiations are performed.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• The second-order case is the usual symmetry of mixed partial derivatives.
  • For a sufficiently smooth scalar function, the third derivative tensor is symmetric under permutations of its indices.
  • Without the needed continuity assumptions, mixed partials can fail to agree.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• For \(f(x,y,z)=x^2yz^3\), the derivatives \(f_{xyz}\), \(f_{xzy}\), and \(f_{zyx}\) agree because \(f\) is a polynomial.
  • For \(f(x,y)=e^{xy}\), \(f_{xxy}=f_{xyx}=f_{yxx}\) at every point because all partial derivatives are continuous.

docs.title: Theorem
docs.text:
In a system \(G(x,y)=0\), the variables \(x\in\mathbb{R}^n\) are treated as exogenous and \(y\in\mathbb{R}^m\) as endogenous. For \(G\colon A\to\mathbb{R}^m\), define the block Jacobians \(D_xG\) and \(D_yG\) by differentiating with respect to the \(x\)-block and \(y\)-block.

Let \(A\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{n+m}\) be open and let \(G\colon A\to\mathbb{R}^m\) be \(C^1\). Suppose \((x_0,y_0)\in A\), \(G(x_0,y_0)=0\), and

\[ \det(D_yG(x_0,y_0))\neq 0. \]

Then there is a neighbourhood \(B\) of \(x_0\) and a \(C^1\) function \(\varphi\colon B\to\mathbb{R}^m\) such that \(\varphi(x_0)=y_0\) and \(G(x,\varphi(x))=0\) for all \(x\in B\). Moreover,

\[ D\varphi(x_0)=-(D_yG(x_0,y_0))^{-1}D_xG(x_0,y_0). \]

For one equation in two variables, this reduces to \(\varphi'(x_0)=-G_x(x_0,y_0)/G_y(x_0,y_0)\).

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: The theorem says that a regular system of equations can locally be solved for the variables that must adjust. It also gives the local response of those adjusting variables when the chosen variables change.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• The determinant condition says the endogenous block is locally pinned down by the equations.
  • The theorem gives local existence, differentiability, and a derivative formula.
  • The one-equation case is the familiar slope formula for an implicit curve.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• For \(G(x,y)=y-x^2\), the theorem gives \(y=\varphi(x)=x^2\) because \(D_yG=1\).
  • For \(G(x,y)=x^2+y^2-1\) near \((0,1)\), the theorem gives the upper circle locally as a function of \(x\).

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
A linear constraint system

\[ Ax=b \]

with \(A\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}\) has independent constraints if the rows of \(A\) are linearly independent, equivalently

\[ \operatorname{rank}A=m. \]

For nonlinear equality constraints \(g_1(x)=0,\ldots,g_m(x)=0\), the corresponding local condition at \(a\) is that the gradients \(\nabla g_1(a),\ldots,\nabla g_m(a)\) are linearly independent.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: Independent constraints each remove a genuinely new direction. Dependent constraints repeat information and can make multiplier tests misleading.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• For \(m\) independent equality constraints in \(\mathbb R^n\), the linearized feasible directions usually form an \((n-m)\)-dimensional space.
  • Independence is a rank condition on the constraint Jacobian.
  • Nondegenerate constraint qualification is the nonlinear optimization version of this idea.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• The constraints \(x+y=1\) and \(2x+2y=2\) are dependent because the second repeats the first.
  • The constraints \(x+y=1\) and \(x-y=0\) are independent because the matrix \(\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\1&-1\end{pmatrix}\) has rank \(2\).

docs.title: Theorem
docs.text:
Let \(f\colon U\subseteq\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^m\) be continuously differentiable near \(a\).

If \(\operatorname{rank}Df(a)=n\) and \(n\le m\), then \(f\) is locally injective near \(a\).

If \(\operatorname{rank}Df(a)=m\) and \(m\le n\), then \(f\) is locally surjective near \(a\).

If \(n=m\) and \(\det Df(a)\neq 0\), then \(f\) is locally bijective near \(a\).

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: Full rank of the Jacobian tells which local behavior survives under linearization: no collapsing for full column rank, no missing nearby outputs for full row rank, and a local inverse in the square case.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• The square case is the multivariable inverse function theorem.
  • Full column rank gives a locally one-to-one parametrized surface or curve.
  • Full row rank means nearby target values can be reached by nearby inputs.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• For \(f(t)=(t,t^2)\), \(Df(t)=(1,2t)^\top\) has rank \(1\), so the curve is locally injective.
  • For \(f(x,y)=x+y\), \(Df=(1\ 1)\) has rank \(1\), so the map is locally surjective onto \(\mathbb R\).

docs.title: Theorem
docs.text:
For the maximization problem

\[ \max_{x\in A} f(x) \quad\text{subject to}\quad g_i(x)\le b_i,\qquad x_h\ge0, \]

define the Kuhn-Tucker Lagrangian

\[ \widetilde L(x,\lambda)=f(x)+\sum_i\lambda_i(b_i-g_i(x)). \]

At a regular local maximum, there exists \(\lambda^\ast\ge0\) such that

\[ \frac{\partial \widetilde L}{\partial x_h}(x^\ast,\lambda^\ast)\le0,\qquad x_h^\ast\frac{\partial \widetilde L}{\partial x_h}(x^\ast,\lambda^\ast)=0,\qquad x_h^\ast\ge0, \]

and

\[ \frac{\partial \widetilde L}{\partial \lambda_i}(x^\ast,\lambda^\ast)\ge0,\qquad \lambda_i^\ast\frac{\partial \widetilde L}{\partial \lambda_i}(x^\ast,\lambda^\ast)=0,\qquad \lambda_i^\ast\ge0. \]

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: Nonnegative variables can be either interior or stuck at the boundary. The Kuhn-Tucker conditions encode that boundary logic together with ordinary inequality slackness.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• If \(x_h^\ast>0\), the derivative condition for that variable becomes equality.
  • If a multiplier is positive, the corresponding ordinary inequality constraint is binding.
  • The conditions are necessary at regular local maxima.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• If \(x_h^\ast>0\), then \(x_h^\ast\partial\widetilde L/\partial x_h=0\) forces \(\partial\widetilde L/\partial x_h=0\).
  • If \(\lambda_i^\ast>0\), then \(\partial\widetilde L/\partial\lambda_i=0\), so the constraint is binding.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
For an optimization problem with equality constraints \(h_i(x)=0\) and inequality constraints \(g_j(x)\le 0\), a Kuhn-Tucker Lagrangian is an expression of the form

\[ L(x,\lambda,\mu) = f(x) +\sum_i \lambda_i h_i(x) +\sum_j \mu_j g_j(x), \]

with sign restrictions such as \(\mu_j\ge 0\) or \(\mu_j\le 0\) depending on the maximization or minimization convention.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: The Kuhn-Tucker Lagrangian brings the objective and all active constraint pressures into one stationarity expression.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Equality multipliers are usually unrestricted in sign.
  • Inequality multipliers have sign restrictions tied to the chosen convention.
  • Complementary slackness connects each inequality multiplier to whether its constraint is binding.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• For maximizing \(f(x)\) subject to \(g(x)\le 0\), one common convention uses \(L=f-\mu g\) with \(\mu\ge 0\).
  • For a nonnegativity condition \(x_i\ge 0\), the KKT system may include a multiplier attached to that boundary condition.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
A Lagrange multiplier is an auxiliary variable attached to a constraint in a Lagrangian. For equality constraints \(h_j(x)=c_j\), a typical course convention writes

\[ L(x,\mu)=f(x)+\sum_{j=1}^m\mu_j(c_j-h_j(x)). \]

At a regular constrained optimum, the multipliers make the gradient of the objective a linear combination of the gradients of the active constraints.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: A multiplier records how a constraint enters the first-order trade-off at a candidate optimum. In parameterized problems, it can also measure the marginal value of relaxing a constraint.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Equality multipliers may be positive, negative, or zero.
  • Inequality multipliers have sign restrictions under the course convention.
  • In the envelope theorem, some multipliers can be interpreted as shadow prices.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• For maximizing \(xy\) subject to \(x+y=10\), the multiplier is attached to the budget equation.
  • For \(L(x,y,\mu)=x^2+y^2+\mu(1-x-y)\), stationarity gives \(2x-\mu=0\) and \(2y-\mu=0\).

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
For a constrained optimization problem with objective \(f\) and equality constraints \(h_j(x)=c_j\), a Lagrangian function is an auxiliary function that combines the objective and the constraints with multiplier variables. Under the course convention for equality constraints,

\[ L(x,\mu)=f(x)+\sum_{j=1}^m \mu_j(c_j-h_j(x)). \]

For inequality constraints, the same idea is used with sign conventions chosen so that multiplier restrictions match the direction of the inequality.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: The Lagrangian rewrites a constrained problem as one expression whose stationary points encode both the objective trade-off and the constraint equations.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Differentiating with respect to the multiplier variables recovers the constraints.
  • Differentiating with respect to the choice variables gives the first-order balance between objective gradients and constraint gradients.
  • Changing the sign convention changes multiplier signs, but not the underlying candidate points when handled consistently.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• For \(\max xy\) subject to \(x+y=10\), one convention uses \(L(x,y,\mu)=xy+\mu(10-x-y)\).
  • For \(\min x^2+y^2\) subject to \(x+y=1\), one can use \(L(x,y,\mu)=x^2+y^2+\mu(1-x-y)\).

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
Let \(f\colon A\to B\) be a function. A left inverse of \(f\) is a function \(\ell\colon B\to A\) such that

\[ \ell\circ f=\operatorname{id}_A. \]

A right inverse of \(f\) is a function \(r\colon B\to A\) such that

\[ f\circ r=\operatorname{id}_B. \]

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: A left inverse undoes the function after the function is applied. A right inverse gives a way to hit every target value.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• A function has a left inverse only if it is injective.
  • A function has a right inverse only if it is surjective, assuming the usual choice of a preimage for every output.
  • A two-sided inverse is both a left inverse and a right inverse.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• The inclusion \(i\colon\mathbb R\to\mathbb R^2\), \(i(t)=(t,0)\), has a left inverse \(\ell(x,y)=x\).
  • The projection \(p\colon\mathbb R^2\to\mathbb R\), \(p(x,y)=x\), has a right inverse \(r(t)=(t,0)\).

docs.title: Theorem
docs.text:
Let \(A\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\), let \(f\colon A\to\mathbb{R}^m\), and let \(x_0\in\operatorname{int}(A)\) with \(b_0=f(x_0)\).

  • \(f\) is locally injective at \(x_0\) if nearby equations \(f(x)=b\) have at most one nearby solution.
  • \(f\) is locally surjective at \(x_0\) if nearby equations \(f(x)=b\) have at least one nearby solution.
  • \(f\) is locally bijective at \(x_0\) if nearby equations \(f(x)=b\) have exactly one nearby solution.

If \(f\) is \(C^1\), then full column rank of \(Df(x_0)\) implies local injectivity, full row rank implies local surjectivity, and square full rank implies local bijectivity.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: These local properties describe whether nearby outputs have no duplicate inputs, no missing inputs, or exactly one input. The Jacobian rank gives the local linear signal for these behaviors.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Full column rank gives local uniqueness of nearby solutions.
  • Full row rank gives local existence of nearby solutions.
  • If \(n=m\) and \(\det(Df(x_0))\neq0\), the function is locally bijective at \(x_0\).

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• The map \(f(x,y)=x\) is locally surjective from \(\mathbb{R}^2\) to \(\mathbb{R}\) at every point.
  • The map \(f(x,y)=(x,y,x+y)\) is locally injective because its Jacobian has full column rank.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
Let \(A\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\), let \(f\colon A\to\mathbb{R}\), and let \(x^\ast\in A\).

  • \(f(x^\ast)\) is a local maximum if there is a neighbourhood \(U\) of \(x^\ast\) such that \(f(x^\ast)\ge f(x)\) for all \(x\in U\cap A\).
  • \(f(x^\ast)\) is a local minimum if there is a neighbourhood \(U\) of \(x^\ast\) such that \(f(x^\ast)\le f(x)\) for all \(x\in U\cap A\).

The extremum is strict if the inequality is strict for all nearby feasible points other than \(x^\ast\).

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: A local extremum is best only against nearby feasible alternatives. It may or may not be globally best.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Interior local extrema of differentiable unconstrained problems must satisfy a first-order necessary condition.
  • Second-order conditions use the Hessian to classify critical points when possible.
  • Local extrema need not be unique and need not be global.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• For \(f(x,y)=x^2+y^2\), \((0,0)\) is a strict local minimum.
  • For \(f(x)=x^3-3x\), \(x=-1\) is a local maximum and \(x=1\) is a local minimum.

docs.title: Method of Lagrange for Constrained Minimization
Theorem
docs.text:
Let \(A\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be open, and let the objective \(f\) and all constraint functions \(g_i,h_j\) be continuously differentiable on \(A\). For

\[ \min_{x\in A} f(x)\quad\text{subject to}\quad g_i(x)\ge b_i,\quad h_j(x)=c_j, \]

the course convention writes the inequality part as \(b_i-g_i(x)\le0\) and defines

\[ L(x,\lambda,\mu)=f(x)+\sum_i\lambda_i(b_i-g_i(x))+\sum_j\mu_j(c_j-h_j(x)). \]

If \(x^\ast\) is a local constrained minimizer, then either NDCQ fails or there are multipliers satisfying

\[ \nabla_xL=0,\qquad \lambda_i^\ast(g_i(x^\ast)-b_i)=0,\qquad g_i(x^\ast)\ge b_i,\qquad h_j(x^\ast)=c_j,\qquad \lambda_i^\ast\ge0. \]

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: For minimization, the inequality is written so the same nonnegative multiplier convention can be used. The resulting conditions are still only a candidate filter.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• The sign of the inequality term in the Lagrangian depends on the feasible side of the constraint.
  • Nonbinding inequalities have zero multipliers.
  • Equality multipliers remain unrestricted.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• For \(\min e^{x-y}\) subject to \(x^2+y^2\ge4\), use \(L=e^{x-y}+\lambda(4-x^2-y^2)\).
  • If \(x+y>1\) at a local minimizer subject to \(x+y\ge1\), complementary slackness forces the multiplier on that constraint to be zero.

docs.title: Method of Lagrange for Equality Constraints
Theorem
docs.text:
Let \(A\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be open. Consider

\[ \max_{x\in A} f(x)\quad\text{subject to}\quad h_j(x)=c_j,\ j=1,\ldots,m, \]

with \(C^1\) data and \(m<n\). Define

\[ L(x,\mu)=f(x)+\sum_{j=1}^m\mu_j(c_j-h_j(x)). \]

If \(f(x^\ast)\) is a local maximum or minimum subject to the constraints, then either NDCQ fails at \(x^\ast\) or there exists \(\mu^\ast\in\mathbb{R}^m\) such that

\[ \nabla L(x^\ast,\mu^\ast)=0. \]

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: A regular equality-constrained optimum must be a critical point of the Lagrangian. Nonregular feasible points are kept as candidates rather than thrown away.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• The theorem gives necessary, not sufficient, conditions.
  • Stationarity in the multiplier variables recovers the equality constraints.
  • Equality constraints can be written on either side because they have no direction.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• Maximizing \(xy\) subject to \(x+y=10\) gives \(L=xy+\mu(10-x-y)\).
  • Minimizing \(x^2+y^2\) subject to \(x+y=1\) uses the same equality-constrained stationarity method.

docs.title: Method of Lagrange for Inequality-constrained Maximization
Theorem
docs.text:
Let \(A\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be open, and let \(f,g_1,\ldots,g_k\colon A\to\mathbb R\) be continuously differentiable. Consider

\[ \max_{x\in A} f(x)\quad\text{subject to}\quad g_i(x)\le b_i,\ i=1,\ldots,k. \]

The course convention writes \(b_i-g_i(x)\ge0\) and defines

\[ L(x,\lambda)=f(x)+\sum_{i=1}^k\lambda_i(b_i-g_i(x)). \]

If \(x^\ast\) is a local constrained maximizer, then either NDCQ fails or there exists \(\lambda^\ast\) such that

\[ \nabla_xL(x^\ast,\lambda^\ast)=0,\qquad \lambda_i^\ast(g_i(x^\ast)-b_i)=0,\qquad \lambda_i^\ast\ge0,\qquad g_i(x^\ast)\le b_i. \]

The condition \(\lambda_i^\ast(g_i(x^\ast)-b_i)=0\) is complementary slackness.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: Inequality constraints are directional, so multiplier signs and slackness matter. A nonbinding constraint has slack and therefore contributes no multiplier force at a regular candidate.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• A binding constraint satisfies \(g_i(x^\ast)=b_i\).
  • A nonbinding constraint has zero multiplier by complementary slackness.
  • The theorem gives necessary, not sufficient, conditions.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• For \(\max xy\) subject to \(x+y\le10\), the Lagrangian is \(xy+\lambda(10-x-y)\).
  • If no inequality is binding at a local maximum, all inequality multipliers are zero and the unconstrained stationarity condition returns.

docs.title: Method of Lagrange for Mixed Constraints
Theorem
docs.text:
Let \(A\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be open, and let the objective \(f\) and all constraint functions \(g_i,h_j\) be continuously differentiable on \(A\). Consider

\[ \max_{x\in A} f(x)\quad\text{subject to}\quad g_i(x)\le b_i,\quad h_j(x)=c_j. \]

The course convention defines

\[ L(x,\lambda,\mu) =f(x)+\sum_i\lambda_i(b_i-g_i(x))+\sum_j\mu_j(c_j-h_j(x)). \]

If \(x^\ast\) is a local constrained maximizer and the binding inequalities are indexed by \(i_1,\ldots,i_\ell\), then either

\[ \operatorname{rank}D(g_{i_1},\ldots,g_{i_\ell},h_1,\ldots,h_m)(x^\ast)<\ell+m, \]

or there exist multipliers satisfying stationarity, complementary slackness, inequality feasibility, equality feasibility, and \(\lambda_i^\ast\ge0\).

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: Mixed problems combine exact equations with one-sided restrictions. The first-order candidate conditions combine equality stationarity with inequality sign and slackness rules.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Only inequalities require nonnegative multipliers.
  • Only binding inequalities are included in the active NDCQ matrix.
  • All equality constraints must hold exactly.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• For \(\max xy\) subject to \(x+y\le10\) and \(x-y=0\), the method uses one nonnegative multiplier and one unrestricted multiplier.
  • If an inequality is nonbinding at the solution, its multiplier is zero and it is not part of the active rank test.

docs.title: Theorem
docs.text:
Let \(A\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\), \(B\subseteq\mathbb{R}^m\), let \(g\colon A\to B\), and let \(f\colon B\to\mathbb{R}^k\). If \(g\) is differentiable at \(x_0\in\operatorname{int}(A)\), \(g(x_0)\in\operatorname{int}(B)\), and \(f\) is differentiable at \(g(x_0)\), then \(f\circ g\) is differentiable at \(x_0\) and

\[ D(f\circ g)(x_0)=Df(g(x_0))Dg(x_0). \]

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: Local changes pass through the inner map first and then through the outer map. This is why the derivative matrices multiply in the same order as the composition acts on changes.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• If \(g\colon\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}^m\) and \(f\colon\mathbb{R}^m\to\mathbb{R}^k\), then the product has size \(k\times n\).
  • If both maps are continuously differentiable near the relevant points, their composition is continuously differentiable near \(x_0\).

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• If \(g(x,y)=(x+y,xy)\) and \(f(u,v)=u^2+v\), then \(D(f\circ g)=Df(g)Dg\).
  • If \(g(t)=(t,t^2)\) and \(f(x,y)=x+y\), the formula gives the curve derivative \(1+2t\).

docs.title: Theorem
docs.text:
Let \(A\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) be open, let \(f\colon A\to\mathbb{R}^n\) be \(C^1\), and let \(x_0\in A\) with \(y_0=f(x_0)\). If

\[ \det(Df(x_0))\neq0, \]

then there exists an open neighbourhood \(V\subseteq A\) of \(x_0\) such that \(f|_V\colon V\to f(V)\) is bijective. Its inverse is \(C^1\) and

\[ D(f|_V^{-1})(y_0)=\left(Df(x_0)\right)^{-1}. \]

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: An invertible Jacobian makes the function locally reversible. Near the reference point, outputs can be used to recover inputs smoothly.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• The determinant condition is the square full-rank condition.
  • The derivative of the local inverse is the inverse matrix of the original derivative.
  • The theorem can be derived from the implicit function theorem and vice versa.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• For \(f(x,y)=(e^x\cos y,e^x\sin y)\), the determinant is \(e^{2x}\), so the map is locally invertible everywhere.
  • For \(f(x,y)=(x^2,y)\) at \((0,0)\), the determinant is \(0\), so the theorem does not apply there.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
Let \(f\colon\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}\) be sufficiently smooth near \(x_0\) and let \(h\) be a small displacement. The first-order approximation is

\[ f(x_0+h)\approx f(x_0)+Df(x_0)h. \]

If \(f\) is \(C^2\) near \(x_0\), the second-order approximation is

\[ f(x_0+h)\approx f(x_0)+Df(x_0)h+\frac12 h^\top Hf(x_0)h. \]

The first correction uses local slope, and the second correction uses local curvature.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: Taylor approximations replace a complicated function near a point by simpler local information. The linear term estimates the immediate change, and the quadratic term corrects for bending.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• For a real-valued function, \(Df(x_0)h=\nabla f(x_0)^\top h\).
  • If \(f\) is \(C^2\), then the Hessian is symmetric and the second-order term is a quadratic form.
  • At a critical point, the quadratic term is the first potentially nonzero correction. It may also vanish, in which case higher-order information is needed.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• For \(f(x,y)=x^2+xy+y^2\) at \((0,0)\), the second-order approximation is exact.
  • For \(f(x,y)=e^{x+y}\) at \((0,0)\), the second-order approximation is \(1+x+y+\frac12(x+y)^2\).

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
For equality constraints \(h_1(x)=c_1,\ldots,h_m(x)=c_m\), the nondegenerate constraint qualification is satisfied at \(x^\ast\) if

\[ \operatorname{rank}(Dh(x^\ast))=m. \]

With inequality constraints, the same rank condition is applied to the gradients of the binding inequality constraints together with the equality constraints.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: NDCQ says the active constraints are locally independent. If it fails, some constraint may be redundant or the feasible set may have a singular shape.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• When NDCQ holds, the regular Lagrange necessary conditions apply at a constrained local optimum.
  • If NDCQ fails, the point remains a candidate that must be checked separately.
  • For inequality problems, nonbinding inequalities are not included in the active rank check.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• For \(h(x,y)=x+y\), NDCQ holds at every point because the gradient is nonzero.
  • For \(h_1(x,y)=x+y\) and \(h_2(x,y)=2x+2y\), NDCQ fails because the gradients are dependent.

docs.title: Nonnegativity Constraint
docs.text: This page presents the Math IV: Multivariate Calculus treatment. See also the treatment in OR Modelling. Mastery is recorded separately for each course context.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
A nonnegativity constraint requires a choice variable to satisfy

\[ x_i\ge 0. \]

In a vector problem this is often imposed componentwise as \(x\ge 0\), meaning \(x_i\ge 0\) for every component \(i\).

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: A nonnegativity constraint says the variable cannot cross below zero, so zero becomes a possible boundary optimum.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• If \(x_i^\ast>0\), the nonnegativity constraint for that component is slack.
  • If \(x_i^\ast=0\), the component is at the boundary and can have a nonzero KKT multiplier.
  • Nonnegativity constraints are common in quantity, probability, and allocation problems.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• In a production problem, labor input \(L\) often satisfies \(L\ge 0\).
  • In a portfolio share problem, a no-short-selling restriction can be written as \(x_i\ge 0\) for each asset.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
A parametric constrained optimization problem is an optimization problem whose objective, constraints, or feasible set depend on a parameter. A typical equality-constrained maximization problem has the form

\[ V(s)=\max_x f(x,s) \quad\text{subject to}\quad g(x,s)=0. \]

The parameter \(s\) is not optimized over; it changes the problem being solved.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: A parametric problem asks how the best choice and best value move when outside conditions change.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• The optimal value as a function of the parameter is the value function.
  • Envelope theorems give derivatives of the value function without fully differentiating the optimizer.
  • Constraint multipliers often measure the marginal value of relaxing parameterized constraints.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• A firm may maximize profit over inputs while the wage rate is a parameter.
  • A consumer may maximize utility over bundles while income is a parameter in the budget constraint.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
Let \(F\colon A\subseteq\mathbb R^{p+q}\to\mathbb R^m\) be differentiable, and write the variables as \((x,y)\) with \(x\in\mathbb R^p\) and \(y\in\mathbb R^q\). The partial Jacobians of \(F\) are the blocks

\[ D_xF(x,y)\in\mathbb R^{m\times p}, \qquad D_yF(x,y)\in\mathbb R^{m\times q}. \]

Together they form the full Jacobian:

\[ DF(x,y)=\begin{pmatrix}D_xF(x,y)&D_yF(x,y)\end{pmatrix}. \]

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: A partial Jacobian isolates how an equation system responds to one chosen block of variables while the other block is held fixed.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Partial Jacobians are the matrix version of holding some variables constant in partial differentiation.
  • The implicit function theorem uses the partial Jacobian with respect to the variables being solved for.
  • Block notation makes comparative statics formulas easier to write and remember.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• For \(F(x,y)=x^2+y^2-1\), \(D_xF=2x\) and \(D_yF=2y\).
  • For \(F(x_1,x_2,y)=(x_1+y,x_2y)\), \(D_xF=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&y\end{pmatrix}\) and \(D_yF=\begin{pmatrix}1\\x_2\end{pmatrix}\).

docs.title: Theorem
docs.text:
Let \(A\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n}\) and let \(I=\{i_1,\ldots,i_k\}\subseteq\{1,\ldots,n\}\). The principal submatrix \([A]_I\) keeps the rows and columns indexed by \(I\), and its principal minor is \(\det([A]_I)\). The \(k\)-th leading principal submatrix is \(A_k=[A]_{\{1,\ldots,k\}}\).

If \(A\) is symmetric, Sylvester's criterion states:

  • \(A\) is positive definite iff \(\det(A_k)>0\) for all \(k=1,\ldots,n\).
  • \(A\) is negative definite iff \((-1)^k\det(A_k)>0\) for all \(k=1,\ldots,n\).
  • Positive and negative semidefinite cases require all principal minors with the corresponding sign pattern.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: Principal minors are determinant snapshots of matched rows and columns. Sylvester's criterion uses their signs to test definiteness without directly computing eigenvalues.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Leading principal minors are enough for positive and negative definiteness.
  • Semidefinite cases require checking all principal minors.
  • The criterion applies to symmetric matrices.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• For \(A=\begin{pmatrix}2&1\\1&2\end{pmatrix}\), the leading minors are \(2\) and \(3\), so \(A\) is positive definite.
  • For \(A=\begin{pmatrix}-2&0\\0&-3\end{pmatrix}\), the alternating sign test shows negative definiteness.

docs.title: Quadratic Form on a Constraint Set
Definition
docs.text:
Let \(q(h)=h^\top Ah\) be a quadratic form and let a constraint system have linearized feasible direction space

\[ T=\{h\in\mathbb R^n:Dg(a)h=0\}. \]

The quadratic form is positive definite on the constraint set at \(a\) if

\[ h^\top Ah>0 \]

for every nonzero \(h\in T\). Negative definiteness on the constraint set is defined similarly with \(h^\top Ah<0\).

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: Under constraints, curvature only matters in directions that are feasible to first order. The same matrix can look indefinite overall but decisive on the allowed directions.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• The relevant directions are tangent to the constraint set.
  • Constrained second-order tests study the Hessian of the Lagrangian on the feasible direction space.
  • Bordered matrix tests are determinant-based ways to check this restricted definiteness.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• For \(q(h_1,h_2)=h_1^2-h_2^2\) with constraint \(h_2=0\), the restricted form is positive definite.
  • For \(q(h_1,h_2)=h_1^2-h_2^2\) with constraint \(h_1=0\), the restricted form is negative definite.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
Let \(f\colon A\to B\) be a function and let \(S\subseteq A\). The restriction of \(f\) to \(S\) is the function

\[ f|_S\colon S\to B, \qquad f|_S(x)=f(x). \]

Only the domain is changed; the rule used to compute the value is the same.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: A restriction focuses the same function on a smaller feasible set. This is the formal move behind optimizing a function subject to constraints.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• The restricted function can have extrema that the unrestricted function does not have.
  • A constraint set often defines the domain of the restricted objective.
  • Properties such as injectivity can change after restriction.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• The function \(f(x,y)=x+y\) restricted to the circle \(x^2+y^2=1\) becomes an objective on that circle only.
  • The function \(f(x)=x^2\) is not injective on \(\mathbb R\), but its restriction to \([0,\infty)\) is injective.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
Let \(f\colon A\subseteq\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R\) and let \(a\in A\). The point \(a\) is a saddle point if it is a stationary point but is neither a local maximum nor a local minimum.

In many two-variable examples, every sufficiently small neighbourhood of \(a\) contains points where \(f\) is larger than \(f(a)\) and points where \(f\) is smaller than \(f(a)\).

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: A saddle point is a flat-looking candidate where the function rises in some directions and falls in others.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• An indefinite Hessian at a critical point is the standard second-order signal for a saddle point.
  • A zero gradient alone does not imply an extremum.
  • Some saddle points require higher-order information because the Hessian test can be inconclusive.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• For \(f(x,y)=x^2-y^2\), \((0,0)\) is a saddle point because values increase along the \(x\)-axis and decrease along the \(y\)-axis.
  • For \(f(x,y)=xy\), \((0,0)\) is a saddle point because \(xy\) takes positive and negative values arbitrarily close to the origin.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
Let \(f\colon E\subseteq\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^k\) be a function and let \(x_i,x_j\) be coordinate variables. A second-order partial derivative is obtained by differentiating a first-order partial derivative again:

\[ \frac{\partial^2 f}{\partial x_j\partial x_i} = \frac{\partial}{\partial x_j} \left( \frac{\partial f}{\partial x_i} \right). \]

When \(i\neq j\), this is called a mixed partial derivative or cross partial derivative.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: A second-order partial derivative measures how one first-order rate of change changes as another input is varied. Mixed partial derivatives compare changes across two different coordinate directions.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• If the relevant mixed partial derivatives are continuous near a point, then their order may be exchanged.
  • Second-order partial derivatives form the entries of the Hessian matrix for scalar-valued functions.
  • Second-order information is the basic input for local curvature and extrema tests.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• For \(f(x,y)=x^2+xy+y^2\), \(\frac{\partial^2 f}{\partial y\partial x}=1\) and \(\frac{\partial^2 f}{\partial x\partial y}=1\).
  • For \(f(x,y)=x^2y^3\), \(\frac{\partial^2 f}{\partial x\partial y}=6xy^2\) and \(\frac{\partial^2 f}{\partial y^2}=6x^2y\).

docs.title: Second-order Sufficient Conditions for Constrained Optimization
Theorem
docs.text:
Let \(L(x,\lambda,\mu)\) be the Lagrangian of a \(C^2\) constrained problem. At a first-order candidate, collect the binding inequality constraints and all equality constraints in \(C(x)\), and let \(r\) be the number of active constraints. The relevant bordered Hessian is

\[ H^\ast= \begin{pmatrix} 0_r & DC(x^\ast)\\ DC(x^\ast)^\top & D^2_{xx}L(x^\ast,\lambda^\ast,\mu^\ast) \end{pmatrix}. \]

Inspect the last \(n-r\) leading principal minors after ignoring the first \(2r\) leading minors. The candidate is a strict local constrained maximizer if these minors alternate in sign and the last one has sign \((-1)^n\). It is a strict local constrained minimizer if these minors all have sign \((-1)^r\).

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: The bordered Hessian checks curvature only along feasible directions. It is the constrained counterpart of using the Hessian in an unconstrained second-order test.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Only binding inequality constraints and equality constraints enter the relevant bordered Hessian.
  • The theorem gives sufficient conditions for strict local constrained optima.
  • Zero or semidefinite cases can be inconclusive.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• With one equality constraint in two variables, the relevant bordered Hessian is a three-by-three matrix.
  • For a maximization problem with three variables and one active constraint, the final relevant determinant must have sign \((-1)^3\).

docs.title: Shadow Price
docs.text: This page presents the Math IV: Multivariate Calculus treatment. See also the treatment in OR Modelling. Mastery is recorded separately for each course context.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
In a constrained optimization problem, a shadow price is the marginal change in the optimal value when a constraint is relaxed slightly. Under the usual regularity assumptions and sign conventions, this marginal change is represented by the associated Lagrange multiplier.

For a constraint written as \(g(x)=b\), one commonly has

\[ \frac{dV}{db}=\lambda \]

or the corresponding sign-adjusted version determined by the Lagrangian convention.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: A shadow price measures how valuable a little extra room in a constraint would be at the optimum.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• A positive shadow price means relaxing the constraint raises the optimal value under the chosen convention.
  • A zero shadow price often corresponds to a nonbinding inequality constraint.
  • The sign depends on whether the constraint is written as a resource, residual, or equality condition.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• If one more unit of a resource increases maximum profit by \(3\), the shadow price of that resource is \(3\).
  • If a budget constraint is slack, its shadow price is typically \(0\) because a small increase in the budget does not improve the optimum.

docs.title: Theorem
docs.text:
Let \(f\colon A\subseteq\mathbb R^n o\mathbb R\) be differentiable at \(a\), and suppose \( abla f(a) eq 0\). Among all unit vectors \(u\), the directional derivative

\[ D_u f(a)= abla f(a)^ op u \]

is maximized when

\[ u= rac{ abla f(a)}{\| abla f(a)\|}. \]

The maximum value is \(\| abla f(a)\|\), and the minimum value is \(-\| abla f(a)\|\) in the opposite direction.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: The gradient points in the direction where the function rises fastest. Its length tells how fast the best immediate rise is.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• The result follows from the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality.
  • The direction of steepest descent is \(-\nabla f(a)/\|\nabla f(a)\|\).
  • If $ abla f(a)=0$, then every directional derivative is zero and there is no unique steepest direction from first-order information.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• For \(f(x,y)=x^2+y^2\) at \((1,2)\), \(\nabla f=(2,4)\), so the steepest ascent direction is \((1,2)/\sqrt5\).
  • For \(f(x,y)=3x-y\) at any point, \(\nabla f=(3,-1)\), so the steepest ascent direction is \((3,-1)/\sqrt{10}\).

docs.title: Theorem
docs.text:
Let \(E\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be open, let \(x_0\in E\), and let \(f\colon E\to\mathbb R^k\). If the two mixed second-order partial derivatives

\[ \frac{\partial^2 f}{\partial x_j\partial x_i} \quad\text{and}\quad \frac{\partial^2 f}{\partial x_i\partial x_j} \]

exist on a neighbourhood of \(x_0\) and are continuous at \(x_0\), then

\[ \frac{\partial^2 f}{\partial x_j\partial x_i}(x_0) = \frac{\partial^2 f}{\partial x_i\partial x_j}(x_0). \]

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: When a function is smooth enough, differentiating first in one coordinate direction and then in another gives the same result as doing those two steps in the opposite order.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• A \(C^2\) function automatically satisfies the hypotheses of the theorem for second-order mixed partial derivatives.
  • For scalar-valued \(C^2\) functions, the Hessian matrix is symmetric.
  • The same idea extends to higher-order partial derivatives when the required higher-order derivatives are continuous.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• For \(f(x,y)=x^2y+e^{xy}\), the mixed derivatives \(f_{xy}\) and \(f_{yx}\) agree at every point because the function is smooth.
  • For \(f(x,y,z)=xyz^2\), the derivatives \(f_{xz}\) and \(f_{zx}\) both equal \(yz\).

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
Let \(D^k f(a)\) be the \(k\)th derivative of a scalar function at \(a\), viewed as a \(k\)-linear map. Its contraction with a displacement \(h\in\mathbb R^n\) is

\[ D^k f(a)[h,\ldots,h]. \]

In a Taylor polynomial, the corresponding \(k\)th-order contribution is

\[ \frac{1}{k!}D^k f(a)[h,\ldots,h]. \]

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: A derivative tensor is useful once it is evaluated on a concrete displacement. Contraction turns the stored derivative information into the actual Taylor correction in that direction.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• For \(k=2\), the contraction is the quadratic form \(h^ op H_f(a)h\).
  • For \(k=3\), the contraction sums all third partial derivatives weighted by three components of \(h\).
  • The factorial corrects for repeated counting in the Taylor expansion.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• If \(H=\begin{pmatrix}2&0\\0&6\end{pmatrix}\) and \(h=(u,v)\), then \(D^2f(a)[h,h]=2u^2+6v^2\).
  • For \(f(x,y)=x^3+xy^2\) at the origin and \(h=(u,v)\), the third-order contraction is \(6u^3+6uv^2\).

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
For a scalar function \(f\colon A\subseteq\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R\) with third-order partial derivatives at \(a\), the third-order derivative tensor is the array

\[ D^3 f(a)=\left(f_{x_i x_j x_k}(a)\right)_{i,j,k=1}^n. \]

It represents the trilinear map

\[ D^3 f(a)[u,v,w] = \sum_{i,j,k=1}^n f_{x_i x_j x_k}(a)u_i v_j w_k. \]

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: The third derivative tensor stores all third-order curvature information in the same way that the Hessian stores all second-order curvature information.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• For \(n\) variables, the raw array has \(n^3\) entries.
  • If the third partial derivatives are continuous, many entries are equal by symmetry.
  • Taylor's third-order term is obtained by feeding the displacement vector into the tensor three times.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• For \(f(x,y)=x^3+xy^2\), entries include \(f_{xxx}=6\), \(f_{xyy}=2\), and \(f_{yyy}=0\).
  • For \(f(x,y,z)=xyz\), all mixed third partials with one \(x\), one \(y\), and one \(z\) equal \(1\).

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
Let \(E\subseteq \mathbb R^n\) be open and let \(f\colon E\to\mathbb R^k\) be a function.

The function \(f\) is continuously differentiable, or \(C^1\), on \(E\) if all first-order partial derivatives of \(f\) exist on \(E\) and are continuous on \(E\).

The function \(f\) is twice continuously differentiable, or \(C^2\), on \(E\) if all second-order partial derivatives of \(f\) exist on \(E\) and are continuous on \(E\).

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: A continuously differentiable function changes smoothly enough that its first local rates of change do not jump. A twice continuously differentiable function has the same smooth behavior one derivative level deeper.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• A \(C^1\) function on an open set is totally differentiable at every point of that set.
  • A \(C^2\) scalar function has symmetric mixed second derivatives.
  • Polynomials and the usual elementary smooth functions are \(C^2\) on the interior of their domains.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• The function \(f(x,y)=x^2+\sin y\) is \(C^2\) on \(\mathbb R^2\).
  • The function \(f(x)=|x|\) is not \(C^1\) on \(\mathbb R\), because it is not differentiable at \(0\).

docs.title: Theorem
docs.text:
Let \(A\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) be open and let \(f\colon A\to\mathbb{R}\).

If \(f\) is \(C^1\) and has a local extremum at an interior point \(x^\ast\), then

\[ Df(x^\ast)=(0,\ldots,0). \]

If \(f\) is \(C^2\), then a local maximum has \(Hf(x^\ast)\) negative semidefinite and a local minimum has \(Hf(x^\ast)\) positive semidefinite. Conversely, if \(x^\ast\) is a critical point, a negative definite Hessian gives a strict local maximum, a positive definite Hessian gives a strict local minimum, and an indefinite Hessian gives a saddle point.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: At an interior unconstrained optimum, first-order movement must disappear. The Hessian then describes the local curvature when the second-order information is decisive.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• First-order stationarity is necessary but not sufficient.
  • Semidefinite Hessians can make the second-order test inconclusive.
  • An indefinite Hessian at a critical point means the point is neither a local maximum nor a local minimum.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• For \(f(x,y)=x^2+y^2\), the Hessian is positive definite and the origin is a strict local minimum.
  • For \(f(x,y)=x^2-y^2\), the Hessian is indefinite and the origin is a saddle point.
