docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
For a parametric optimization problem, the value function assigns to each parameter value the optimized objective value. For example,

\[ V(s)=f(x^\ast(s),s) \]

when \(x^\ast(s)\) solves the problem at parameter \(s\).

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: The value function records the best achievable outcome after the decision variables have been chosen optimally.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• The value function depends on parameters, not directly on arbitrary feasible choices.
  • Envelope theorems provide formulas for derivatives of value functions under regularity conditions.
  • A value function can be nonsmooth if the optimizer changes abruptly or constraints switch status.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• If \(V(I)\) is the maximum utility attainable with income \(I\), then \(V\) is a value function.
  • If \(V(K)\) is maximum profit when available capital is \(K\), then changing \(K\) changes the optimization problem and hence the value.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
Let \(\gamma\colon I\to\mathbb R^n\) be a differentiable path. If each component \(\gamma_i\) is differentiable at \(t_0\), then the velocity vector of \(\gamma\) at \(t_0\) is

\[ \gamma'(t_0)= \begin{pmatrix} \gamma_1'(t_0)\\ \vdots\\ \gamma_n'(t_0) \end{pmatrix}. \]

The velocity is the tangent vector to the curve at the point \(\gamma(t_0)\).

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: The velocity vector records the instantaneous direction and rate of motion along an already chosen path.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Velocity is computed component by component.
  • If \(\gamma'(t_0)\neq 0\), then \(\gamma'(t_0)\) gives a tangent direction to the image of the curve.
  • The speed of the curve is \(\|\gamma'(t_0)\|\) when a norm is being used.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• For \(\gamma(t)=(t,t^2)\), the velocity is \(\gamma'(t)=(1,2t)\), so at \(t=1\) the curve passes through \((1,1)\) with velocity \((1,2)\).
  • For \(\gamma(t)=(\cos t,\sin t)\), the velocity is \(\gamma'(t)=(-\sin t,\cos t)\), which is tangent to the unit circle.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
Adam's Law with extra conditioning: for rvs \(X,Y,Z,\)

\[ \begin{align*} \E{\E{Y\given X,Z}\given Z}=\E{Y\given Z}. \end{align*} \]

This is Adam's Law with \(Z\) kept as background information. It implies LOTP with extra conditioning by taking \(Y=\mathbf{1}_A\) and letting \(X\) encode the partition \(\{B_i\}\). Equivalently, once we condition on \(C\), we can treat \(C\) as the new background information and apply the ordinary LOTP inside that conditional world. Here the events \(B_i\) still form a partition, but all probabilities are now computed under the assumption that \(C\) has occurred:

\[ \begin{align*} \P{A\given C} &= \sum_i \P{A\given B_i,C}\P{B_i\given C}. \end{align*} \]

docs.title: Definition

Central limit theorem (CLT): for iid \(X_1,X_2,\ldots\) with mean \(\mu\) and variance \(\sigma^2>0,\) the sample mean \(\bar X_n=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n X_i\) satisfies

\[ \begin{align*} \frac{\bar X_n-\mu}{\sigma/\sqrt{n}}\xrightarrow{d}\Norm{0,1}. \end{align*} \]

Equivalently, for the sum \(S_n=\sum_{i=1}^n X_i,\)

\[ \begin{align*} \frac{S_n-n\mu}{\sigma\sqrt{n}}\xrightarrow{d}\Norm{0,1}. \end{align*} \]

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
Conditional CDF: for continuous \(X,Y\) and \(f_Y(y)>0,\)

\[ \begin{align*} F_{X\mid Y}\rb{x\given y} =\int_{-\infty}^x f_{X\mid Y}\rb{t\given y}\,\d t. \end{align*} \]

Here

\[ \begin{align*} f_{X\mid Y}\rb{t\given y}=\frac{f_{X,Y}(t,y)}{f_Y(y)}. \end{align*} \]

We write \(F_{X\mid Y}\rb{x\given y}=\P{X\leq x\given Y=y}\). Note that for continuous \(Y\), this cannot be defined by the elementary formula \(\P{A\given B}=\P{A\cap B}/\P{B}\), because \(\P{Y=y}=0\).

Conditional density given an event: for an event \(A\) with \(\P(A)>0\) and continuous \(Y,\)

\[ \begin{align*} F_{Y\mid A}(y)=\P{Y\leq y\mid A}. \end{align*} \]

Where the derivative exists,

\[ \begin{align*} f_{Y\mid A}(y)=\frac{\d}{\d y}F_{Y\mid A}(y). \end{align*} \]

Equivalently, by Bayes' rule,

\[ \begin{align*} f_{Y\mid A}(y)=\frac{\P{A\mid Y=y}f_Y(y)}{\P(A)}. \end{align*} \]

docs.title: Conditional Variance Given a Random Variable
docs.text: This page keeps the Probability Distributions treatment of conditional variance given a random variable. The event-based foundational treatment remains in Probability Theory for EOR.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
Let \(X\) and \(Y\) be random variables. The conditional variance of \(Y\) given \(X\) is the random variable

\[ \operatorname{Var}(Y\mid X) =E[Y^2\mid X]-\bigl(E[Y\mid X]\bigr)^2, \]

provided the conditional expectations exist.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: Conditional variance measures the remaining spread in one random variable after another random variable is known. It is itself random because the amount of remaining uncertainty can depend on the observed value.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• \(\operatorname{Var}(Y\mid X)\) is a function of \(X\).
  • If \(Y\) is determined by \(X\), then \(\operatorname{Var}(Y\mid X)=0\).
  • Eve's law decomposes total variance using \(E[\operatorname{Var}(Y\mid X)]\) and \(\operatorname{Var}(E[Y\mid X])\).

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• If \(Y=X+Z\) where \(Z\) is independent noise with variance \(\sigma^2\), then \(\operatorname{Var}(Y\mid X)=\sigma^2\).
  • If \(Y\) is Bernoulli with success probability \(X\), then \(\operatorname{Var}(Y\mid X)=X(1-X)\).

docs.title: Density of an Order Statistic
docs.text: This page keeps the Probability Distributions density formula for order statistics. The basic definition of order statistics remains in Probability Theory for EOR.

docs.title: Theorem
docs.text:
Let \(X_1,\ldots,X_n\) be iid continuous random variables with CDF \(F\) and PDF \(f\). For the \(k\)th order statistic \(X_{(k)}\), the density is

\[ f_{X_{(k)}}(x) = n\binom{n-1}{k-1} f(x)F(x)^{k-1}\bigl(1-F(x)\bigr)^{n-k}. \]

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: The formula counts how one observation lands near the chosen value, while the right number of observations fall below and above it.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• For \(k=1\), the formula gives the density of the sample minimum.
  • For \(k=n\), the formula gives the density of the sample maximum.
  • The binomial coefficient counts which observations fall below the order statistic.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• For iid uniform random variables on \([0,1]\), \(f_{X_{(k)}}(x)=n\binom{n-1}{k-1}x^{k-1}(1-x)^{n-k}\).
  • For the sample maximum \(X_{(n)}\) from iid continuous variables, the density is \(n f(x)F(x)^{n-1}\).

docs.title: Expectation of a Continuous Random Variable
Definition
docs.text:
For a continuous random variable \(X\) with density \(f_X\),

\[ E[X]=\int_{-\infty}^{\infty} x\,f_X(x)\,dx. \]

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: The expectation is the average value obtained by weighting each value by its density.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• The integral is taken over the support of the density, or over all real numbers.
  • The expectation exists when the integral is well-defined.
  • Continuous expectations use integration instead of summation.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• A continuous uniform distribution on \([a,b]\) has expectation \((a+b)/2\).
  • A normal distribution has expectation equal to its location parameter \(\mu\).

docs.title: Expectation of a Discrete Random Variable
Definition
docs.text:
For a discrete random variable \(X\) with probability mass function \(p_X\),

\[ E[X]=\sum_x x\,p_X(x). \]

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: The expectation is the probability-weighted average value of a discrete random variable.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• The sum is taken over all possible values of \(X\).
  • The expectation exists when the relevant sum is well-defined.
  • It is the special case of LOTUS with \(g(x)=x\).

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• The expectation of a fair die roll is \(3.5\).
  • If \(X\sim\operatorname{Bernoulli}(p)\), then \(E[X]=p\).

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
A random variable \(X\) has a gamma distribution with shape \(\alpha>0\) and rate \(\lambda>0\) if its probability density is

\[ f_X(x)= \frac{\lambda^\alpha}{\Gamma(\alpha)} x^{\alpha-1}e^{-\lambda x}, \qquad x>0, \]

and \(f_X(x)=0\) for \(x<0\). The value assigned to the density at zero does not affect probabilities. The scale parametrization uses \(\theta=1/\lambda\) instead of the rate \(\lambda\).

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: The gamma distribution models positive waiting times built from several exponential-like stages. The shape controls how many stages are accumulated, while the rate controls the time scale.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• \(E[X]=\alpha/\lambda\) and \(\operatorname{Var}(X)=\alpha/\lambda^2\) in the shape-rate parametrization.
  • With scale \(\theta=1/\lambda\), the mean is \(\alpha\theta\) and the variance is \(\alpha\theta^2\).
  • If independent gamma random variables have the same rate, their sum is gamma with shape equal to the sum of the shapes.
  • When \(\alpha=1\), the gamma distribution reduces to an exponential distribution.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• With shape \(\alpha=2\) and rate \(\lambda=3\), the density is \(f_X(x)=9xe^{-3x}\) for \(x>0\), the mean is \(2/3\), and the variance is \(2/9\).
  • The waiting time until the \(n\)th arrival in a Poisson process with rate \(\lambda\) has a gamma distribution with shape \(n\) and rate \(\lambda\).

docs.title: Geometric Series
docs.text: This page presents the Probability Distributions treatment. See also the treatment in Math I: Calculus. Mastery is recorded separately for each course context.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
For \(|\alpha|<1\),

\[ \sum_{i=0}^{\infty}\alpha^i=\frac{1}{1-\alpha}. \]

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: A geometric series adds powers of a fixed ratio. The sum is finite exactly when the powers decay to zero.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• The common ratio is \(\alpha\).
  • The condition \(|\alpha|<1\) is needed for convergence.
  • The formula is often used to normalize geometric probabilities.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• \(\sum_{i=0}^{\infty}(1/2)^i=2\).
  • If \(q=1-p\) and \(0<p<1\), then \(\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}q^k p=1\).

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
For a discrete random variable \(X\) and a function \(g\),

\[ E[g(X)]=\sum_x g(x)p_X(x). \]

Equivalently, the sum may be taken over \(\operatorname{supp}(X)\).

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: LOTUS computes the expectation of a transformed random variable directly from the original distribution, without first deriving the transformed distribution.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• For \(g(x)=x\), LOTUS gives the usual formula for \(E[X]\).
  • For \(g(x)=x^2\), LOTUS gives \(E[X^2]\).
  • LOTUS is often the cleanest way to compute moments.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• \(E[X^2]=\sum_x x^2p_X(x)\).
  • If \(X\) is a die roll, \(E[X^2]=\sum_{x=1}^{6}x^2/6\).

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
Generalized Markov's inequality: if \(f\) is non-negative and non-decreasing with \(f(a)>0,\) then

\[ \begin{align*} \P{X\geq a}\leq \frac{\E{f(X)}}{f(a)}. \end{align*} \]

Choosing \(f(x)=x\) gives Markov's inequality: for \(X\geq 0\) and \(a>0,\) \(\P{X\geq a}\leq \E X/a.\)

docs.title: Taylor Series
docs.text: This page presents the Probability Distributions treatment. See also the treatment in Math III: Analysis. Mastery is recorded separately for each course context.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
The Taylor series of the exponential function is

\[ e^x=\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\frac{x^k}{k!}. \]

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: The exponential function can be represented as an infinite polynomial. This is useful when simplifying limits, approximations, and probability generating formulas.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• The series is valid for every real number \(x\).
  • Truncating the series gives a polynomial approximation of \(e^x\).
  • The first terms are \(1+x+x^2/2+x^3/6+\cdots\).

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• For small \(x\), \(e^x\) is often approximated by \(1+x\).
  • The Poisson probability formula contains the factor \(e^{-\lambda}\).
